short_description: Botulism immune globulin, human, for intravenous use
lay_term: Immunoglobulin is a very complex protein, that is produced by certain cells in the body to protect itself from various types of infections and produces a passive immunity. BIG–IV (Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous) are derivation of pooled plasma from adults, immunized with pentavalent botulinum toxoid. Explanation In this procedure, the provider administers a botulism immune globulin intravenously. The injection is administered slowly into the patient's vein using an appropriately sized needle to provide the desired pharmacological action. The intravenous infusion is done to produce a short–term immunity as the complex protein from the immune globulin injection circulates through the body and helps protect the body against Botulism. Terminology Botulism: A serious illness caused by a neurotoxin produced by the bacteria clostridium botulinum that causes respiratory and muscular paralysis; the disease typically occurs through ingestion of contaminated food, intestinal infection in infants, wound infections, and by inhalation. CMV immunoglobulin: A preparation of human immunoglobulin for intravenous administration. Tips Report the administration code separately. Read Less

short_description: Rabies immune globulin (RIg), human, for intramuscular and/or subcutaneous use
lay_term: Immunoglobulin is a very complex protein that is produced by certain cells in the body to protect it from various types of infections and provide passive immunity. RIg (rabies immunoglobulin) contains gamma globulin derived from pooled human plasma, sourced from non–remunerated healthy donors, with a high titer of antibodies to the rabies virus. These are used to prevent or treat category III rabies. Explanation In this procedure, the provider administers a rabies immunoglobulin (RIg). The provider slowly administers an injection into the patient's muscle or under the skin using an appropriately sized needle to provide a desired pharmacological action. The injection is done to produce short–term immunity as the antibodies from the injection of this gamma globulin circulate through the body and help the body prevent or treat category III rabies. Terminology Rabies: A potentially deadly viral infection that attacks the brain and central nervous system; infected or rabid animals such as bats, raccoons, skunks, foxes, ferrets, cats, or dogs spread the virus in their bite and saliva. Tips For heat–treated human rabies immune globulin (RIg–HT) for intramuscular and/or subcutaneous use, see 90376. For rabies vaccine for intramuscular use, see 90675. For rabies vaccine for intradermal use, 90676. Read Less

short_description: Rho(D) immune globulin (RhIgIV), human, for intravenous use
lay_term: Immunoglobulin is a very complex protein, that is produced by certain cells in the body to protect itself from various types of infections and produces a passive immunity. Rho(D) (Rhesus D immunoglobulin ) is obtained from the plasma of healthy Human volunteers which have been specifically immunized against the rhesus antigen. This antibody is used to prevent Rhesus disease or hemolytic disease of a newborn. Explanation In this procedure, the provider administers an intravenous dose of human rhesus D immunoglobulin, or RhIgIV, to the patient. The provider first inspects the injection site. Then she slowly administers the injection into the patient's vein using an appropriately sized needle to provide the desired pharmacological action. The infusion is done to produce a short–term immunity as the antibodies from the injection help the body to prevent rhesus disease or hemolytic disease of a newborn. short_description: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) (coronavirus disease [COVID-19]) vaccine, recombinant spike protein nanoparticle, saponin-based adjuvant, 5 mcg/0.5 mL dosage, for intramuscular use Notes: (Report 91304 with administration code 90480)
lay_term: This code represents a SARS–CoV–2 vaccine product administered by intramuscular injection to prevent the patient from contracting COVID–19. The dosage is 5 mcg/0.5 mL. Explanation This code represents a SARS–CoV–2 vaccine product administered to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting COVID–19. This is a recombinant spike protein nanoparticle, saponin–based adjuvant vaccine. The vaccine uses a purified protein encoded by the SARS–CoV–2 spike protein’s genetic sequence. The spike protein is what the coronavirus uses to bind to host cells. The spike protein nanoparticles in the vaccine trigger an immune response that helps protect the patient from getting COVID–19. short_description: Dengue vaccine, quadrivalent, live, 2 dose schedule, for subcutaneous use
lay_term: This code represents a quadrivalent live vaccine product administered subcutaneously to protect against dengue virus, which causes dengue fever. The product has a two–dose schedule. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting dengue disease, caused by dengue virus. This is a live vaccine, containing a weakened version of the live virus. The vaccine is quadrivalent, meaning it protects against four types of the virus. The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route is subcutaneous, an injection into the fatty layer beneath the skin. The vaccine has a two–dose schedule. Dengue virus is mosquito–borne. The first infection with dengue virus typically results in no symptoms or a mild illness. Subsequent infection can lead to severe dengue, including hemorrhagic fever, which can be fatal. Symptoms may include stomach pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, confusion, and difficulty breathing. Tips This code represents the vaccine product. A separate code represents vaccine administration. Read Less

The CPT® Editorial Panel, in recognition of the public health interest in vaccine products, has chosen to publish new vaccine product codes prior to approval by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). These codes are indicated with the âš¡ symbol and will be tracked by the AMA to monitor FDA approval status. Once the FDA status changes to approval, the âš¡ symbol will be removed. CPT® users should refer to the AMA CPT® website (ama-assn.org/cpt-cat-i-immunization-codes) for the most up-to-date information on codes with the âš¡ symbol. Codes 90476-90759, 91304, 91318, 91319, 91320, 91321, 91322 identify the vaccine product only. To report the administration of a vaccine/toxoid other than SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus disease [COVID-19]), the vaccine/toxoid product codes (90476-90759) must be used in addition to an immunization administration code(s) (90460, 90461, 90471, 90472, 90473, 90474). To report the administration of a SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus disease [COVID-19]) vaccine, the vaccine/toxoid product codes 91304, 91318, 91319, 91320, 91321, 91322 should be reported with the corresponding immunization administration code (90480). Do not report 90476-90759 in conjunction with the SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus disease [COVID-19]) immunization administration code 90480, unless both a SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus disease [COVID-19]) vaccine/toxoid product and at least one vaccine/toxoid product from 90476-90759 are administered at the same encounter. Modifier 51 should not be reported with vaccine/toxoid codes 90476-90759, 91304, 91318, 91319, 91320, 91321, 91322, when reported in conjunction with administration codes 90460, 90461, 90471, 90472, 90473, 90474, 90480. If a significantly separately identifiable Evaluation and Management (E/M) service (eg, office or other outpatient services, preventive medicine services) is performed, the appropriate E/M service code should be reported in addition to the vaccine and toxoid administration codes. To meet the reporting requirements of immunization registries, vaccine distribution programs, and reporting systems (eg, Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System) the exact vaccine product administered needs to be reported. Multiple codes for a particular vaccine are provided in the CPT® codebook when the schedule (number of doses or timing) differs for two or more products of the same vaccine type (eg, hepatitis A, Hib) or the vaccine product is available in more than one chemical formulation, dosage, or route of administration. The "when administered to" age descriptions included in CPT® vaccine codes are not intended to identify a product's licensed age indication. The term "preservative free" includes use for vaccines that contain no preservative and vaccines that contain trace amounts of preservative agents that are not present in a sufficient concentration for the purpose of preserving the final vaccine formulation. The absence of a designation regarding a preservative does not necessarily indicate the presence or absence of preservative in the vaccine. Interim updates to vaccine code descriptors will be made following abbreviation approval by the ACIP on a timely basis via the AMA CPT® website (ama-assn.org/cpt-cat-i-immunization-codes). The accuracy of the ACIP vaccine abbreviation designations in the CPT® code set does not affect the validity of the vaccine code and its reporting function. short_description: Hepatitis A vaccine (HepA), pediatric/adolescent dosage-2 dose schedule, for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a vaccine product administered into a muscle to protect against hepatitis A, a liver infection. This code is specific to a pediatric/adolescent dosage with a two–dose schedule. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting hepatitis A (HepA), caused by the hepatitis A virus. This code is specific to the pediatric/adolescent dosage. This vaccine has a two–dose schedule. The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route is intramuscular, meaning an injection into a muscle. Hepatitis A is a highly contagious liver infection that can cause inflammation and affect liver function. Symptoms range from mild to severe and can include fever, malaise (general feeling of discomfort or being unwell), appetite loss, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and jaundice (a yellowing of the eyes and skin). Tips This code represents the vaccine product. A separate code represents vaccine administration. Read Less

short_description: Hepatitis A and hepatitis B vaccine (HepA-HepB), adult dosage, for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a vaccine product administered into a muscle to protect against hepatitis A and hepatitis B, which are liver infections. This code is specific to an adult dosage. Hepatitis A and hepatitis B are highly contagious liver infections that can cause inflammation and affect liver function. Symptoms range from mild to severe and can include fever, malaise (general feeling of discomfort or being unwell), appetite loss, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and jaundice (a yellowing of the eyes and skin). short_description: Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine (Hib), PRP-OMP conjugate, 3 dose schedule, for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine product administered into the muscle to protect against Hib disease. This formulation uses a PRP–OMP conjugate and follows a three–dose schedule. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting Hib disease, a bacterial infection that can cause severe illnesses such as meningitis (inflammation of the protective membranes of the brain and spinal cord) and pneumonia. The vaccine contains a PRP–OMP conjugate, which means the bacterial polysaccharide (PRP) is linked to an outer membrane protein (OMP) from another bacteria to enhance the immune response. The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route of administration is intramuscular, meaning the vaccine is injected directly into the muscle. The vaccine follows a three–dose schedule. Tips This code represents the vaccine product. Report a separate code for vaccine administration. Read Less

short_description: Respiratory syncytial virus vaccine, preF, subunit, bivalent, for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a bivalent prefusion F vaccine product administered into the muscle to protect against respiratory syncytial virus. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease. The vaccine is bivalent, meaning it protects against two types of the virus. The vaccine is composed of two prefusion F (preF) proteins to improve protection against RSV A and B strains. PreF is a form of the viral fusion protein (F) that RSV uses to enter human cells. Antibodies specific to the preF may block virus infection. An antibody is a protein produced by the body as an immune–system response. The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route is intramuscular, an injection into the muscle. RSV is a common respiratory virus that can be serious, especially for infants and older adults. Symptoms may be similar to a mild cold, but RSV also may cause more severe issues, such as bronchiolitis, an inflammation of the small airways in the lung, and pneumonia, an infection of the lungs. Tips This code represents the vaccine product. A separate code represents vaccine administration. Read Less

short_description: Influenza virus vaccine, quadrivalent (qIRV), mRNA; 30 mcg/0.5 mL dosage, for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a quadrivalent, mRNA–based influenza vaccine administered by intramuscular injection to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting influenza. The dosage is 30 mcg/0.5 mL. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting influenza. It is quadrivalent, meaning it protects against four different types of the flu virus. This is an mRNA–based vaccine that uses modified messenger RNA (modRNA) technology. The modRNA in the vaccine carries instructions for the body’s cells to produce pieces of the virus. Once these proteins are produced, the immune system recognizes them as foreign and mounts an immune response. This response includes the production of antibodies that are specific to these proteins. If the person is later exposed to the actual flu virus, their immune system is already primed to recognize and fight off the virus because of the antibodies. The dosage is 30 mcg/0.5 mL. The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route is intramuscular, meaning into the muscle. Terminology Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin (Ig). Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. short_description: Typhoid vaccine, Vi capsular polysaccharide (ViCPs), for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents an intramuscular vaccine product used to protect against typhoid fever. The vaccine contains Vi capsular polysaccharide, a purified bacterial component. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to reduce the patient’s risk of contracting typhoid fever. The vaccine contains Vi capsular polysaccharide (ViCPs), a substance taken from the outer surface of Salmonella Typhi bacteria. This component helps the immune system recognize and fight the bacteria. The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route is intramuscular, meaning the vaccine is injected directly into the muscle. Typhoid fever is a potentially severe bacterial illness that spreads through contaminated food or water and can cause fever, weakness, and stomach symptoms. Tips This code represents the vaccine product. A separate code represents vaccine administration. Read Less

short_description: Diphtheria, tetanus toxoids, acellular pertussis vaccine and inactivated poliovirus vaccine (DTaP-IPV), when administered to children 4 through 6 years of age, for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a combination vaccine product administered into the muscle to protect young children (4 to 6 years of age) against diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough), and polio. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product given to children aged 4 through 6 to reduce their risk of contracting four serious diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough), and poliovirus. The vaccine contains diphtheria and tetanus toxoids (inactivated toxins), acellular pertussis components (purified parts of the bacteria that cause whooping cough), and inactivated poliovirus (killed virus). The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route is intramuscular, an injection into the muscle. These diseases can lead to complications such as breathing problems, paralysis, or death, if contracted. Tips This code represents the vaccine product. A separate code represents vaccine administration. Read Less

short_description: Diphtheria, tetanus toxoids, acellular pertussis vaccine, inactivated poliovirus vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b PRP-OMP conjugate vaccine, and hepatitis B vaccine (DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB), for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a combination vaccine product administered into the muscle to protect against six diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and hepatitis B. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to protect children against six serious diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough), poliovirus, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and hepatitis B. The vaccine contains diphtheria and tetanus toxoids (inactivated toxins), acellular pertussis components (purified parts of the pertussis bacteria), inactivated poliovirus (killed virus), PRP–OMP conjugate Hib vaccine (a type of Hib vaccine using a sugar from the bacteria linked to a protein to help trigger immunity), and hepatitis B surface antigen (a part of the hepatitis B virus). The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. The route is intramuscular, meaning the vaccine is injected into the muscle. These diseases can cause serious complications including breathing problems, brain damage, paralysis, blood infections, and liver disease. Tips This code represents the vaccine product. A separate code represents vaccine administration. Read Less

short_description: Diphtheria, tetanus toxoids, and acellular pertussis vaccine (DTaP), when administered to individuals younger than 7 years, for intramuscular use
lay_term: This code represents a DTaP vaccine product administered into the muscle to protect against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (whooping cough). It is used for children younger than 7 years of age. Explanation This code represents a vaccine product administered to help prevent three bacterial diseases. Diphtheria can cause a thick coating in the throat that leads to breathing problems, heart failure, or paralysis. Tetanus (lockjaw) causes painful muscle stiffness and spasms and can be fatal. Pertussis (whooping cough) is a contagious respiratory disease causing severe coughing fits and difficulty breathing. This is an acellular pertussis vaccine, meaning it uses purified components of the pertussis bacteria instead of the whole bacteria to generate an immune response. The vaccine is administered intramuscularly, meaning it is injected directly into the muscle. The provider performs separately reportable administration of the vaccine. Tips This code represents the vaccine product. A separate code represents vaccine administration. Read Less

short_description: Tetanus, diphtheria toxoids and acellular pertussis vaccine (Tdap), when administered to individuals 7 years or older, for intramuscular use
lay_term: The provider uses this combination vaccine as a booster to help protect patients who are 7 years old or older from lockjaw, diphtheria, and whooping cough. Explanation The provider presents the parent/guardian or patient with the options for immunization. She reviews the risks and benefits along with the potential side effects then administers the vaccine intramuscularly directly into the arm or thigh muscle. A single dose of this three–in–one vaccine of diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis, abbreviated as Tdap, is generally given to children 7 through 10 years old, when they did not get any or all five DTaP vaccines. Children 11 and 12 years old get a single booster dose if they had all five DTaP shots when younger. Adults, especially those 65 years or older who have never had Tdap, get one shot of Tdap. Pregnant women receive a single dose during each pregnancy. Terminology Combination vaccine: A vaccine with components that protect against multiple illnesses Diphtheria: Diphtheria causes a thick covering in the back of the throat that can lead to breathing problems, paralysis, or heart failure. DTaP vaccine: A combination vaccine to protect against diphtheria, tetanus toxoids, and acellular pertussis (whooping cough) given in 5 doses between 2 months and 4 to 6 years of age. Intramuscular: An injection directly into the muscle. Pertussis: Pertussis or whooping cough causes uncontrollable coughing so bad that there is potential for choking spells or coughing so hard that the patient vomits. It is especially dangerous for infants as it makes it hard for them to eat, drink, or breathe. Tetanus: Tetanus or lockjaw causes painful muscle spasms, often all over the body. Tetanus can lead to tightening of the jaw muscles so the patient cannot open his or her mouth or swallow Toxoid: A toxoid stimulates the immune system to produce specific antitoxin antibodies that destroy the toxins that bacteria release. This provides effective and long lasting immunity. Include sufficient documentation from your provider explaining the product administered, administration route, and purpose. short_description: Meningococcal conjugate vaccine, serogroups C & Y and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine (Hib-MenCY), 4 dose schedule, when administered to children 6 weeks-18 months of age, for intramuscular use
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider administers a combination vaccine that protects against specific strains of meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae B, bacteria that cause meningitis, a serious disease that attacks the meninges, the covering of the brain and spinal cord. He injects the vaccine into a muscle in an infant between 6 weeks and 18 months of age as part of a multiple dose schedule. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider injects a meningococcal conjugate vaccine, serogroups C and Y, and Haemophilus influenzae B vaccine into the muscle as part of a multi–dose schedule for children at 6 weeks to 18 months of age. He counsels the family along with providing instructions and precautions before administration of the vaccine. This combination vaccine is also called Hib–MenCY. Terminology Haemophilus influenzae B, or Hib: Bacterial infection that causes meningitis, an inflammation of the meninges, the covering of the brain and spinal cord, resulting in brain damage and other complications. HibMenCY: Combination vaccine that protects against Hemophilus influenza B and the C and Y serogroups, or strains, of meningococcus, bacteria that cause meningitis, a disease that attacks the meninges, the covering of the brain and spinal cord; conjugate vaccines combine a weak form of an antigen, or infectious agent, with a carrier molecule to induce a strong immune response in a patient. Immunization: Use of a modified form of an infectious agent to protect against an infectious disease. Intramuscular: Within muscle tissue. Meningococcal conjugate vaccine, serogroups C and Y: Vaccine that provides protection against specific strains of meningococcal bacteria that causes meningitis, an inflammation of the meninges, the covering of the brain and spinal cord, resulting in brain damage and other complications. Meningococcus: Common name for Neisseria meningitidis, an infectious bacterium that causes meningitis, an inflammation of the meninges, the covering of the brain and spinal cord. Toxoid: A substance that has had its toxic, or disease causing, properties rendered harmless so that it causes an immune state in the body by triggering the production of antitoxins. Vaccine: A preparation that triggers an immune response to an infectious disease, usually through the introduction of some form of the agent that causes the disease, providing protection to the patient over a long period of time. Tips When coding for immunizations, report separate codes for vaccine administration, the actual vaccine, and an office visit. Include sufficient documentation from your provider explaining the product administered, administration route, and purpose. Select from other forms of this vaccine in the section Vaccines, toxoids. lay_term: Use 90749 to report unlisted vaccine or toxoid procedures that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider administers an unlisted vaccine or toxoid that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Terminology Antibody: Proteins produced in the blood and activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses, also called immunoglobulin. Antigen: Foreign bodies, such as bacteria, that enter the human body, or substances that form within the body, that cause an immune response, such as antibody production, and possibly infection; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Antitoxin: An antibody that counterbalances the toxin secreted by the antigen. Immune: Protected against infection. Toxoids: Inactive bacterial infection that stimulates the immune system to produce specific antitoxin antibodies that destroy the toxins released by bacteria. Vaccine: An altered form of a virus given to an individual for long term protection against the disease that a virus causes. Virus: An infectious agent that can reproduce only inside other living cells, generally invisible even with a microscope. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. lay_term: This add–on code represents increased work intensity of psychotherapy services that adds difficulty to delivery of service. Explanation This add–on code represents communication factors that add to the difficulty of service delivery and increase the intensity of effort required of the provider in a particular treatment session. There are various factors that make the psychotherapy session more intensive in effort like high reactivity or disagreement among family members, emotions or behavior of the caregiver that hinder execution of the treatment plan, situations involving abuse or neglect that the provider must legally report, use of play equipment or other objects to assist communication, or the need for an interpreter or translator because of the patient’s lack of fluency or undeveloped verbal skills. Tips Because +90785 is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary psychotherapy or evaluation and management services code. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Code 90785 is an add-on code for interactive complexity to be reported in conjunction with codes for diagnostic psychiatric evaluation (90791, 90792), psychotherapy (90832, 90833, 90834, 90836, 90837, 90838), and group psychotherapy (90853). Interactive complexity refers to specific communication factors that complicate the delivery of a psychiatric procedure. Common factors include more difficult communication with discordant or emotional family members and engagement of young and verbally undeveloped or impaired patients. Typical patients are those who have third parties, such as parents, guardians, other family members, agencies, court officers, or schools involved in their psychiatric care. Psychiatric procedures may be reported "with interactive complexity" when at least one of the following is present: 1. The need to manage maladaptive communication (related to, eg, high anxiety, high reactivity, repeated questions, or disagreement) among participants that complicates delivery of care. 2. Caregiver emotions or behavior that interferes with the caregiver's understanding and ability to assist in the implementation of the treatment plan. 3. Evidence or disclosure of a sentinel event and mandated report to third party (eg, abuse or neglect with report to state agency) with initiation of discussion of the sentinel event and/or report with patient and other visit participants. 4. Use of play equipment or other physical devices to communicate with the patient to overcome barriers to therapeutic or diagnostic interaction between the physician or other qualified health care professional and a patient who has not developed, or has lost, either the expressive language communication skills to explain his/her symptoms and response to treatment, or the receptive communication skills to understand the physician or other qualified health care professional if he/she were to use typical language for communication. Interactive complexity must be reported in conjunction with an appropriate psychiatric diagnostic evaluation or psychotherapy service, for the purpose of reporting increased complexity of the service due to specific communication factors which can result in barriers to diagnostic or therapeutic interaction with the patient. When provided in conjunction with the psychotherapy services (90832-90838), the amount of time spent by a physician or other qualified health care professional providing interactive complexity services should be reflected in the timed service code for psychotherapy (90832, 90834, 90837) or the psychotherapy add-on code (90833, 90836, 90838) performed with an evaluation and management service and must relate to the psychotherapy service only. Interactive complexity is not a service associated with evaluation and management services when provided without psychotherapy. Section Specific Guideline Psychiatry services include diagnostic services, psychotherapy, and other services to an individual, family, or group. Services may be provided by a physician or other qualified health care professional. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a psychiatric evaluation of the patient with the aim of making a diagnosis. In addition to the diagnostic evaluation, he also renders some additional medical services. Explanation The provider performs a diagnostic evaluation that includes collecting information about present and past behavior concerns as well as past family, medical, and social history. He may check the patient's vital signs, perform an examination and review of systems, and assess the patient’s condition. The provider may order and interpret lab tests and imaging. The provider may also evaluate the patient for adverse drug reactions. He also performs diagnostic tests to work up the diagnoses. He may also interview the family members and friends of the patient to make a definite diagnosis. He then may prescribe medication and devise the psycho–social comprehensive treatment plan. He may also refer the patient for psychological, neuropsychological, developmental, or speech, language, and occupation therapy evaluations as a supplement for a full diagnostic evaluation. This code applies to new patients or to patients undergoing re–evaluation. Tips Use this code only once per day regardless of the number of sessions or time that the provider spends with the patient on the same day. Read Less

guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Psychotherapy is the treatment of mental illness and behavioral disturbances in which the physician or other qualified health care professional, through definitive therapeutic communication, attempts to alleviate the emotional disturbances, reverse or change maladaptive patterns of behavior, and encourage personality growth and development. The psychotherapy service codes 90832-90838 include ongoing assessment and adjustment of psychotherapeutic interventions, and may include involvement of informants in the treatment process. Codes 90832, 90833, 90834, 90836, 90837, 90838 describe psychotherapy for the individual patient, although times are for face-to-face services with patient and may include informant(s). The patient must be present for all or a majority of the service. See codes 90846, 90847 when utilizing family psychotherapy techniques, such as focusing on family dynamics. Do not report 90846, 90847 for family psychotherapy services less than 26 minutes. Codes 90832, 90833, 90834, 90836, 90837, 90838 may be reported on the same day as codes 90846, 90847, when the services are separate and distinct. In reporting, choose the code closest to the actual time (ie, 16-37 minutes for 90832 and 90833, 38-52 minutes for 90834 and 90836, and 53 or more minutes for 90837 and 90838). Do not report psychotherapy of less than 16 minutes duration. (See instructions for the usage of time in the Introduction of the CPT® code set.) For psychotherapy for crisis, see "Other Psychotherapy." Code 90785 is an add-on code to report interactive complexity services when provided in conjunction with the psychotherapy codes 90832-90838. For family psychotherapy, see 90846, 90847. The amount of time spent by a physician or other qualified health care professional providing interactive complexity services should be reflected in the timed service code for psychotherapy (90832, 90834, 90837) or the psychotherapy add-on code performed with an evaluation and management service (90833, 90836, 90838). To report both E/M and psychotherapy, the two services must be significant and separately identifiable. These services are reported by using codes specific for psychotherapy when performed with evaluation and management services (90833, 90836, 90838) as add-on codes to the evaluation and management service. Medical symptoms and disorders inform treatment choices of psychotherapeutic interventions, and data from therapeutic communication are used to evaluate the presence, type, and severity of medical symptoms and disorders. For the purposes of reporting, the medical and psychotherapeutic components of the service may be separately identified as follows: 1. The type and level of E/M service is selected based on medical decision making. 2. Time spent on the activities of the E/M service is not included in the time used for reporting the psychotherapy service. Time may not be used as the basis of E/M code selection and prolonged services may not be reported when psychotherapy with E/M (90833, 90836, 90838) are reported. 3. A separate diagnosis is not required for the reporting of E/M and psychotherapy on the same date of service. short_description: Psychotherapy for crisis; first 60 minutes
lay_term: In this service, the provider performs psychotherapy for a crisis situation when the patient is in a life–threatening state and needs immediate attention. The treatment session typically lasts anywhere between 30 to 74 minutes. Explanation Psychotherapy is a type of therapy in which the provider uses a series of techniques to treat the mental and emotional health problems of a patient. Psychotherapy includes the interactive process between the provider and the patient. The provider involves the patient in this therapeutic interaction with the aim to explore the thoughts, feelings, and behavior of the patient. The provider uses a variety of techniques based on relationship building, communication, and behavior change that target improvement of the mental health of the patient. Use this code when the provider performs psychotherapy for a patient in a state of crisis. A crisis state is defined as a life–threatening or complex state requiring immediate attention to a patient in high distress. The provider primarily aims the treatment at mobilization of resources to defuse the crisis and restore safety of the patient to minimize the potential for psychological trauma. For this code, the provider should spend approximately 60 minutes but no less than a minimum of 30 minutes and a maximum of 74 minutes face–to–face with the patient. Tips You may not report 90839 more than once per day. See 90840 for each additional 30 minutes. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Psychotherapy for crisis is an urgent assessment and history of a crisis state, a mental status exam, and a disposition. The treatment includes psychotherapy, mobilization of resources to defuse the crisis and restore safety, and implementation of psychotherapeutic interventions to minimize the potential for psychological trauma. The presenting problem is typically life threatening or complex and requires immediate attention to a patient in high distress. Codes 90839, 90840 are used to report the total duration of time face-to-face with the patient and/or family spent by the physician or other qualified health care professional providing psychotherapy for crisis, even if the time spent on that date is not continuous. For any given period of time spent providing psychotherapy for crisis state, the physician or other qualified health care professional must devote his or her full attention to the patient and, therefore, cannot provide services to any other patient during the same time period. The patient must be present for all or some of the service. Do not report with 90791 or 90792. Code 90839 is used to report the first 30-74 minutes of psychotherapy for crisis on a given date. It should be used only once per date even if the time spent by the physician or other health care professional is not continuous on that date. Psychotherapy for crisis of less than 30 minutes total duration on a given date should be reported with 90832 or 90833 (when provided with evaluation and management services). Code 90840 is used to report additional block(s) of time, of up to 30 minutes each beyond the first 74 minutes. lay_term: In this add on service, after initial psychotherapy intervention for crisis, the provider performs an additional 30 minutes of psychotherapy for crisis. The crisis state is a life–threatening condition requiring immediate attention to the patient. Explanation Psychotherapy is a type of therapy in which the provider uses a series of techniques to treat the mental and emotional health problems of a patient. Psychotherapy includes the interactive process between the provider and the patient. The provider involves the patient in this therapeutic interaction with the aim to explore the thoughts, feelings, and behavior of the patient. The provider uses a variety of techniques based on relationship building, communication, and behavior change that target improvement of the mental health of the patient. Use this code when the provider performs psychotherapy for a patient in a state of crisis. A crisis state is defined as a life–threatening or complex state requiring immediate attention to a patient in high distress. The provider primarily aims the treatment at mobilization of resources to diffuse the crisis and restore safety of the patient to minimize the potential for psychological trauma. For this code, the provider performs the service for additional time, up to 30 minutes, after initial psychotherapy intervention lasting 74 minutes. Tips Because +90840 is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without the primary code: 90839. Code +90840 represents each additional block of time, up to 30 minutes, after the initial psychotherapy reported using 90839. Code 90839 specifies it is for the first 60 minutes, but you may not report +90840 until you’ve reached the halfway point of the 30 minutes mentioned in the code descriptor. Consequently, 90839 covers the first 74 minutes of treatment. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Psychotherapy for crisis is an urgent assessment and history of a crisis state, a mental status exam, and a disposition. The treatment includes psychotherapy, mobilization of resources to defuse the crisis and restore safety, and implementation of psychotherapeutic interventions to minimize the potential for psychological trauma. The presenting problem is typically life threatening or complex and requires immediate attention to a patient in high distress. Codes 90839, 90840 are used to report the total duration of time face-to-face with the patient and/or family spent by the physician or other qualified health care professional providing psychotherapy for crisis, even if the time spent on that date is not continuous. For any given period of time spent providing psychotherapy for crisis state, the physician or other qualified health care professional must devote his or her full attention to the patient and, therefore, cannot provide services to any other patient during the same time period. The patient must be present for all or some of the service. Do not report with 90791 or 90792. Code 90839 is used to report the first 30-74 minutes of psychotherapy for crisis on a given date. It should be used only once per date even if the time spent by the physician or other health care professional is not continuous on that date. Psychotherapy for crisis of less than 30 minutes total duration on a given date should be reported with 90832 or 90833 (when provided with evaluation and management services). Code 90840 is used to report additional block(s) of time, of up to 30 minutes each beyond the first 74 minutes. short_description: Psychoanalysis
lay_term: The provider uses an analytical technique to increase insight into a person's unconscious motivations and conflicts to effect a change in maladaptive actions. Explanation A trained, credentialed provider, such as a physician or licensed psychologist, uses various techniques to change a patient’s behaviors, feelings, and thoughts by uncovering the unconscious meanings and motivations behind them. These insights then lead the patient to understanding and change. Psychoanalysis includes such work by the analyst as his review of related medical, legal, and administrative documentation, arrangement of all appointments as necessary to develop a trusting relationship with the patient; intently listening to and observing the patient to gain insight and identify issues; assessment of the patient’s mental processes and experiences; use of analytical techniques, and questioning and patient feedback to facilitate the patient’s introspection and self–understanding to overcome barriers and adapt change. Therapy sessions typically occur between one and four times a week and include monitoring and reassessment of any medications. Terminology Maladaptive: Not adequately or appropriately able to adjust to the environment or situation. Tips 90845 refers to the practice of psychoanalysis, do not confuse this code with psychotherapy codes, 90832 to 90838, and 90846 to 90853. Report psychoanalysis per day. Read Less

short_description: Family psychotherapy (without the patient present), 50 minutes
lay_term: A provider meets with the patient’s family without the patient present to counsel the family on the psychological issues affecting the patient and the family. Explanation Psychotherapy, also known as talk therapy, is a type of therapy in which the provider uses a series of techniques to treat mental and emotional health problems. A provider or qualified psychotherapist meets with a patient’s family without the patient present to counsel the family members and help them understand the patient’s problem and how they respond to the patient can negatively affect or benefit the patient. The emphasis during family psychotherapy is on the patient's care and the family’s involvement in the patient’s treatment. The therapist may discuss family dynamics as they relate to the patient including family interaction and communication and conflict resolution. Terminology Psychotherapy: Interaction between a trained professional and patient on issues related to mood, behavior, feelings, and thoughts. Tips The term, family, may apply to traditional family members, significant others involved in the care of the patient or live–in companions. Read Less

lay_term: Group psychotherapy is provided to a group of people who are normally not acquainted with each other but might be sharing similar kinds of psychological issues. The psychotherapist selects a group of patients who are not members of the same family, involving no more than 12 participants, and leads the group therapy session for 45 to 60 minutes. Explanation A trained therapist, also known as a facilitator, conductor, or leader, selects the members of the group based on their compatibility with the group in terms of problems and psychological background. Personal and group dynamics are discussed and explored in a therapeutic setting allowing emotional catharsis, instruction, insight, and support. Under the supervision and observation of the therapist, the group members share their problems, issues, and thoughts with the whole group while the group reacts through feedback, support, criticism, and sharing of their own problems. Group therapy helps people in relating with others and knowing as well as overcoming their personal shortcomings in terms of behavior, self–esteem, interpersonal relations, social interactions, and adaptability. Tips Group therapy, since it involves psychotherapy, must be led by a person who is licensed or otherwise authorized by the state in which he or she practices to perform this service. This will usually mean a psychiatrist, psychologist, clinical social worker, clinical nurse specialist, or other person authorized by the state to perform this service. Registered nurses with special training may also be considered eligible for coverage. For Medicare coverage, group therapy does not include: socialization, music therapy, recreational activities, art classes, excursions, sensory stimulation or eating together, cognitive stimulation, or motion therapy, etc. Read Less

short_description: Narcosynthesis for psychiatric diagnostic and therapeutic purposes (eg, sodium amobarbital (Amytal) interview)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider administers a narcotic drug to induce a hypnotic state that helps in psychiatric diagnosis and treatment. Explanation Narcosynthesis is a psychiatric treatment technique that involves administering a narcotic drug that allows the patient to release thoughts that might be suppressed or repressed. Amytal or sodium amobarbital is a sedative hypnotic that providers most commonly use for psychiatric diagnosis and treatment. An Amytal interview is a test in which the provider administers a small amount of the drug, by vein, every few minutes. Intravenous Amytal causes a feeling of relaxation, warmth, and closeness to the provider; while in this state, the provider questions the patient. The provider uses the interview to evaluate memory and to elicit information from a person who is voluntarily guarding against its revelation. Amytal interviews have a role in the assessment and initial management of catatonia and unexplained muteness as well as in distinguishing between depressive, schizophrenic, and organic stuporous states. Terminology Catatonia: A state of apparent unresponsiveness to external stimuli in a person who is apparently awake. Hypnotic state: A relaxed state of mind that providers may induce to treat mainly psychological or emotional disorders. Schizophrenic: A mental health condition that causes a range of different psychological symptoms. Stuporous: A state of mental numbness. Read Less

short_description: Therapeutic repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treatment; initial, including cortical mapping, motor threshold determination, delivery and management Notes: (Report only once per course of treatment) (Do not report 90867 in conjunction with 90868, 90869, 95860, 95870, 95928, 95929, 95939, 0889T, 0890T, 0891T, 0892T) (For peripheral nerve transcutaneous magnetic stimulation, see 0766T, 0767T)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, a procedure that uses magnetic fields to stimulate nerve cells in the brain to improve symptoms of depression. Use this code for initial treatment that includes cortical mapping, motor threshold determination, delivery, and management. Explanation Transcranial magnetic stimulation, abbreviated as TMS, is a noninvasive method that uses a magnetic field to stimulate neurons, which are brain nerve cells. When the patient is appropriately prepared, the provider places an electromagnetic coil over the patient’s scalp, focused on an area of the brain thought to play a role in mood regulation. The aim of using transcranial magnetic stimulation is to treat depression in a patient who does not respond to medications. This procedure includes repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in which the provider administers magnetic impulses in rapid succession, producing long lasting changes in the brain activity. Use this code for only the initial treatment that includes cortical mapping, motor threshold determination, delivery, and management. Terminology Cortical mapping: Identifying the areas in the brain cortex that perform various functions, such as language, motor, and sensory areas. Motor threshold: A minimum stimulus intensity that produces a miminal motor evoked response. Read Less

lay_term: The provider performs a subsequent redetermination of the minimum intensity of electrical pulses necessary to elicit the desired response in brain activity for a patient undergoing therapeutic transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, a therapy that uses a magnet to generate electric pulses that stimulate nerve cells in the brain. He delivers and manages the therapy based on his findings. He performs the procedure to treat depression in a patient who does not respond to medications. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepared, the provider places the transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS device, over the patient’s scalp, over the limbic area of the brain, the area thought to control mood and behavior, in a patient undergoing therapeutic TMS treatments. The magnet generates electric pulses in rapid succession and produces changes in the brain activity. The provider redetermines the motor threshold, or minimum intensity of electrical pulses that elicits the desired response in brain activity. He delivers and manages the therapy based on this information. Terminology Motor evoked response: The electrical response from the central nervous system by any independent stimulus that causes the spinal cord and the peripheral nerves to harvest neuroelectrical signals. Motor threshold: A minimum stimulus intensity that produces a minimal motor evoked response. Stimulus: An agent which induces the activity. Tips For the same service with subsequent delivery and management per session, use 90868, Therapeutic repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation or TMS treatment; subsequent delivery and management, per session. short_description: Electroconvulsive therapy (includes necessary monitoring)
lay_term: The provider applies an electric current to the patient's brain for the purpose of producing a seizure or series of seizures to alleviate symptoms of various mental disorders. Explanation Electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, is a psychiatric treatment a provider performs on a patient for whom conventional lines of treatment, such as prescribed medications and other psychotherapy, are not working. ECT’s primary use is for the treatment of depression, but the provider may also consider ECT for other conditions, such as persistent life–threatening psychoses when the patient is suicidal or homicidal, and there is a need for a rapid alleviation of symptoms. ECT causes changes in brain chemistry that quickly reverses some mental illness symptoms. After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider, usually a trained psychiatrist, applies an electric current to the brain for a fraction of a second through scalp electrodes to intentionally trigger a brief seizure that usually lasts less than 60 seconds. ECT can be unilateral, in which electrical currents focus on one side of the brain, or bilateral, in which both sides of the brain receive the electrical currents. The code includes the psychiatrist evaluation prior to performing an ECT procedure; time the physician takes to monitor the patient during the convulsive phase including the management of the seizure time by electroencephalographic tracing, and observation, and monitoring during the recovery phase. Decision making regarding further treatment is part of the monitoring, as well. Terminology Electroencephalographic tracing or EEG: Test that records the electrical activity in the brain. Homicidal: Thoughts, unusual preoccupation with, or actions relating to killing someone. Suicidal: Thoughts, unusual preoccupation with, or actions relating to killing oneself. Tips Report one unit of 90870 only once per session. If the provider evaluates the patient for a significant and separately identifiable evaluation and management service, you can report it with the appropriate established patient E/M code. Append a modifier such as 25, Significant, separately identifiable evaluation and management services by the same physician or other qualified health care professional on the same day of the procedure or other service, to the E/M code that you are reporting for the service to override the edit. The exception is the psychodiagnostic evaluation code 90792, which you bundle with 90870. You cannot report these two codes together under any circumstances for physician services. Only 90870 is payable if you provide both services to the same patient on the same date. Read Less

Services are provided in all settings of care and psychiatry services codes are reported without regard to setting. Services may be provided by a physician or other qualified health care professional. Some psychiatry services may be reported with evaluation and management services (98000-98016, 99202-99255, 99281-99285, 99304-99316, 99341-99350) or other services when performed. Evaluation and management services (98000-98016, 99202-99285, 99304-99316, 99341-99350) may be reported for treatment of psychiatric conditions, rather than using psychiatry services codes, when appropriate. Hospital inpatient or observation care in treating a psychiatric inpatient or partial hospitalization may be initial or subsequent in nature (see 99221-99233). Some patients receive hospital evaluation and management services only and others receive hospital evaluation and management services and other procedures. If other procedures such as electroconvulsive therapy or psychotherapy are rendered in addition to hospital evaluation and management services, these may be listed separately (eg, hospital inpatient or observation care services [99221-99223, 99231-99233] plus electroconvulsive therapy [90870]), or when psychotherapy is done, with appropriate code(s) defining psychotherapy services. Consultation for psychiatric evaluation of a patient includes examination of a patient and exchange of information with the primary physician and other informants such as nurses or family members, and preparation of a report. These services may be reported using consultation codes (see Consultations). (Do not report 90785-90899 in conjunction with 90839, 90840, 97151, 97152, 97153, 97154, 97155, 97156, 97157, 97158, 0362T, 0373T) Psychiatric diagnostic evaluation is an integrated biopsychosocial assessment, including history, mental status, and recommendations. The evaluation may include communication with family or other sources and review and ordering of diagnostic studies. Psychiatric diagnostic evaluation with medical services is an integrated biopsychosocial and medical assessment, including history, mental status, other physical examination elements as indicated, and recommendations. The evaluation may include communication with family or other sources, prescription of medications, and review and ordering of laboratory or other diagnostic studies. In certain circumstances one or more other informants (family members, guardians, or significant others) may be seen in lieu of the patient. Codes 90791, 90792 may be reported more than once for the patient when separate diagnostic evaluations are conducted with the patient and other informants. Report services as being provided to the patient and not the informant or other party in such circumstances. Codes 90791, 90792 may be reported once per day and not on the same day as an evaluation and management service performed by the same individual for the same patient. The psychiatric diagnostic evaluation may include interactive complexity services when factors exist that complicate the delivery of the psychiatric procedure. These services should be reported with add-on code 90785 used in conjunction with the diagnostic psychiatric evaluation codes 90791, 90792. Codes 90791, 90792 are used for the diagnostic assessment(s) or reassessment(s), if required, and do not include psychotherapeutic services. Psychotherapy services, including for crisis, may not be reported on the same day. (Do not report 90791-90899 in conjunction with 90839, 90840, 97151, 97152, 97153, 97154, 97155, 97156, 97157, 97158, 0362T, 0373T)

short_description: Environmental intervention for medical management purposes on a psychiatric patient's behalf with agencies, employers, or institutions
lay_term: In this service, the provider works with outside agencies, employers, or other healthcare providers regarding the patient’s physical environment to help manage a psychiatric patient’s medical care. Explanation In this service, the provider works with outside agencies, employers, or other healthcare providers to achieve some changes in the physical environment of a psychiatric patient to aid in his medical management. This could include discussions about the impact of the environment on the patient’s condition. For example, if the patient is having difficulty coping with a stressful work situation, the provider might talk with the patient’s manager to determine if anything can be done to alleviate the situation. It might also involve working with the state’s office of vocational rehabilitation to help to retrain the patient for a new career if he is unable to continue to work at his previous job due to a mental disorder. Terminology Vocational rehabilitation: Providing training in a specific trade with the aim of gaining employment. Read Less

short_description: Unlisted psychiatric service or procedure
lay_term: Use 90899 to report psychiatric services or procedures that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a psychiatric service or procedure that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

short_description: Biofeedback training by any modality
lay_term: The provider trains patients to control involuntary bodily functions by altering brain activity, blood pressure, heart rate, and other bodily functions that are normally not controlled voluntarily. Explanation The provider uses equipment that measures and responds to very slight changes in the body, such as changes in their temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and muscle tension, and provides feedback to the patient via lights, sounds, and meters. By using this equipment, and other therapeutic methods, the provider guides the patient through practices to alter their bodily functions and learn to control their reactions to help treat their disorders. Conditions treated by this self–therapeutic technique include asthma, addiction, high blood pressure, chronic pain, depression, headache, incontinence, and many others. Terminology Biofeedback: A self–guided treatment that teaches a patient to control muscle tension, pain, body temperature, brain waves, and other bodily functions through processes such as relaxation, visualization, and other cognitive control techniques; biofeedback is also referred to as applied psychophysiological feedback. short_description: Biofeedback training, perineal muscles, anorectal or urethral sphincter, including EMG and/or manometry, when performed; initial 15 minutes of one-on-one physician or other qualified health care professional contact with the patient
lay_term: The provider, a physician or other qualified healthcare professional, trains a patient to control involuntary bodily functions by altering brain activity, blood pressure, heart rate, and other bodily functions that the patient cannot normally control voluntarily. This service is done for conditions such as fecal or urinary incontinence. EMG and manometry, if performed, are included with this service. Report this code for the first 15 minutes of face–to–face service with the patient. Explanation The provider uses equipment that measures and responds to very slight changes in the body, such as changes in temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and muscle tension, and provides feedback to the patient via lights, sounds, and meters. By using this equipment, and other therapeutic methods, the provider guides the patient through practices to alter his bodily functions and learn to control his reactions to help treat his disorders. In this service, the provider is usually a urologist who first assesses and documents that reasons why the patient is a good candidate for biofeedback. The provider then uses biofeedback–assisted pelvic muscle education (PME) which may include measurement of muscle contraction through an electromyography (EMG) and vaginal or rectal sensors and/or rectal manometry devices to help the patient become more aware of the pelvic muscles and assist in their movement. The service may also include other techniques, such as relaxation, to help control involuntary bodily movements. The provider places printouts from the testing and his written interpretation of each of the tests in the patient’s medical record. Report this code for the first 15 minutes that a provider, a physician or other qualified healthcare professional, spends face–to–face with the patient for biofeedback training. Terminology Anorectal: Refers to the anus and rectum. Biofeedback: A self–guided treatment that teaches a patient to control muscle tension, pain, body temperature, brain waves, and other bodily functions through processes such as relaxation, visualization, and other cognitive control techniques; biofeedback is also known as applied psychophysiological feedback. Electromyography (EMG): A diagnostic test that evaluates the health of muscles and the nerves that control them by measuring their electrical activity. Manometry: A procedure in which a catheter (manometer) typically containing evenly spaced recording side holes or pressure sensors that measure different pressures depending upon the orientation of the holes is used to measure the pressure or variations in pressure in the biliary tree, colon, or urinary tract. Perineal muscles: Refers to pelvic muscles. Urethral sphincter: Refers to muscles responsible for controlling the retention and release of urine from the bladder. Tips Report +90913 for each additional 15 minutes of service in conjunction with 90912 for the first 15 minutes of face–to–face biofeedback training. Some payers still consider biofeedback bladder training to be investigational or apply frequency limits for biofeedback performance and reimbursement. Biofeedback sessions often have limits of four to six treatments over a four–week period. As a result, payers will deny claims that exceed the frequency limit unless you can prove that the patient's specific condition requires additional services. Some payers may require modifier GP, Services delivered under an outpatient physical therapy plan of care. Read Less

lay_term: Hemodialysis is a procedure that involves drawing blood via an intraarterial or intravenous catheter, then sieving it through a semipermeable membrane to remove the impurities and finally transfusing the blood back into body. Along with performing hemodialysis, the same physician may also carry out an E/M service related to the dialysis on the same day, which is also included in this code. Explanation The dialysis specialist or physician provider performs hemodialysis on the patient as per the established schedule and physician’s order and follows all prescribed parameters. This service requires the provider to repeat evaluations due to an adverse event during dialysis, such as a hypotensive episode, or drop in blood pressure, and respiratory problems, but may or may not result in considerable alterations to the dialysis order. During this procedure, the blood is taken from the body and passes through a special type of filter or dialyzer where waste and extra fluids are removed, and the clean filtered blood is returned to the body. Along with the procedure, the physician may also conduct an E/M service related to the dialysis procedure on the patient on the same day. lay_term: The provider monitors the blood flow in a patient’s vascular access site, or where the provider joined blood vessels together, to ensure it remains patent, or open, and to prevent blood clots and complications. Explanation The long term need for and use of dialysis access requires the preservation of an open, unobstructed, and well–functioning dialysis fistula to prevent vascular access problems. Flow studies measure blood flow to ensure the vascular site meets established guidelines for the type of access while the patient receives hemodialysis. Flow assessment uses measuring techniques, such as an indicator dilution method. A protocol for a urea–based measurement of recirculation, for example, begins approximately 30 minutes after the start of treatment and after the provider turns off the ultrafiltration system. The provider then draws arterial and venous blood samples, reduces the blood flow rate, and then turns the dialysis pump off. He then clamps the arterial line right above the sampling port and draws another arterial sample from the arterial port. The provider unclamps the line and continues the patient’s dialysis treatment. He measures the blood urea and nitrogen, or BUN, in all three samples and calculates the percentage of recirculation. Terminology Arteriovenous fistulae: A provider surgically creates a direct connection between an artery and vein. Arteriovenous graft: A provider surgically connects a vein to an artery using a soft plastic tube or an organic material from a person or animal. Dialysis pump or dialysis machine: Equipment that mixes and monitors the fluid that helps remove toxins from a patient’s blood during hemodialysis. Hemodialysis: A method of cleaning the blood of impurities or wastes by drawing blood outside of the body and filtering the blood through a dialysis machine and then returning the blood to the patient. Indicator dilution: A method for measuring cardiac output by putting an indicator substance into the blood and withdrawing blood and measuring its concentration downstream. Sampling port: A small medical device installed beneath the skin that allows drugs to be injected or blood samples withdrawn. Ultrafiltration system: Dialysis equipment responsible for removal of excess water during hemodialysis. Read Less

short_description: Dialysis procedure other than hemodialysis (eg, peritoneal dialysis, hemofiltration, or other continuous renal replacement therapies), with single evaluation by a physician or other qualified health care professional Notes: (For home infusion of peritoneal dialysis, use 99601, 99602)
lay_term: The provider evaluates the patient and chooses one of several methods to perform dialysis, except hemodialysis. Explanation The provider administers a dialysis procedure other than hemodialysis, such as peritoneal dialysis, hemofiltration, or other continuous renal replacement therapy. Before he performs dialysis, the provider or other qualified health care professional examines the patient. If he chooses to place the patient on peritoneal dialysis, the provider introduces a large volume of fluid or dialysate containing glucose into the abdomen, typically through a previously placed access port. Electrolytes, waste products and fluid in the blood pass into this fluid, typically over a period of two to six hours, a period of time known as dwell. He then drains out the fluid and replaces it with fresh fluids. If he chooses to use hemofiltration, the provider pumps the blood through a filter but does not use a dialysate. The filter removes the waste elements in the blood. The provider replaces the salts and water lost from the blood during the process with an infusion drip. The provider sometimes chooses other continuous renal replacement therapies, particularly for critically ill patients who cannot tolerate the more rapid changes in fluid volume of other treatments. These procedures more closely mimic the actual function of the kidneys and take up to 24 hours to complete. Terminology Dialysis: Artificial restoration of kidney function by removing toxic product from blood through filtration. Electrolytes: Potassium, sodium, calcium, and magnesium; minerals important for maintaining fluid balance, nerve and muscle function, and a regular heart rhythm. Hemodialysis: A procedure that removes waste products from the blood and extra fluid from body tissues; it helps correct electrolyte imbalances for patients with impaired kidney function. Tips Do not use this code for hemodialysis; it is for other types of dialysis procedures than hemodialysis. short_description: End-stage renal disease (ESRD) related services monthly, for patients younger than 2 years of age to include monitoring for the adequacy of nutrition, assessment of growth and development, and counseling of parents; with 4 or more face-to-face visits by a physician or other qualified health care professional per month
lay_term: The provider manages all the services associated with the monthly care of a patient who is younger than 2 years old and has a condition known as end stage renal disease, or ESRD. For this service, the provider sees the patient face–to–face at least four times during the month to accomplish this care. Explanation The provider manages all outpatient ESRD related services for a one–month period for a patient who is younger than 2 years old. The provider sees the patient face–to–face during dialysis sessions four or more times during the month. The care bundled into this code includes such services as scheduled and episodic examinations for management of the disease; establishment and changes to the patient’s dialysis schedule and prescription; oversight of each dialysis visit; review of laboratory tests, medications, and supplement needs; monitoring the patient’s growth and developmental progress with intervention for delayed milestones; ongoing assessment of feeding and nutrition requirements and adjustments as necessary; telephone and electronic communications regarding the patient; and care coordination and regular counseling and support of the parents and/or caregivers and siblings. Terminology End stage renal disease or ESRD: Term used to define the final stage of kidney failure where a patient is not able to live without dialysis or a transplant because of the complete or nearly complete irreversible loss of renal function; ESRD is also referred to as end–stage kidney disease, end–stage kidney failure, and end–stage renal failure. Tips The 90951 service does not include dialysis treatment. See 90935–90937 to report hemodialysis. For payment of ESRD–Related Services under the Monthly Capitation Payment, Medicare considers a month as referring to a calendar month. The first month the patient starts dialysis treatments is the date the dialysis treatments begin through the end of that calendar month. Thereafter, month refers to each calendar month. Read Less

short_description: Hemoperfusion (eg, with activated charcoal or resin)
lay_term: This is a process which removes substances from the blood using a charcoal or resin working like an artificial kidney. This process can also be used in the treatment of life–threatening drug overdoses, for patients with or without renal failure. Explanation At the start of the treatment, the patient is fitted with two catheters: one is placed in an artery in the arm, and the second is placed in the closest large vein in the same arm. Both catheters are connected to the treatment unit, which includes the column of adsorbent material, and the catheter inserted in the vein is also connected to a blood pressure monitor. Throughout treatment, the patient is given small doses of heparin to prevent blood clotting. Using this special equipment and vascular access the physician draws blood from the patient, which is pumped directly through a column of adsorbent material (charcoal or amberlite resin). This removes the toxic material and lipid soluble drugs from the circulation. After the cleansing of blood, it is transfused back again into the patient's body using needle and catheter. Terminology Hemoperfusion is a medical process used to remove toxic substances from a patient's blood. The technique involves passing large volumes of blood over an adsorbent substance (resin, activated charcoal, etc). Tips If hemoperfusion is performed concurrently with dialysis, Medicare considers that payment for the hemoperfusion reflects only the additional care rendered over and above the care given with dialysis. However, hemoperfusion is not a covered service when used to improve the results of hemodialysis. Hemoperfusion in conjunction with deferoxamine (DFO) in treating symptomatic patients with iron overload is not covered. But if hemoperfusion in conjunction with DFO for aluminum toxicity is performed, then it is covered. Read Less

short_description: Esophageal motility (manometric study of the esophagus and/or gastroesophageal junction) study with interpretation and report
lay_term: The provider uses a manometer to analyze esophageal muscle pressure and movement in a patient with gastroesophageal reflux disease or GERD. He interprets the findings and prepares a report. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a catheter into the nostril. He gradually moves the catheter into the esophagus, he asks the patient to gulp to help in opening the esophagus. He asks the patient to swallow 10 to 20 sips of water. When the patient sips the water, the computer records the pressure, force, and pattern of esophageal muscle contractions. The provider also takes readings while the patient swallows a light meal. The electrodes transmit the data to a recording device. The provider then removes the catheter. The provider then analyzes the recorded data and prepares a written interpretation. Terminology Esophageal manometric study: A motility test that measures esophageal muscle pressure and movement, coordination, and strength of esophageal contractions. Esophagus: The muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx, which is behind the mouth, down to the stomach. Gastroesophageal junction, or esophagogastric junction: The point at which the esophagus enters the stomach; providers identify this point by changes in the lining, or epithelium, of the esophagus. Gastroesophageal reflux disease: Backward flow or regurgitation of bile and stomach acid stomach into the esophagus causing heartburn, esophagitis, and erosion or ulcer of the esophageal tissues; this condition can lead to Barrett esophagus, precancerous changes in the esophageal tissues at the cellular level. Impedance electrodes: A conductor that measures current when a certain voltage is applied to a circuit. Manometer: Equipment which measures pressure. Tips If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26, Professional component to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Gastric motility (manometric) studies
lay_term: The provider uses a manometer to analyze stomach muscle pressure and movement to assess the motility and peristaltic movement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider administers radiopharmaceuticals to the patient and captures the emitted radiation by external detectors. Analysis of the hydrogen or methane levels is done from the samples taken at different time intervals to identify which compound causes more hydrogen/methane production in the body.
