short_description: Rectal sensation, tone, and compliance test (ie, response to graded balloon distention) Notes: (For biofeedback training, see 90912, 90913) (For anorectal manometry, use 91122)
lay_term: The provider uses graded balloon distention of the rectum to test its sensation, tone, and compliance. He performs the procedure because the patient has fecal incontinence, constipation or irritable bowel syndrome. Explanation The provider asks the patient to empty the rectum and anus prior to the procedure. When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider places a balloon catheter with two channels into the anus and advances it to the rectum. He inflates one channel of the balloon with air to distend the rectum, and a sensory in the other channel of the catheter senses and records the pressure, muscular tone, and sensitivity inside the rectum. He repeats the inflation and measurements again and again with the rectum at rest and after he administers a substance to stimulate contractions. He removes the catheter after adequate examination. short_description: Anorectal manometry Notes: (Do not report 91120, 91122 in conjunction with 91117)

short_description: Ophthalmological services: medical examination and evaluation with initiation of diagnostic and treatment program; intermediate, new patient Notes: (Do not report 92002 in conjunction with 99173, 99174, 99177, 0469T)
lay_term: Lay Term
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline (For distinguishing between new and established patients, see Evaluation and Management guidelines) Section Specific Guideline (For surgical procedures, see Surgery, Eye and Ocular Adnexa, 65091 et seq) Definitions Intermediate ophthalmological services describes an evaluation of a new or existing condition complicated with a new diagnostic or management problem not necessarily relating to the primary diagnosis, including history, general medical observation, external ocular and adnexal examination and other diagnostic procedures as indicated; may include the use of mydriasis for ophthalmoscopy. For example: a. Review of history, external examination, ophthalmoscopy, biomicroscopy for an acute complicated condition (eg, iritis) not requiring comprehensive ophthalmological services. b. Review of interval history, external examination, ophthalmoscopy, biomicroscopy and tonometry in established patient with known cataract not requiring comprehensive ophthalmological services. Comprehensive ophthalmological services describes a general evaluation of the complete visual system. The comprehensive services constitute a single service entity but need not be performed at one session. The service includes history, general medical observation, external and ophthalmoscopic examinations, gross visual fields and basic sensorimotor examination. It often includes, as indicated: biomicroscopy, examination with cycloplegia or mydriasis and tonometry. It always includes initiation of diagnostic and treatment programs. Intermediate and comprehensive ophthalmological services constitute integrated services in which medical decision making cannot be separated from the examining techniques used. Itemization of service components, such as slit lamp examination, keratometry, routine ophthalmoscopy, retinoscopy, tonometry, or motor evaluation is not applicable. For example: The comprehensive services required for diagnosis and treatment of a patient with symptoms indicating possible disease of the visual system, such as glaucoma, cataract or retinal disease, or to rule out disease of the visual system, new or established patient. Initiation of diagnostic and treatment program includes the prescription of medication, and arranging for special ophthalmological diagnostic or treatment services, consultations, laboratory procedures and radiological services. Special ophthalmological services describes services in which a special evaluation of part of the visual system is made, which goes beyond the services included under general ophthalmological services, or in which special treatment is given. Special ophthalmological services may be reported in addition to the general ophthalmological services or evaluation and management services. For example: Fluorescein angioscopy, quantitative visual field examination, refraction or extended color vision examination (such as Nagel's anomaloscope) should be separately reported. Prescription of lenses, when required, is included in 92015. It includes specification of lens type (monofocal, bifocal, other), lens power, axis, prism, absorptive factor, impact resistance, and other factors. Interpretation and report by the physician or other qualified health care professional is an integral part of special ophthalmological services where indicated. Technical procedures (which may or may not be performed personally) are often part of the service, but should not be mistaken to constitute the service itself.

short_description: Ophthalmological services: medical examination and evaluation, with initiation or continuation of diagnostic and treatment program; intermediate, established patient Notes: (Do not report 92012 in conjunction with 99173, 99174, 99177, 0469T)
lay_term: For this CPT® code, an Ophthalmologist sees an established patient for an intermediate level eye examination. Generally, a patient is considered to be "established" if the same physician, or any physician in the group practice (or any physician of the same specialty who is billing under the same group number), has seen the patient for a face–to–face service within the past 36 months. Explanation For this CPT® code, an Ophthalmologist sees an established patient for an intermediate level eye examination. Generally, a patient is considered to be "established" if the same physician, or any physician in the group practice (or any physician of the same specialty who is billing under the same group number), has seen the patient for a face–to–face service within the past 36 months. Tips Intermediate ophthalmological service describes an evaluation of a new or existing condition complicated with an acute problem that may not be related to the primary diagnosis including the review of previous history, a general examination, a few diagnostic procedures. It may include mydriasis for conducting ophthalmoscopy. The main difference between 92012 and 92014 is that 92014 requires dilation unless medically contraindicated. A comprehensive exam (92014 for an established patient or 92004 for a new patient) also includes more exam components than an intermediate exam (92012 for an established patient or 92002 for a new patient). For example, an insurer may require that you include nine or more of these elements in a comprehensive exam: Visual acuity (not including refractive error), gross visual fields, eyelids and adnexa, ocular mobility, pupils, iris, conjunctiva, cornea, anterior chamber, lens, intraocular pressure, retina (vitreous, macula, periphery, and vessels), and optic disc. Some insurers may require that certain elements, such as gross visual field tests and ocular mobility tests, be covered in all comprehensive tests. Examination of the eyelids and adnexa may be mandatory for an intermediate exam. Most dilated exams will include nine or more of the above items. Even though CPT® does not support this restriction, some insurers consider 92002–92014 to be used only for routine vision exams. Be sure to check your carrier for its rules. Read Less

short_description: Ophthalmological services: medical examination and evaluation, with initiation or continuation of diagnostic and treatment program; comprehensive, established patient, 1 or more visits Notes: (Do not report 92014 in conjunction with 99173, 99174, 99177, 0469T) (For surgical procedures, see Surgery, Eye and Ocular Adnexa, 65091 et seq)
lay_term: An ophthalmologist sees an established patient for a comprehensive level eye examination. Generally, a patient is considered to be "established" if the same physician, or any physician in the group practice (or any physician of the same specialty who is billing under the same group number), has seen the patient for a face–to–face service within the past 36 months. Explanation The physician may initiate new treatment or continue with the existing treatment plan based on the patient's problem and symptoms. The physician reviews the patient's medical history, performs a complete general external examination, and may conduct a few diagnostic eye tests such as slit–lamp viewing, exophthalmometry, tonometry, biomicroscopy, retinoscopy, etc. for detailed examination purposes. Code an intermediate exam (92002 or 92012) if three of these elements are documented. short_description: Determination of refractive state Notes: (Do not report 92015 in conjunction with 99173, 99174, 99177) (For instrument-based ocular screening, use 99174, 99177)
lay_term: The provider determines the process of determining if a patient's vision is less than 20/20 and by what amount so that corrective lenses or contact lenses can be prescribed and produced. Explanation With the patient looking at a standardized vision chart, such as a Snellen chart, the provider determines the patient's refractive state. He adds lenses of varying power and adjusts other settings while asking the patient if his vision is better or worse. The process is carried out until the patient's vision is corrected as near to normal vision, called 20/20 vision, as possible. The settings used and power of lenses used are then written as a prescription so that eyeglasses or contact lenses can be produced. Tips You can bill a patient for 92015 even if the ophthalmologist doesn't give the patient a new prescription. You did the work and should be paid for your time. Code the work performed, with or without prescription, just as you would an E/M service. You probably already know that Medicare won't pay for 92015 (Determination of refractive state). Some private payers might, so be sure to check with the patient's payer so you can discuss potential payment issues with him before the procedure. If insurance won't cover it, the patient is responsible for paying for the service. As a noncovered service, refractions don't require an advance beneficiary notice, but you should inform the patient that refraction is not covered and, as such, he will be responsible for payment. short_description: Ophthalmological examination and evaluation, under general anesthesia, with or without manipulation of globe for passive range of motion or other manipulation to facilitate diagnostic examination; complete
lay_term: Code 92018 describes examination and evaluation of the eye while the patient is asleep under general anesthesia. The exam may include not only evaluation of the internal structure of the eye, but tests the eyeball's ability to move either passively or with manipulation of the eyeball directly by the physician (for example, by pulling on the individual muscles controlling movement of the eye). Explanation This procedure is most often performed on children or uncooperative adults when a detailed examination of the eye cannot otherwise be performed. While the patient is asleep under general anesthesia, the physician (ophthalmologist) can make a detailed examination of the internal aspects of the eye (fundoscopic examination) to check for conditions such as glaucoma, retinal abnormalities, or other conditions such as presence of tumors. He may take pictures of the internal components of the eye, take special measurements of the eye, perform ultrasound examination, or perform actual treatment of various conditions. In addition, he examines the outside aspect of the eye and may test the movement of the eyeball by pulling on the various external muscles that cause the eye to move. This latter procedure may be important in cases of double vision or strabismus to determine if there are mechanical obstructions to movement of the eye. Tips You cannot report an add–on code without a primary procedure code, and most of the primary procedure codes now include 92018 and 92019. Therefore, you are effectively prevented from reporting 92018 or 92019 with any payable eye surgery code, without an appropriate modifier. Read Less

short_description: Computerized corneal topography, unilateral or bilateral, with interpretation and report Notes: (Do not report 92025 in conjunction with 65710-65771) (92025 is not used for manual keratoscopy, which is part of a single system Evaluation and Management or ophthalmological service)
lay_term: The provider measures the curvature of one or both corneas, interprets the findings, and prepares a report. Explanation With the assistance of a computer, the shape or curvature of the cornea (the clear outer part of the eye over the iris and pupil) is measured and displayed on a monitor, often as a colored map of the corneal surface. The computer allows detection of much finer detail than other methods of examination and has the advantage that the data can be stored for later comparison if needed. The process is painless and involves the patient looking into an illuminated sphere, which, most often, has a pattern of concentric rings. This pattern is reflected back from the cornea to a digital camera at the back of the illuminated sphere. Distortion of the concentric pattern caused by alterations of the cornea can then be measured and stored. The provider interprets the results and writes a report. Computerized corneal topography is also known as computer–assisted videokeratography (CAVK) and corneal mapping. Tips Many insurers exclude routine preoperative or postoperative corneal topography for refractive surgery such as LASIK or radial keratotomy. Some covered indications for this procedure include central corneal ulcers, corneal dystrophy, bullous keratopathy, or complications of a transplanted cornea, diagnosis and monitoring of keratoconus, difficult fitting of contact lenses, and post–traumatic corneal scarring. short_description: Orthoptic training; under supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional Notes: (Do not report 92066 in conjunction with 92065, 0687T, 0688T, when performed on the same day)
lay_term: A provider under the supervision of a physician or other qualified healthcare professional trains the patient to perform exercises for vision therapy. Explanation A provider prescribes exercises to correct the patient’s eye problems, particularly for issues with binocular vision and eye movements. Examples of conditions include amblyopia (also called lazy eye; it can result in decreased vision because the brain favors one eye over the other), strabismus (misalignment of the eyes), and convergence insufficiency (the eyes drift outward when looking at near objects). At the session, a provider under the supervision of a physician or other qualified healthcare professional (QHP) trains the patient to perform the exercises, such as a dot card exercise (the patient holds the card up to their nose and focuses on a series of dots) or pencil pushups (focusing on a pencil moving closer to the patient’s eyes until it appears double, and then reversing the direction until the double image disappears). Tips See 92065 for orthoptic training by a physician or other QHP. Read Less

short_description: Visual field examination, unilateral or bilateral, with interpretation and report; limited examination (eg, tangent screen, Autoplot, arc perimeter, or single stimulus level automated test, such as Octopus 3 or 7 equivalent)
lay_term: The provider may use one or more methods to determine the extent of a patient's visual field of one or both eyes; he interprets the results and prepares a report. Report this code for a limited examination of the patient's visual field. Explanation The provider performs a limited examination of the extent of a patient's visual field, that is, how far inward, outward (laterally), upward (superiorly), and downward (inferiorly) the patient can see an object while his vision is fixed on a stationary point in front of the eye. Basically, the test determines how much peripheral vision a patient possesses using techniques or methods such as tangent screen (use of a white object on the end of a black stick in front of a black screen), Auto–Plot® (a variation on a tangent screen that can change the size and color of the stimulus), arc perimeter (a device to keep the stimulus at a static distance from the eye), or single–stimulus level automated test, such as an Octopus 3 or 7 equivalent, which is a computer–aided visual field test. This code is for a very limited screening test only and is used for screening either one or both eyes. The provider interprets the findings and writes a report. Terminology Isopter: Connected points of equal retinal sensitivity to an object of a given size, testing distance, level of illumination, and color; the isopter line is generated by connecting all the points where the patient first sees the test object. Peripheral: Existing along the margins of an object or surface or outer limits of vision; may also be used to refer to the extremities. Visual field: The extent to which one can see an object positioned superiorly, laterally, inferiorly, and nasally when vision is fixed on a spot directly in front of the eye; a blind spot (scotoma) exists at 15 degrees laterally where the optic nerve exits the eye. Tips The most important responsibility of the provider is that copies of the visual field results themselves are not sufficient to justify billing a special ophthalmological service code. The documentation must show that a visual field test is necessary for diagnosis and future treatment and prognosis. Code 92082 and 92083 are very similar to 92081, the difference being that the test methodology is more sensitive than that described for 92081. Code 92082 uses at least 2 isopters for testing by the Goldmann perimeter method, that is, at least two targets of differing size, color, and intensity. The other listed methods are various brands of perimetry testing equipment and associated computer programs for enhanced sensitivity. Similarly, 92083 is for an extended examination with 3 isopters plotted, static determination within the central 30 degrees, or full threshold visual field analysis. Codes 92081, 92082, or 92083 for limited, intermediate, and extended examinations are all considered bilateral procedures in the Medicare program. The use of the term bilateral means that payment for the service code includes payment for both eyes. When reporting these services on an electronic or paper claim, submission of the code 92081, 92082, or 92083 without a modifier communicates to the carrier that the service was performed on both eyes. Although the descriptors state that these visual field codes are "unilateral or bilateral," Medicare payers and those that follow Medicare rules, don't see it that way. Medicare's fee schedule gives codes 92081 to 92083 a bilateral indicator of "2," meaning that it sees the codes as inherently bilateral. CMS bases the relative value units (RVUs) assigned to 92081 to 92083 on the assumption that the ophthalmologist performs the work in both eyes. So, you should not append modifiers LT (Left side), RT (Right side), or 50 (Bilateral procedure) to the code when you report bilateral visual fields. The payment from Medicare will reflect the work performed on both eyes. However, if the service is performed on just one side, you should append the modifiers, and the payment may be reduced. short_description: Serial tonometry (separate procedure) with multiple measurements of intraocular pressure over an extended time period with interpretation and report, same day (eg, diurnal curve or medical treatment of acute elevation of intraocular pressure) Notes: (For monitoring of intraocular pressure for 24 hours or longer, use 0329T) (Ocular blood flow measurements are reported with 0198T. lay_term: Code 92100 describes multiple measurements of intraocular pressure taken over a given time period on a single day in order to monitor response to treatment or document pressure changes throughout the day. Explanation Tonometry is part of the examination for glaucoma. The test measures the intraocular pressure of the eye, similar to measuring tire pressure on your car. The pathophysiology of glaucoma is that there is increased intraocular pressure above normal which results in damage to the delicate nerve fibers that run across the retina. The greater and more prolonged the intraocular pressure, the greater the damage. This damage initially results in diminution or shrinking of the patient's field of vision, thus the value of performing perimetry (codes 92081–92083). There are multiple differing methods for measuring intraocular pressure, some of which require initial numbing of the cornea with a local anesthetic so that the measuring device can be placed on the cornea without patient discomfort. The physician then measures and records the pressure. Normal range is 10–21. In cases of acute glaucoma, there is a rapid rise of pressure. Following instillation of eyedrops to treat the condition, the physician can measure the intraocular pressure repeatedly over time to assess the response to treatment. There is a normal pressure variation during the day with higher morning and lower evening pressures. In early glaucoma there is an exaggeration of this variation. Tips Question: Is there a code for "diurnal curve testing" for glaucoma, during which the ophthalmologist checks pressures over the course of several hours? Answer: Code 92100 describes diurnal curve testing. Most Medicare carriers require that the ophthalmologist perform three tests over six or more hours before it can be considered serial tonometry. Don't report 92100 just because the ophthalmologist performed tonometry once or twice during an eye exam. Medicare and CPT® both consider tonometry incidental to an intermediate or comprehensive exam for a new or established patient (92002–92014) or E/M service. This is true even if the ophthalmologist repeats the tonometry. Don't miss: The ophthalmologist may not perform all of the serial tonometry tests in the same day, but even if he spreads the test out over several days, you should report 92100 only once. Medicare considers the procedure bilateral, so only code one unit whether the physician tests one or both eyes. Read Less

short_description: Computerized ophthalmic diagnostic imaging (eg, optical coherence tomography [OCT]), anterior segment, with interpretation and report, unilateral or bilateral Notes: (Do not report 92132 in conjunction with 0730T) (For computerized ophthalmic diagnostic imaging of the optic nerve and retina, see 92133, 92134, 92137) (For specular microscopy and endothelial cell analysis, use 92286) (For tear film imaging, use 0330T)
lay_term: The provider performs computerized diagnostic imaging of the anterior segment (front part) of the eye, interprets the data, and provides a report. The service may be on one or both eyes. Explanation Computerized ophthalmic diagnostic imaging for the anterior segment is a noninvasive procedure that allows a provider to capture high–resolution, cross–sectional images of the front part of the eye, including the cornea, iris, and anterior chamber. The cornea is the clear, outer layer of the eye that helps focus light, the iris is the colored part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil and regulates light entry, and the anterior chamber is the fluid–filled space between the cornea and iris. A typical service is optical coherence tomography (OCT), in which the patient sits in front of the OCT machine and rests their chin on a support to keep their head steady. The provider aligns the machine to ensure the eye is properly positioned for scanning. The OCT device uses light waves to take detailed images of the structures of the anterior segment, allowing the provider to assess issues like corneal thickness, anterior chamber depth, or any abnormalities such as scarring or lesions. Once the scan is completed, the provider reviews the images on a computer. These images are highly detailed and allow for precise analysis of the tissues without the need for invasive techniques. After interpretation, the provider compiles a report summarizing the findings, which can include measurements, visual analysis, and any indications of disease or abnormalities. This report helps guide further treatment or monitoring plans. The provider may perform the service on one eye (unilateral) or both eyes (bilateral), depending on the patient’s condition. Tips This code is specific to the anterior segment. Read Less

lay_term: The provider performs computerized diagnostic imaging of the optic nerve in the posterior segment (back part) of the eye, interprets the data, and provides a report. The service may be on one or both eyes. Explanation Computerized ophthalmic diagnostic imaging of the optic nerve is a noninvasive imaging technique used to capture detailed cross–sectional images of the optic nerve in the eye’s posterior segment. A typical service is optical coherence tomography (OCT), in which the patient sits in front of the OCT machine, which is equipped with a chin rest and forehead support to ensure proper alignment. The provider adjusts the device to focus on the optic nerve in either one eye (unilateral) or both eyes (bilateral), depending on the patient’s condition. The OCT machine uses light waves to penetrate the layers of the retina and optic nerve, producing high–resolution images that allow the provider to evaluate the health of the optic nerve fibers. Once the scan is complete, the provider reviews the captured images, looking for signs of thinning, swelling, or other abnormalities in the optic nerve that could indicate disease progression or damage. These images provide precise data on the structural integrity of the optic nerve and help monitor changes over time. After interpreting the findings, the provider prepares a detailed report, summarizing the results and indicating any potential concerns or need for further treatment. After the scan, the provider reviews both the structural and vascular images, looking for any signs of retinal thinning, swelling, or abnormal blood vessel growth or leakage. Following the interpretation of the images, the provider prepares a detailed report summarizing the findings, including any recommendations for treatment or further monitoring. short_description: Corneal hysteresis determination, by air impulse stimulation, unilateral or bilateral, with interpretation and report

He applies pressure over the cornea through metered air pulses that deform the cornea and move it inward. short_description: Ophthalmoscopy, extended; with retinal drawing and scleral depression of peripheral retinal disease (eg, for retinal tear, retinal detachment, retinal tumor) with interpretation and report, unilateral or bilateral
lay_term: The provider performs an extended ophthalmoscopy, typically with an indirect ophthalmoscope which utilizes a bright light and a hand–held indirect lens rather than the common hand–held one–piece direct ophthalmoscope. Using a headlamp or other bright light source and a hand–held indirect lens, he meticulously examines the Interior of the eye, looking for retinal or choroidal tumors, retinal tears or detachments or retinal defects without detachment, choroidal detachment, hemorrhages, exudative detachments, and retinal landmarks. To make sure he is able to examine the complete posterior fundus and retinal periphery, the provider inserts the tip of a thimble, flat double–ended, or cotton–tipped scleral depressor between the globe (eyeball) and the orbit (eye socket) to help visualize the peripheral part of the retina obscured by the iris or crystalline lens. The space occupied by the depressor displaces the retina inward and elevates it, enhancing contrast between any lesion and the peripheral retinal tissue. Scleral depression helps identify poorly defined lesions, retinal holes, tears or vitreoretinal adhesions. The provider makes one or more detailed retinal drawings that reveal the extent of his examination, interprets his findings, and prepares a report. He may, before or after the extended ophthalmoscopy, obtain fundus photographs, which may or may not be reported separately, to establish a baseline or compare with previous photographs to document disease progression. Glaucoma: Eye disorder characterized by increased intraocular pressure, the pressure caused by the fluid inside the eye, the aqueous humor, that helps maintain the shape of the eye. Hemorrhage: Bleeding; typically refers to uncontrolled, rapid and/or excessive bleeding. Lens: Transparent eye structure that focuses light onto the retina; also called crystalline lens. Macula: The point of sharpest vision within the retina, tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation. Ophthalmoscopy: Examination of the internal surfaces of the hollow eye cavity through a dilated pupil; in indirect ophthalmoscopy the machine produces an inverted image of the fundus of the eye. Optic nerve: One of the pair of second cranial nerves that connect the eyes to the brain; it carries impulses from the retina of the eye to the brain. Orbit: Bony cavity that holds the eyes; the orbital area is formed by seven bones, the frontal, lachrymal, ethmoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, and sphenoid bones. Peripheral: Existing along the margins of an object or surface of the body; may also be used to refer to the extremities. Retina: Tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation. Retinal detachment: A medical condition in which the retina is separated from its attachment to the supporting layers within the eye. Sclera: The white outer part of the eye that covers all of the eyeball except for the cornea. Vitreoretinal: Pertaining to the retina and the vitreous body (the gelatinous substance filling the eyeball between the lens and the retina). lay_term: The provider injects two different special dyes into one or both eyes that cause the blood vessels to stand out in photographic images timed so that multiple frames are taken in rapid succession. He interprets the findings and prepares a report. Indications for the study include disorders of the eye vessels and optic nerve, tumors, and preparation for some forms of laser treatment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider injects fluorescein dye into a patient's vein. The dye, when exposed to light of a certain wavelength, emits light itself (fluoresces) and allows the blood flow in the small vessels of the eye to be photographed. The dye reaches the retina in 10 to 15 seconds after injection and can be seen for 10 seconds. During this period, the provider captures multiple images using multiframe timing. He takes photos or videos of the blood vessels of the fundus, or inner back part of eye to examine the structure of the retinal blood vessels and detect any leaks. Following the fluorescein procedure, he injects a second fluorescent dye, indocyanine–green, which provides better images of the tiny vessels in the choroid at the back of the eye, and again captures multiple images. He then interprets the images and prepares a report that summarizes pertinent findings, compares the findings to any previous studies, and documents how the test will affect clinical management or prognosis. Terminology Choroid: Highly vascular membrane of the eye that lies between the sclera and the retina. Optic nerve: One of the pair of second cranial nerves that connect the eyes to the brain; it carries impulses from the retina of the eye to the brain. short_description: Fundus photography with interpretation and report
lay_term: Code 92250 describes the taking of fundus photographs, that is, photographs of the posterior segment of the inner aspect of the eye, to document alterations in the optic nerve head, retinal vessels, and retinal epithelium. It can be used to document baseline retinal findings and track disease progression. Explanation Medical necessity must be documented, but common conditions for which fundus photographs are used are glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, choroidal nevus, optic neuritis, papilledema, and age–related macular degeneration. Photos are usually taken at the end of a comprehensive eye exam when the eyes have been fully dilated. The usual requirement for a formal report and interpretation exists. Report should include vertical and horizontal cup/disc ratio based upon vessel pattern and/or coloration, presence or absence of diffuse or focal pallor (paleness, loss of color), asymmetry, progression, or any of the above. Photos should be labeled as to which eye, date taken, and date reviewed. Implications for patient diagnosis, management, and prognosis should be included. Terminology Choroid: Highly vascular membrane of the eye that lies between the sclera and the retina. Choroidal nevus: A pigmented area something like a freckle on the choroidal membrane. Diabetic retinopathy: A complication of diabetes that affects the retina of the eye, causing blockages of the blood vessels and subsequent abnormal blood vessel growth. Epithelium: The outer layer of cells that covers all the free surfaces of the body including the skin and mucous membranes that communicate with the outside of the body. Glaucoma: Eye disorder characterized by increased intraocular pressure, the pressure caused by the fluid inside the eye, the aqueous humor, that helps maintain the shape of the eye. Macular degeneration (MD): A slowly progressive eye disease that causes deterioration of the photoreceptor cells (the cells for detecting light and enabling sight). Neuritis: Inflammation of a nerve. Optic nerve: One of the pair of second cranial nerves that connect the eyes to the brain; it carries impulses from the retina of the eye to the brain. Papilledema: Swelling (edema) of the optic disk (papilla), often resulting from increased intracranial pressure, obstruction of blood flow in the central retinal vein, or malignant hypertension; also known as a "choked disk." Retina: Tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation. Tips If only one eye is photographed it is recommended to add modifier 52 and modifier for which eye was photographed. short_description: Ophthalmodynamometry Notes: (For ophthalmoscopy under general anesthesia, use 92018)
lay_term: Code 92260 describes measurement of arterial blood pressure in the retina. Explanation This is a technique used to measure the pressure of the ophthalmic artery, a branch vessel of the internal carotid. It has been used as a non–invasive method for assessing carotid artery insufficiency and ischemic retinopathy. It can also measure pressure of the central retinal vein which has been shown to correlate well with intracranial pressure and has the advantage over current methods of measuring ICP in that it is non–invasive. Several differing methods are described with one procedure involving use of a Goldmann contact lens fitted with a pressure sensor; other procedures describe use of a Doppler device. It is suggested that the procedure not be performed on patients with high myopia or previous intraocular surgery. Also, in that it requires dilation of the eyes, it is not recommended in comatose patients where pupillary reaction and size is a critical physical finding and prognostic indicator. Tips This is a bilateral procedure with comparison of values between sides being of diagnostic value for predicting vessel insufficiency/occlusion. While CPT® makes no requirement for interpretation and report, it is probably a good idea to document the medical necessity of the procedure and results. Read Less

short_description: Electro-oculography with interpretation and report Notes: (For vestibular function tests with recording, see 92537, 92538, 92540, 92541, 92542, 92544, 92545, 92546, 92547, 92548) (Do not report 92270 in conjunction with 92537, 92538, 92540, 92541, 92542, 92544, 92545, 92546, 92547, 92548, 92549) (To report saccadic eye movement testing with recording, use 92700)
lay_term: The provider performs electro–oculography, which measures the electrical potential between electrodes placed at points close to the eye to assess eye movements after which he interprets the results and prepares a report. It is done first with the patient in the dark and then with the patient in a brightly lit room. The maximum voltage obtained in the light is then divided by the minimum voltage recorded in the dark (the Arden ratio). Terminology Electrocardiogram (ECG): A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. short_description: Electroretinography (ERG), with interpretation and report; full field (ie, ffERG, flash ERG, Ganzfeld ERG)
lay_term: The provider performs an electrophysiologic test of retinal function, which may be referred to as conventional, full–field or Ganzfeld (ffERG) or flash/focal (fERG) electroretinography to assess outer or generalized retinal function. Explanation The test is performed on a patient who has been dark adapted and whose eyes have been dilated (these two components add about one hour of time to the study). The provider instills a local anesthetic into the eyes and fits the patient with a recording contact lens and a reference electrode attached to the patient's forehead. Light flashes are then produced, and the electrical activity generated by the retina is recorded. The response is a waveform that looks somewhat like an electrocardiogram. Normal waveforms have an a–wave, b–wave and c–wave that are generated by the rods and cones, the bipolar cells, and pigmented epithelium respectively. Any deviation in waveform represents disease in the corresponding anatomic component. The test can detect changes before ophthalmoscopic changes occur or when cataracts or corneal opacity prevent ophthalmoscopic exam. The procedure may even be performed on babies. The provider interprets the results and prepares a formal report. It should document medical necessity and how the test results will affect the patient’s management and prognosis. Terminology Electrophysiologic: Relating to the electrical impulse generation phenomena of cells and tissues. Tips For multifocal electroretinography (mfERG), see 92274; mfERG uses multiple sequences to stimulate many retinal areas and records retinal responses from different regions simultaneously. The test is similar to but different from visual evoked potentials which measure the brain's electrical activity after light flashes and is useful for detecting abnormalities of the optic nerve and visual pathways of the brain. Check with your payer's local coverage decision (LCD) for diagnoses supporting medical necessity. This test may require preauthorization. Read Less

short_description: Electroretinography (ERG), with interpretation and report; multifocal (mfERG) Notes: (For pattern ERG, use 0509T) (For electronystagmography for vestibular function studies, see 92541 et seq) (For ophthalmic echography (diagnostic ultrasound), see 76511-76529)
lay_term: The provider performs an electrophysiologic test of retinal function, which consists of multifocal electroretinography (mfERG) to detect localized retinal abnormalities or cone–rod dysfunction. The retina of the eye is responsible for visual image formation, and the rods and cones are involved in dark adaptation and color vision. Explanation The test is performed on a patient who has been dark adapted and whose eyes have been dilated (these two components add about one hour of time to the study). The provider instills a local anesthetic into the eyes and fits the patient with a recording contact lens and a reference electrode attached to the patient's forehead. Light flashes, alternating with dark, are presented on a video monitor in pattern of hexagons (six–sided shapes) that are smaller in the center and larger in the outer regions of the pattern. The electrical activity generated by the retina is recorded. The response is a waveform similar to that of the full–field electroretinogram (ffERG). Normal waveforms have a negative deflection or N1 (corresponding to the a–wave on ffERG), positive deflection or P1 (b–wave) and a second negative deflection or N2 (c–wave). Any deviation in waveform represents disease in the corresponding anatomic component. The test can detect changes before ophthalmoscopic changes occur or when cataracts or corneal opacity prevent ophthalmoscopic exam. The provider interprets the results and prepares a formal report. It should document medical necessity and how the test results will affect the patient’s management and prognosis. Multifocal ERGs may be performed to detect localized retinal abnormalities in eye conditions such as retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited degenerative eye disease where the light sensitive retina slowly and progressively degenerates resulting in gradual loss of peripheral vision and eventual blindness. The study may also help identify or diagnose branch retinal artery occlusion and fundus flavimaculatus or Stargardt disease (a type of inherited macular dystrophy); mfERG may also help detect the degree of retinal toxicity related to certain drugs and early visual field defects due to glaucoma. Terminology Electrophysiologic: Relating to the electrical impulse generation phenomena of cells and tissues. Tips For full field (ffERG), flash ERG, or Ganzfeld ERG, see 92273. short_description: Color vision examination, extended, eg, anomaloscope or equivalent Notes: (Color vision testing with pseudoisochromatic plates [such as HRR or Ishihara] is not reported separately. It is included in the appropriate general or ophthalmological service, or 99172)
lay_term: The provider uses an optical instrument, such as a Nagel anomaloscope, that uses long wavelengths of yellow–green light, which a patient adjusts, to match a predetermined ratio of red to green light; this test is used to determine whether the patient has color blindness, typically red–green color blindness. Explanation Typically, after a positive color blindness test using flash cards, such as Ishihara plates, the provider retests the patient using an optical instrument that allows adjustment of long wavelengths of yellow–green light to match a predetermined ratio of red–green light. The patient looks through an eye piece and sees a circle, the upper half of which is yellow, the lower half a combination of red and green light. The patient adjusts the color in the top half of the circle until it matches the color in the bottom half. Some instruments allow the patient to adjust both halves of the circle until the colors match in hue and intensity. Some anomaloscopes can be configured to use short wavelengths of light with an adjustable aqua test light and a constant, predetermined ratio of violet and blue–green for other types of color blindness, such as violets and yellows. Another advanced color vision test based on the anomaloscope is the anomaloscope plate test (APT–5) which uses plates of yellow and red–green light–emitting diodes (LEDs); the intensity and chromaticity of the yellow LEDs can be controlled, and the patient matches patterns in the red–green LEDs. Other color vision tests that use plates include the Farnsworth–15 and the Farnsworth–Munsell 100 Hue color vision test, which use 15 and 100 color plates, blocks, or pegs respectively, that have to be arranged in the correct color order. Terminology Color blindess: The inability to distinguish between certain colors or intensity of color; the degree of red–green color blindness varies, but some patients cannot discriminate between red and green at all, except by external clues such as brightness; types of color blindness include the following: Cone monochromacy: An autosomal recessive disorder which causes trouble distinguishing colors due to dysfunction of two of the three cone cell photopigments (red, green, and blue); when only one type of cone works, the brain cannot compare the signals from different types of cones in order to see color; blue cone monochromacy may be associated with reduced visual acuity, near–sightedness, and nystagmus (uncontrollable eye movements). Deuteranomaly: The most common form of color blindness, it affects about 5 percent of men; an X–linked inherited disorder in which yellow and green appear redder and distinguishing violet from blue is difficult, , usually mild and does not interfere with daily living. Deuteranopia: An X–linked inherited disorder affecting about 1 percent of men in which they see reds as brownish–yellow and greens as beige. Protanomaly: An X–linked inherited disorder affecting about 1 percent of men in which red, orange, and yellow appear greener and colors are not as bright, usually mild and does not interfere with daily living. Protanopia: An X–linked inherited disorder affecting about 1 percent of men in which red looks black and certain shades of orange, yellow, and green all appear yellow. Rod monochromacy or achromatopsia: An autosomal recessive disorder present at birth and the most severe form of color blindness in which none of the cone cells have functional photopigments; individuals with this disorder see everything as black, white, and gray. And since rods respond to dim light, photophobia (light intolerance) and nystagmus (uncontrollable eye movements) are usually associated with this disorder. Tritanomaly: An extremely rare, autosomal dominant disorder in both men and women in which blue appears greener and distinguishing yellow and red from pink is difficult due to dysfunctional blue cone (tritan) cells. Tritanopia: An extremely rare, autosomal dominant disorder in both men and women in which blue appears green and yellow appears violet or light grey due to absent blue cone (tritan) cells. Ishihara test: Cards with colored dots that imbed images within other dots of different colors, used to test for color blindness. Tips If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26, Professional component to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Diagnostic dark adaptation examination with interpretation and report
lay_term: The provider assesses the ability of a patient’s eyes to adapt to changes in lighting. The results may indicate retinal disease, nutritional deficiencies, and other conditions. The provider interprets the findings and generates a report. Explanation The provider places the patient in a dark room. The patient looks into a machine designed to test dark adaptation, the ability of the rod photoreceptors (retina cells that function in low light) to increase their sensitivity in the dark. For instance, a test may involve a bright light blinking at different intensities. The patient hits a button when they see the light, allowing the machine to test the threshold of the patient’s rod function. Impaired dark adaptation is associated with various eye conditions. The provider interprets the results and generates a report of the findings. Terminology Retina: Tissue at the back of the eye that is sensitive to light and helps in visual image formation. Read Less

lay_term: Code 92285 describes photography of abnormalities using any of the methods described for documentation purposes and later comparison. Explanation A separate report and interpretation needs to be reported. It should document which eye is photographed, date taken and reviewed, and abnormalities labeled. The camera should be of a special type capable of taking magnified images. Explanation The provider prescribes corneal contact lenses for both eyes in a patient who is aphakic. The provider specifies the optical and physical characteristics of the lenses, including power, curvature, size, flexibility, and gas permeability. The provider supervises the adaptation and direction of fitting of the lenses by an independent technician. Terminology Aphakia: Absence of the lens of an eye, either by surgical removal or due to wound or congenital absence. Tips Aphakia lenses are placed when the eye has no lens, either congenitally or from an injury that requires removal of the natural lens. This differs from fixing a regular refractive error. Use 92315 for prescription by a specialist and supervision of fitting by an independent technician for one eye and 92316 for both eyes. With aphakic contact lenses, there is also a supply issue. Aphakic patients are legally blind without their contact lenses. If they wear aphakic contact lenses, Medicare is required to replace one per aphakic eye a year as medically necessary. Medicare carriers will only pay once per eye per lifetime for a patient with an intraocular lens. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline The prescription of contact lens includes specification of optical and physical characteristics (such as power, size, curvature, flexibility, gas-permeability). It is not a part of the general ophthalmological services. The fitting of contact lens includes instruction and training of the wearer and incidental revision of the lens during the training period. Follow-up of successfully fitted extended wear lenses is reported as part of a general ophthalmological service (92012 et seq). The supply of contact lenses may be reported as part of the service of fitting. It may also be reported separately by using the appropriate supply codes. (For therapeutic or surgical use of contact lens, see 68340, 92071, 92072) Section Specific Guideline (For surgical procedures, see Surgery, Eye and Ocular Adnexa, 65091 et seq) Definitions Intermediate ophthalmological services describes an evaluation of a new or existing condition complicated with a new diagnostic or management problem not necessarily relating to the primary diagnosis, including history, general medical observation, external ocular and adnexal examination and other diagnostic procedures as indicated; may include the use of mydriasis for ophthalmoscopy. For example: a. Review of history, external examination, ophthalmoscopy, biomicroscopy for an acute complicated condition (eg, iritis) not requiring comprehensive ophthalmological services. b. Review of interval history, external examination, ophthalmoscopy, biomicroscopy and tonometry in established patient with known cataract not requiring comprehensive ophthalmological services. Comprehensive ophthalmological services describes a general evaluation of the complete visual system. The comprehensive services constitute a single service entity but need not be performed at one session. The service includes history, general medical observation, external and ophthalmoscopic examinations, gross visual fields and basic sensorimotor examination. It often includes, as indicated: biomicroscopy, examination with cycloplegia or mydriasis and tonometry. It always includes initiation of diagnostic and treatment programs. Intermediate and comprehensive ophthalmological services constitute integrated services in which medical decision making cannot be separated from the examining techniques used. Itemization of service components, such as slit lamp examination, keratometry, routine ophthalmoscopy, retinoscopy, tonometry, or motor evaluation is not applicable. For example: The comprehensive services required for diagnosis and treatment of a patient with symptoms indicating possible disease of the visual system, such as glaucoma, cataract or retinal disease, or to rule out disease of the visual system, new or established patient. Initiation of diagnostic and treatment program includes the prescription of medication, and arranging for special ophthalmological diagnostic or treatment services, consultations, laboratory procedures and radiological services. Special ophthalmological services describes services in which a special evaluation of part of the visual system is made, which goes beyond the services included under general ophthalmological services, or in which special treatment is given. Special ophthalmological services may be reported in addition to the general ophthalmological services or evaluation and management services. For example: Fluorescein angioscopy, quantitative visual field examination, refraction or extended color vision examination (such as Nagel's anomaloscope) should be separately reported. Prescription of lenses, when required, is included in 92015. It includes specification of lens type (monofocal, bifocal, other), lens power, axis, prism, absorptive factor, impact resistance, and other factors. Interpretation and report by the physician or other qualified health care professional is an integral part of special ophthalmological services where indicated. Technical procedures (which may or may not be performed personally) are often part of the service, but should not be mistaken to constitute the service itself.

short_description: Fitting of spectacle prosthesis for aphakia; monofocal
lay_term: Code 92352 describes the fitting of eyeglasses with one specified focal length for patients who have undergone removal of the native crystalline lens, i.e., those who have had cataract surgery. Explanation The physician component of determination of the refractive state is covered with code 92015. This code is strictly for the fitting of the eyeglasses which takes into account measurements of the patient's facial features, and alignment of the lenses to the patient's visual axis and other fitting adjustments to the eyeglass frames so that the eyeglasses fit comfortable and result in good vision for the patient. The physician need not be present for fitting of the frames. The physician must prescribe the eyeglasses and sign the order and date it in order for Medicare coverage. Tips Medicare covers the cost of standard frames and the lenses even if the cataract surgery occurred before the patient was eligible for Medicare and Medicare will cover the cost of both lenses even if only one eye had cataract surgery. Medicare still covers the cost of spectacles even if you have an intraocular lens implant. Medicare covers 80% of the cost, and the patient is responsible for the remaining 20%. If the patient upgrades beyond standard frames, Medicare pays only the cost of standard frames. Read Less

When provided, fitting of spectacles is a separate service and is reported as indicated by 92340-92371. Fitting includes measurement of anatomical facial characteristics, the writing of laboratory specifications, and the final adjustment of the spectacles to the visual axes and anatomical topography. Presence of the physician or other qualified health care professional is not required. Supply of materials is a separate service component; it is not part of the service of fitting spectacles. Section Specific Guideline (For surgical procedures, see Surgery, Eye and Ocular Adnexa, 65091 et seq) Definitions Intermediate ophthalmological services describes an evaluation of a new or existing condition complicated with a new diagnostic or management problem not necessarily relating to the primary diagnosis, including history, general medical observation, external ocular and adnexal examination and other diagnostic procedures as indicated; may include the use of mydriasis for ophthalmoscopy. For example: a. Review of history, external examination, ophthalmoscopy, biomicroscopy for an acute complicated condition (eg, iritis) not requiring comprehensive ophthalmological services. b. Review of interval history, external examination, ophthalmoscopy, biomicroscopy and tonometry in established patient with known cataract not requiring comprehensive ophthalmological services. Comprehensive ophthalmological services describes a general evaluation of the complete visual system. The comprehensive services constitute a single service entity but need not be performed at one session. The service includes history, general medical observation, external and ophthalmoscopic examinations, gross visual fields and basic sensorimotor examination. It often includes, as indicated: biomicroscopy, examination with cycloplegia or mydriasis and tonometry. It always includes initiation of diagnostic and treatment programs. Intermediate and comprehensive ophthalmological services constitute integrated services in which medical decision making cannot be separated from the examining techniques used. Itemization of service components, such as slit lamp examination, keratometry, routine ophthalmoscopy, retinoscopy, tonometry, or motor evaluation is not applicable. For example: The comprehensive services required for diagnosis and treatment of a patient with symptoms indicating possible disease of the visual system, such as glaucoma, cataract or retinal disease, or to rule out disease of the visual system, new or established patient. Initiation of diagnostic and treatment program includes the prescription of medication, and arranging for special ophthalmological diagnostic or treatment services, consultations, laboratory procedures and radiological services. Special ophthalmological services describes services in which a special evaluation of part of the visual system is made, which goes beyond the services included under general ophthalmological services, or in which special treatment is given. Special ophthalmological services may be reported in addition to the general ophthalmological services or evaluation and management services. For example: Fluorescein angioscopy, quantitative visual field examination, refraction or extended color vision examination (such as Nagel's anomaloscope) should be separately reported. Prescription of lenses, when required, is included in 92015. It includes specification of lens type (monofocal, bifocal, other), lens power, axis, prism, absorptive factor, impact resistance, and other factors. Interpretation and report by the physician or other qualified health care professional is an integral part of special ophthalmological services where indicated. Technical procedures (which may or may not be performed personally) are often part of the service, but should not be mistaken to constitute the service itself.

short_description: Unlisted ophthalmological service or procedure
lay_term: Use 92499 to report ophthalmological procedures that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs an ophthalmological procedure that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Terminology Ophthalmological: Related to conditions affecting the eyes. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

short_description: Otolaryngologic examination under general anesthesia
lay_term: The provider examines the ears, nose, and throat of a patient that he places under general anesthesia. He performs this in the case of an uncooperative child or an adult, and for a trauma victim who has already had administration of anesthesia. Explanation This service describes the examination of the ears, nose, and throat of a patient who requires general anesthesia for the test. These include patients such as an uncooperative child or an adult, who is difficult to handle during the test when in a conscious or active state. It also applies to trauma victims who are already anesthetized before the examination. With the patient under anesthesia, the provider completes an otoscopy and examines the nose and larynx of the patient as well. Terminology Anesthesia: A medication–induced state that reduces or eliminates sensitivity to pain, depending upon the type of anesthesia administered; general anesthesia renders the patient completely unconscious; sedation, depending on the level, induces a drowsy but aware or a sleeping state; and local or regional anesthesia reduces sensation to pain in specific areas of the body. Anterior rhinoscopy: Examination of the front part of the nose. Cerumen: Ear wax. Impaction: Condition characterized by a deposit of ear wax in such a way that it tightly packs in the outer ear and blocks it. Larynx: Respiratory organ that contains the vocal cords, positioned between the thorax, or throat, and the trachea, the tubes that ultimately lead to the lungs; also called the voice box. Otolaryngology: Study of diseases of the ears, nose, and throat. Otoscope: A medical instrument with a light source and lenses for magnification that helps the provider to visualize both the internal and external ear. Otoscopy: Examination of the ear using an instrument specially designed for the procedure. Tuning fork test: Medical test to determine the type of hearing loss in patients with the help of an instrument with a handle and two prongs that vibrate at a set frequency, and assess the ability of a person to hear. Tips If the provider examines only a patient’s nose for a possible nasal fracture, report 92502 for the exam. Otolaryngologists rarely perform a complete ENT exam under general anesthesia. Because the provider places the child under general anesthetic to perform a medically necessary procedure, due to the patient's age, the otolaryngologic exam meets 92502's requirements. Therefore, you should not append modifier 52, Reduced services, to 92502. Do not report diagnostic or treatment procedures like otoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy, removal of nonimpacted cerumen, or tuning fork test separately if the provider reports them as evaluation and management (E/M) services. However, 92502 is a special diagnostic test that is not included in an E/M service. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Section Specific Guideline Diagnostic or treatment procedures that are reported as evaluation and management services (eg, otoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy, tuning fork test, removal of non-impacted cerumen) are not reported separately. Special otorhinolaryngologic services are those diagnostic and treatment services not included in an evaluation and management service, including office or other outpatient services (99202-99215) or office or other outpatient consultations (99242, 99243, 99244, 99245). Codes 92507, 92508, 92520, 92521, 92522, 92523, 92524, and 92526 are used to report evaluation and treatment of speech sound production, receptive language, and expressive language abilities, voice and resonance production, speech fluency, and swallowing. Evaluations may include examination of speech sound production, articulatory movements of oral musculature, oral-pharyngeal swallowing function, qualitative analysis of voice and resonance, and measures of frequency, type, and duration of stuttering. Evaluations may also include the patient's ability to understand the meaning and intent of written and verbal expressions, as well as the appropriate formulation and utterance of expressive thought. (For laryngoscopy with stroboscopy, use 31579)

short_description: Treatment of speech, language, voice, communication, and/or auditory processing disorder; individual Notes: (Do not report 92507 in conjunction with 97153, 97155)
lay_term: The provider treats a patient with communication and hearing difficulties by directly interacting with the patient. He assesses the patient with impairment in his ability to make sounds, along with significant receptive and expressive deficit, to identify if the sound signals reach the brain through the ears. Explanation The provider performs articulation therapy to teach sounds and words to the patient, so that the patient may distinguish between sounds, react to different sounds in different ways, and integrate various sounds in words and phrases. The provider also executes such treatment as oral strength and control exercises, language therapy, both receptive and expressive; and he communicates with the patient through action and lip movements. He records the response of the patient and guides him to perform his daily activities properly. Terminology Anterior rhinoscopy: Examination of the front part of the nose. Articulation: Correct pronunciation of sounds. Auditory processing disorder: A neurological condition characterized by a learning disability, behavioral problem, and or the inability to differentiate between sounds in words, due to the inability of the brain to process the auditory information. Binocular microscope: An instrument with a lens to enlarge small parts and consisting of two eyepieces in order to use both the eyes for visualization. Cerumen: Ear wax. Expressive language: Ability to use language to convey wants, needs, and ideas. Impaction: Condition characterized by a deposit of ear wax in such a way that it tightly packs in the outer ear and blocks it. Otoscopy: Examination of the ear using an instrument specially designed for the procedure. Receptive language: Ability to understand and follow directions. Tuning fork test: Medical test to determine the type of hearing loss in patients with the help of an instrument with a handle and two prongs that vibrate at a set frequency, and assess the ability of a person to hear. Tips Do not report the diagnostic or treatment procedures like otoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy, removal of nonimpacted cerumen, or tuning fork test, separately if the provider reports them as evaluation and management services. However, 92507 is a special diagnostic test that is not included in an evaluation and management service. If the provider offers the service in a group, use code 92508, Treatment of speech, language, voice, communication, and or auditory processing disorder; group, two or more individuals. Speech–language pathology services are necessary for the diagnosis and treatment of speech–language disorders that result in communication disabilities. 92507 is not a time–based code. Therefore, it is incorrect to bill multiple units on the same day, regardless of the time spent with the patient. Local Medicare carriers specify varying guidelines, but many require that ongoing speech therapy services be provided by a speech–language pathologist (SLP). Read Less

short_description: Nasal function studies (eg, rhinomanometry)
lay_term: The provider uses this diagnostic test to evaluate the respiratory function of the nose by measuring the airflow during inhalation and exhalation as well as the air pressure in the nose. Explanation The provider assesses airflow and pressure using several different methods of rhinomanometry. One of the more common methods is anterior rhinomanometry that measures airflow separately in each of the nasal passages to diagnose an anatomical or mucosal abnormality. The service begins with the patient sitting upright. The provider has the patient blow her nose and then places a pressure sensing probe into one nostril. Next, the patient puts a facemask tightly over her face, and the mask is connected to a rhinomanometer. The provider takes measurements in each nostril; the patient inhales a nasal decongestant, and the measurements are repeated. A difference in resistance between the two measurements indicates to the provider there is nasal mucosal congestion. If there is not a considerable improvement after inhalation of the decongestant, it indicates to the provider that an obstruction is more likely. Terminology Rhinomanometer: A device used to measure the air pressure in the nose. Rhinomanometry: Diagnostic test to access and measure nasal airflow and pressures. lay_term: A caloric vestibular test refers to a qualitative test that involves sequentially irrigating both ears with warm and cold water while evaluating the patient’s eye movements. This helps measure the disturbance in the patient’s vestibular system and assesses the function of the nerves involved in hearing. Explanation In this study, using electronystagmography electrodes placed around the patient’s eyes or infrared videonystagmography goggles, technologies which record eye movements and help to diagnose balance or vestibular disorders, the provider flushes the patient’s ears sequentially with warm and cold water. This irrigation creates nystagmus, regular, repetitive, and involuntary rhythmic horizontal, vertical, and/or rotary eye movements. The provider observes the patient for any differences in reaction during the left and right ear irrigations and records the findings. The provider sometimes refers to the test as vestibular caloric stimulation. Terminology Bithermal: Dual temperature. Electronystagmography, or ENG: Test to record movement of eye; can also be used to test the patient’s vestibular functions, which manages the balance of the body. Infrared: Invisible form of light with wavelength beyond the visible range. Monothermal: Single temperature. Vestibular system: The sensory system of the body that contributes to movement and provides a sense of balance. Videonystagmography, or VNG: Test to record the functioning of the inner ear; can be used to determine the cause of a patient’s dizziness and balance disorder. Tips For monothermal irrigation, i.e., one irrigation in each ear, use code 92538, Caloric vestibular test with recording, bilateral; monothermal (i.e., one irrigation in each ear for a total of two irrigations). short_description: Sinusoidal vertical axis rotational testing Notes: (Do not report 92546 in conjunction with 92270)
lay_term: The provider measures various parameters of normal and pathological vestibular systems and also estimates the patient's visual acuity by checking the visual–vestibular interaction using sinusoidal vertical–axis rotation testing. Explanation The patient is prepared for the test by placement of electronystagmography (ENG) electrodes which are placed over the skin at eye level; one additional electrode is placed at the forehead level. The patient is then asked to sit in a rotational chair, and the electrodes are connected to a computer for analysis of the nystagmus. The test is usually performed in complete darkness with the chair placed in a lightproof chamber. The patient is asked to keep his eyes open and the head is held by a head restraint device. The chair is rotated in a specific direction, and it is controlled by a computer program. Frequently, the head restraint device tilts the patient's head forward at 30, thus placing the horizontal labyrinth canals inside the inner ear perpendicular to the plane of gravity. short_description: Computerized dynamic posturography sensory organization test (CDP-SOT), 6 conditions (ie, eyes open, eyes closed, visual sway, platform sway, eyes closed platform sway, platform and visual sway), including interpretation and report
lay_term: The provider performs computerized dynamic posturography sensory organization testing to evaluate the patient's motor, sensory, and integrative processes used to maintain balance and stability. The test is carried out using 6 specific conditions specified in the descriptor. This code represents both the technical and professional components of the service. Explanation This code represents the technical and professional components of a service in which the provider evaluates the patient’s posture and balance under various conditions. The patient stands on a support platform that can tilt up and back and rotate. The provider assesses the patient’s balance with tests involving elements such as the sense of touch in the lower extremities, vision, and the vestibular system of the inner ear and brain. To collect the data, the provider asks the patient to stand on a platform with force plates surrounded by a visual field. The patient wears a harness so that he does not fall. The provider begins the automated test, which often starts by altering the angle of the platform on which the patient is standing and shifting the visual field. The provider monitors visual and vestibular information relevant to postural control. The stages of the tests vary but must include testing with the patient’s eyes open and closed on a fixed platform, shifting of the visual field (visual sway), moving the platform (platform sway), platform sway with eyes closed, and combined visual and platform sway. Each stage is conducted for 30 seconds. The provider records these changes using electromyography. The provider reviews any unusual or inconsistent findings before completion of the study so that he can repeat testing fully or in part as needed. The provider interprets the findings and prepares a report. Terminology Electromyography: A procedure to evaluate the health of muscles and the nerves that control them by placing electrodes at strategic points to transmit or detect electrical signals; a needle EMG involves inserting a needle electrode into a muscle to evaluate the electrical signals in that muscle. Electronystagmography device (ENG): A medical instrument a provider uses to evaluate the movement of the eyes to rule out any neurological disorder, meaning disorders of the nervous system including the brain, the spinal cord, and the nerves. Proprioception: Perception of position and movement of parts of the body. Vestibular evaluation: A number of tests that help determine if there is something wrong with the vestibular (balance) portion of the inner ear. Vestibular–evoked myogenic potentials (VEMP): Balance testing based on how certain muscles in the neck (cVEMP) or eyes (oVEMP) respond to high–level acoustic stimulation in the inner ear. Vestibular ocular reflex (VOR) test: A test to determine whether an individual's visual acuity adjusts normally or fails to adjust to movement of the head and body; testing methods include patient–initiated side–to–side or rotational head movement, technician–controlled similar head movements, patient placed in a rotating chair, or devices attached to the head to move the head; electrodes attached to eye muscles detect oculomyographic responses. Tips To report the same procedure with the addition of motor control test (MCT) and adaptation test (ADT), see 92549. If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Vestibular evoked myogenic potential (VEMP) testing, with interpretation and report; cervical (cVEMP) Notes: (Do not report 92517 in conjunction with 92270, 92518, 92519)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider measures the patient’s response to high–level acoustic stimuli (sound) using electrodes placed on the neck (cervical region). The service includes interpretation and report. VEMP testing checks how muscles respond when sound reaches the inner ear as part of evaluating diseases of the ear and vestibular system. Explanation Cervical vestibular evoked myogenic potential (cVEMP) testing is a neurophysiologic diagnostic test that determines function of the otolith (inner ear structure that senses gravity and straight–line acceleration) and vestibular nerve (which provides balance information). The provider places surface electrodes on the sternocleidomastoid muscles (SCM), which turn and nod the neck, to detect sound evoked potentials. In an example test, the VEMPs may be recorded using an evoked response computer and a sound generator. The provider may instruct the patient to lie down and turn or lift the head up to contract the muscles. Then loud sound from an inserted earphone stimulates the saccule (a small sac in the inner ear), which in turn activates the inferior vestibular nerves. The provider then monitors the recordings, interprets them, and reports the response. The tests help in evaluation of suspected auditory and balance or dizziness disorders. Terminology Evoked potentials: Electrical signals generated by the nervous system in response to external physiological or electrical stimuli; also known as evoked response, sensory–evoked potentials, or stimulus–evoked response. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: A neck muscle that helps turn and bend the neck, so named because it originates at the top of the sternum and the clavicle (cleido–) and has its insertion at the mastoid process of the temporal bone of the skull. Tips Report 92518 for ocular VEMP (oVEMP) with interpretation and report. Report 92519 for both cervical VEMP (cVEMP) and ocular VEMP (oVEMP) with interpretation and report. Read Less

short_description: Tympanometry and reflex threshold measurements Notes: (Do not report 92550 in conjunction with 92567, 92568)
lay_term: The provider uses this global service code, which bundles tympanometry and reflex threshold measurement when the provider performs both tests to evaluate the middle ear and inner ear, respectively, for various ear diseases. Explanation The provider uses tympanometry to determine problems in the middle ear by creating variations of air pressure in the ear canal. The provider performs tympanometry by presenting a tone into the ear canal by placing a probe into the canal. The probe changes the pressure in the ear, generates the tones, and then measures the sound that reflects back. The provider also performs a reflex threshold measurement known as an acoustic reflex test (ART). ART measures the contraction of the stapedius muscle in response to a loud sound. In this service, the provider places an earphone on one ear and the probe on the other and then switches them to test the other ear. The provider obtains a total of four test conditions and the reflex measurements of each ear at different levels of frequencies. Terminology Reflex threshold measurements: A test to evaluate the inner ear, which helps diagnose the type and degree of hearing loss. Stapedius muscle: The muscle that transmits vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear. Tympanometry: A test to evaluate the middle ear and the condition of the eardrum (tympanic membrane) to assess for fluid, determine disease, or measure function of the middle ear.
