short_description: Pure tone audiometry (threshold); air and bone
lay_term: The provider presents the patient with a series of tones at varying intensities to identify the softest level at which the patient can hear to access hearing and determine the type and amount of hearing loss. He also places a vibrating device over the mastoid bone behind the patient's ear and tests the patient's bone conduction. Explanation The provider uses this test to measure a patient’s hearing sensitivity. The service begins with the patient seated and wearing headphones or inserted earbuds. The patient may also be in a soundproof booth with speakers. The provider delivers tones of different intensity, and the patient responds to the sounds or tones he hears. For the bone conduction part of the study, the provider uses a headband on the forehead or a vibration device placed over the mastoid bone behind the patient’s ears to conduct sound through the bones of the skull. The patient senses the tones as vibrations through the bones to the inner ear. short_description: Speech audiometry threshold; with speech recognition
lay_term: The provider measures a patient’s ability to recognize familiar words and repeat them to diagnose hearing disorders. Explanation The provider measures the minimum hearing level for which a patient can recognize and correctly repeat fifty percent of familiar disyllable, or two–syllable, words. The lowest level the patient was able to repeat fifty present of the time is the patient’s speech reception threshold or SRT. Then the provider assesses how well the patient understands words by asking the patient to again repeat the words he hears. This time, the provider gives one–syllable words that we use in ordinary conversation to the patient who is listening with headphones. The words are given at a level louder than the SRT so the patient typically has no problem hearing the words, and the patient repeats the words he hears. The provider measures the patient’s clarity or ability to understand speech. Depending on the percentage of words the patient is able to successfully identify, the provider may determine that the patient could benefit from a hearing aid in the affected ear. short_description: Comprehensive audiometry threshold evaluation and speech recognition (92553 and 92556 combined) Notes: (For hearing aid evaluation and selection, see 92590-92595) (For automated audiometry, see 0208T-0212T)
lay_term: The provider assesses a patient’s hearing with a series of tones at varying intensities to identify the softest level at which the patient can hear. He also measures the patient’s ability to recognize familiar words and repeat them. Explanation The provider places the patient in a soundproof booth with speakers or fits him with headphones. He presents the patient with a series of tones at varying levels of intensity. He places a headband on the forehead or against the bone behind the patient’s ears and conducts sound through the bones of the skull, which the patient senses as vibrations through the bones to the inner ear. The provider identifies the response of the patient to different sounds and establishes the softest level at which the patient can hear. The provider then conducts a speech audiometry test where the patient repeats the words heard while wearing headphones, beginning with sounds of low intensity to determine the speech reception threshold, which is the lowest level of sound easily understood and repeated by the patient. short_description: Stenger test, pure tone
lay_term: The provider delivers two tones of the same frequency simultaneously to both ears to detect if a patient has unilateral hearing loss or has a pseudohypacusis condition. Explanation The provider administers this functional hearing test delivering two tones of the same frequency simultaneously to both ears then increasing the intensity level of the deficient ear and gauging the patient’s response. In this service, the provider first determines the hearing threshold of both ears. The provider then gives the tone to both ears at a level over the threshold in the good ear and below the level of the good ear, in the suspected deficient ear. The provider continues the test by increasing the intensity level of the suspected deficient ear. If the patient keeps responding to the signal, the hearing loss is genuine, as he is responding to the tone being heard in the better ear. If the patient stops responding when the level of the suspected ear exceeds the signal in the good ear, the patient is faking the hearing loss. The provider knows this because when the same type of sound is given simultaneously to both ears, the patient only perceives the louder of the two similar tones. The patient does not respond because he thinks this is the correct reaction to the louder sound he hears in the supposedly bad ear. The patient may be simulating the hearing loss due to a psychogenic or malingering condition. Terminology Malingering hearing loss: A simulated hearing loss where the patient is deliberately pretending to be deaf. Pseudohypacusis: Fabricating or exaggerating the symptoms of a hearing loss; patient’s hearing loss is not consistent with a clinical or audiological evaluation. Psychogenic hearing loss: A hearing loss that is due to a mental or emotional disorder or trauma and has no evidence of a cause or insufficient evidence to explain it. Tips This service includes testing of both ears. Use modifier 52, reduced services, if a test is applied to one ear instead of both. Read Less

short_description: Acoustic immittance testing, includes tympanometry (impedance testing), acoustic reflex threshold testing, and acoustic reflex decay testing Notes: (Do not report 92570 in conjunction with 92567, 92568)
lay_term: The provider uses this global service code which bundles a tympanometry, reflex threshold measurement, and reflex decay testing when the provider performs all three tests. This group of services measures the functional integrity of the eardrum and middle ear anatomy and helps identify what part of the ear may be the cause of hearing loss. Explanation Acoustic immittance testing evaluates a number of elements of the ear functionality, including the eardrum, and the middle ear space behind it, as well as a muscle reflex that involves the eardrum, middle and inner ear, auditory nerve, auditory brainstem pathways, and the facial nerve. In this service, the provider performs tympanometry by presenting a probe tone into the ear canal and measuring the immittance as a function of change in atmospheric pressure in the ear canal. The provider also performs a reflex threshold measurement, known as an acoustic reflex test, or ART. In this service, the provider places an earphone on one ear and the probe on the other and then switches them to test the other ear. The provider obtains a total of four test conditions and the reflex measurements of each ear at different levels of frequencies. The last test in the group that the provider performs is the reflex decay testing, also known as acoustic reflex adaptation. He delivers one or two longer louder tones of approximately 10 seconds each to each ear to determine if the muscle reflex contraction is maintained or weakens. Terminology Immittance: The ease and speed in which sound travels from one material to another, as in evaluation of middle ear function. Tympanometry: A test to evaluate the middle ear and the condition of the ear drum, or tympanic membrane, to assess for fluid, determine disease, or measure function of the middle ear. Reflex decay testing: A test to measure whether the middle ear reflex contraction is maintained or weakens with constant acoustic stimulation. Reflex threshold measurements: A test to evaluate the inner ear which helps diagnose the type and degree of hearing loss. Tips If the provider performs three out of four tests, you should report 92570 with modifier 52, reduced services. If your audiologist performs only one of the tests in the global service, do not use the global code with modifier 52. Use the individual codes representing each test. Read Less

short_description: Filtered speech test
lay_term: The provider tests a patient’s hearing using distorted words to assess the patient’s ability to understand and repeat words. This test helps diagnose a variety of auditory processing disorders, or APDs. Explanation The provider uses this service to test if a patient can identify a word after hearing only a part of the word. An individual with normal hearing can recognize speech even when parts of the signal are missing, but a patient with an APD is often unable to distinguish the words. In this service, the patient sits while wearing earphones, and the provider instructs the patient to repeat the words she hears. The provider then delivers single syllable words through a filter that distorts them, first to one ear then to the other and asks the patient to repeat the distorted words. Terminology Auditory processing disorders, or APDs: A variety of disorders that affect the way the brain processes sounds, especially speech, also known as central auditory processing disorder, or CAPD. Tips This service includes testing of both ears. Use modifier 52, reduced services, if a test is applied to one ear instead of both. Read Less

short_description: Staggered spondaic word test
lay_term: The provider performs this dichotic test, where the patient receives different information in each ear in an overlapping manner, to access central auditory processing. Explanation The provider uses this test to evaluate the patient’s ability to separate and interpret competing speech, which the provider presents to both a patient’s ears in an overlapping manner. In this service, the patient sits while wearing earphones. The provider instructs the patient to repeat the words heard in the same order he hears them. The provider then delivers two syllable words, in two–word pairs, with a partial overlapping of the words. This means the provider gives the first syllable of the first word in one ear and the last syllable of the word in the same ear, but simultaneously delivers the first syllable of the second word in the other ear. The second syllable of the second word follows in that same ear, but the provider delivers it alone without overlap. The patient responds after each pair of disyllable, or two syllable, words, and the provider scores the response for each ear. Terminology Auditory processing disorders or APDs: A variety of disorders that affect the way the brain processes sounds, especially speech; also known as central auditory processing disorder or CAPD. Dichotic: Stimulating each ear simultaneously with different sounds. Spondaic: Relating to spondee words which are disyllabic words, or words with two syllables, that are pronounced with equal emphasis on both syllables. Tips This service includes testing of both ears. Use modifier 52, reduced services, if a test is applied to one ear instead of both. Read Less

short_description: Sensorineural acuity level test
lay_term: The provider performs this service as an alternative to conventional bone conduction testing for patients with hearing impairments. Explanation The provider uses this indirect method of testing bone conduction hearing thresholds for a patient to determine the amount of sensorineural loss. In this service, the provider tests the patient’s air conduction hearing threshold two times. The first time, the provider does a standard tonal or speech pure tone air conduction procedure. The patient sits in a quiet environment while wearing earphones. The provider delivers tones or speech of different intensity, and the patient responds to the words or tones he hears. The second time, he conducts the test with a background masking noise the patient receives from a bone vibrator placed on the forehead. The provider then compares the results of the two tests with established normal values to determine the amount of sensorineural loss. Terminology Bone conduction testing: Hearing test using a headband on the forehead or on the mastoid bone behind the patient’s ears to conduct sound through the bones of the skull to test the cochlea, or inner ear. Pure tone air conduction testing: Hearing test using headphones to determine the faintest tones a person can hear at selected frequencies or pitches. Sensorineural: Relates to the effect of the sensory nerves on hearing. Tips This service includes testing of both ears. short_description: Stenger test, speech
lay_term: The provider delivers words of the same frequency simultaneously to both ears to detect if a patient has unilateral hearing loss or has a pseudohypacusis condition. Explanation The provider administers this functional hearing test delivering words of the same frequency simultaneously to both ears then increasing the intensity level of the worse ear and gauging the patient’s response. In this service, the patient wears earphones, and the provider first determines the hearing threshold of both ears. The provider then gives the speech to both ears at a level over the threshold in the good ear and below the level of the good ear in the suspected deficient ear. The provider continues the test by increasing the intensity level of the suspected deficient ear. If the patient keeps responding to the signal, the hearing loss is genuine, as he is responding to the words being heard in the better ear. If the patient stops responding when the level of the suspected deficient ear exceeds the signal in the good ear, the patient is simulating the hearing loss. The provider knows this because when the same type of sound is given simultaneously to both ears, the patient only perceives the louder of the two similar tones. The patient does not respond because he thinks this is the correct reaction to the louder sound he hears in the allegedly bad ear. The patient may be simulating the hearing loss due to a psychogenic or malingering condition. Terminology Malingering hearing loss: A simulated hearing loss where the patient is deliberately pretending to be deaf. Pseudohypacusis: Fabricating or exaggerating the symptoms of a hearing loss; the patient’s hearing loss is not consistent with a clinical or audiological evaluation. Psychogenic hearing loss: A hearing loss that is due to a mental or emotional disorder or trauma and has no evidence of a cause or insufficient evidence to explain it. short_description: Auditory evoked potentials; screening of auditory potential with broadband stimuli, automated analysis
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider measures the patient’s response to sound stimuli to screen auditory potential (electrical response). The screening uses frequency nonspecific stimuli and automated analysis. Explanation The provider places electrodes behind the patient’s ears and on his forehead. Earphones are placed over the patient’s ears. One or more sounds are presented through the earphones, and a computer attached to the electrodes records the electrical responses (auditory evoked potentials) to the auditory stimuli. The test uses broadband stimuli, which may include clicks, chirps, or other noises. The results (pass or fail) are generated through automated analysis that requires minimal human assistance. Terminology Evoked potentials: Electrical signals generated by the nervous system in response to external physiological or electrical stimuli; also known as evoked response, sensory–evoked potentials, or stimulus–evoked response. Tips This code is for automated analysis, which gives a pass or fail result and may be performed in the office of a primary care provider. Patients with a fail result may then be referred to an otolaryngology specialist for further evaluation. CPT® provides multiple codes for auditory evoked potentials in the range 92650–92653. short_description: Distortion product evoked otoacoustic emissions; limited evaluation (to confirm the presence or absence of hearing disorder, 3-6 frequencies) or transient evoked otoacoustic emissions, with interpretation and report
lay_term: Code 92587 is in the Medicine/Special Otorhinolaryngologic Services Section. It involves special procedures of the ears/nose/throat. This code is for screening purposes with interpretation and report. An OAE is a simple, noninvasive, test for hearing defects in newborn babies and young children. The healthy cochlea does not just receive sound; it also produces low–intensity sounds called OAEs. These sounds are produced specifically by the cochlea hair cells as they expand and contract. Explanation The provider has a computer with an ear probe tip. She places the ear probe tip into the patient's ear canal. For the distortion product otoacoustic emission test, the probe emits pairs of tones at specific frequencies, typically three to six frequency levels. For the transient evoked otoacoustic emissions test, the probe emits broad frequency range clicks or brief bursts of pure tone. The sound passes through the tympanic membrane, the middle ear and the inner ear. At the inner ear, the sound is picked up by the hair cells of the cochlea. The computer records the echo off the cochlea hair cells. When the test is complete, the provider interprets the findings and prepares a report. The provider performs the test to assess the presence or absence of a hearing disorder. Tips Before you file another claim for 92587, check that the tests meet this criterion: an audiologist or other qualified healthcare provider administers them. Reporting these codes would be inappropriate if they are performed by a computer instead of a healthcare professional. New technology opened the door to potential misuse of 92587. This code's descriptors and valuations do not take into account automated administration of these tests. Using the traditional codes for automated tests overcompensates you by paying you for non–performed work. Computer–administered tests do not rely on the administration and oversight of a professional to determine the outcome. After the patient has the earphones placed and some introductory instructions, these tests can be self–administered. The computer administers each test, automatically determines the accuracy of the outcome, scores the results where scoring is necessary, and prints the results in a written output. Read Less

short_description: Distortion product evoked otoacoustic emissions; comprehensive diagnostic evaluation (quantitative analysis of outer hair cell function by cochlear mapping, minimum of 12 frequencies), with interpretation and report Notes: (For central auditory function evaluation, see 92620, 92621)
lay_term: The provider performs this noninvasive, diagnostic test to help detect inner ear abnormalities to identify such conditions as functional hearing loss or differentiate between sensory and neural hearing impairment. Explanation The provider uses a computer with an ear probe tip. She places the ear probe tip into the patient's ear canal. This probe emits either a distortion product which are two closely spaced, simultaneous, pure tone frequencies, given at a moderate intensity level or a transient sound, which are very brief noises, such as clicks or tone bursts. The sound passes through the tympanic membrane, the middle ear, and the inner ear. The inner ear then picks up the sound in the hair cells of the cochlea, and the computer records the echo off the cochlear hair cells, a technique called quantitative analysis of outer hair cell function by cochlear mapping. The provider repeats the test at different intensity levels and for at least twelve ranges of frequencies, and the computer records the results. The provider then compares the results to normative data, interprets results, and prepares a report. The provider performs the test to assess the presence or absence of a hearing disorder. Terminology Cochlea: Part of the inner ear that contains the microscopic nerve endings that relay sound to the brain, the organ of hearing. Cochlear mapping: Process where adjustments are made to a cochlear implant to optimize how sounds are heard. Functional hearing loss: A hearing loss that is due to a mental or emotional disorder or trauma and has no evidence of a cause or insufficient evidence to explain it; also known as psychogenic hearing loss. Neural hearing impairment: Hearing loss involving the hearing nerve. Normative data: Benchmark or baseline data that depict what is usual. Otoacoustic emissions or OAEs: Low–intensity sounds emerging from the ear, which reflect movement of the outer hair cells in the cochlea and that can be measured in the external ear canal. Pure tone frequency: Basic single frequency sound; a sine wave. Sensory hearing impairment: Hearing loss involving the inner ear. Tympanic membrane: Thin membrane that separates the middle ear from the external ear; eardrum. Tips This service includes testing of both ears. Use modifier 52, reduced services, if a test is applied to one ear instead of both. Read Less

short_description: Electroacoustic evaluation for hearing aid; monaural
lay_term: This code is for evaluating one hearing aid; monaural means one ear. The provider checks the hearing aid whenever the wearer has a problem with the hearing aid or else it can also be a routine check. The provider does electroacoustic evaluation of the hearing aid, which is more accurate than a normal hearing aid check. Explanation To see how well the patient’s hearing aid compares to its original specifications, the provider uses an electroacoustic analyzer. An electroacoustic analyzer has a multi–channel signal analyzer, which gives accurate measurements and allows for recording and storage of data. The analyzer provides information on various specifications, including gain and output characteristics, such as the difference between the input signal and hearing aid’s output; frequency response characteristics, such as determining the hearing aid’s frequency range; input noise, such as the amount of noise from the aid’s electronic current; and various other specifications. Tips Use 92595 for evaluating hearing aids of both ears. Audiologists often provide these services. Check payer policy to see if you should report HCPCS V codes for hearing aid services. Read Less

short_description: Ear protector attenuation measurements
lay_term: With the patient wearing ear protectors, such as plugs or protective ear muffs, the provider checks a patient’s ability to hear tones at various levels using a number of possible methods. This code represents the technical component of the service only. Explanation This code represents the technical component of a service in which the provider uses various testing methods to measure hearing sensitivity. The test may include subjective approaches or objective approaches depending upon whether the person responds directly, or an instrument is used to gauge the patient’s reaction to test tones. These tests help determine the effectiveness of the hearing protection device, or HPD, being tested. When the provider uses the REAT, or real–ear attenuation at threshold, method, for example, he performs a standard pure–tone assessment in a quiet test environment, typically a soundproof booth or a sound–field, with and without the HPD. The provider performs the test to determine the insertion loss or the difference between the sound levels before and after the HPD and/or the noise reduction capabilities of the ear protectors. The provider follows a basic procedure that involves familiarizing the patient with the test signal, to assure the provider that the participant understands and can perform the response task, and then taking threshold measurements. Regardless of the method used the provider records the results on a chart or form, reporting the data values in either decibels or percent of noise level exposure, documenting both loudness and time exposed during the test. Terminology Attenuation: The reduction of the strength of a sound signal. Objective test: Hearing test in which an instrument reading is used to gauge the patient’s reaction. Sound fields or free–field: Hearing test that uses speakers to transmit sound signals to infants, toddlers, and others with special needs; the test uses different techniques such as games or toys that light and animate when the patient responds to sound to help provider’s measure responses. Subjective test: Hearing test that requires the patient to hear, listen, and actively respond to test tones. Tips Code 92596 represents the technical component of the service only, so you should not append modifier 26 or TC. Read Less

short_description: Diagnostic analysis of cochlear implant, patient younger than 7 years of age; with programming
lay_term: The provider analyzes a cochlear implant previously placed in a patient younger than 7 years of age. The provider does all programming required to make the implant work properly and also counsels the patient and family on how to take proper care of the device. Explanation The provider starts by placing a transmitter magnet opposite the cochlear implant’s receiver, which is under the patient’s skin. The patient is under the age of 7. The provider makes sure the patient is comfortable and confirms the magnet isn’t preventing blood flow or causing problems at the implant site. He then connects the transmitter, microphone, and cable to the external speech processor. He places the speech processor under computer control for programming. The provider ensures that the stimulator system is working properly and that all electrodes in the cochlea are properly positioned. The provider adjusts the implant settings, such as the volume and the stimulator according the patient’s specific needs. The provider activates the electrodes in succession, while continuing to assess the patient’s comfort level. He counsels the family on how to use the external speech processor controls, position the microphone and transmitter, insert the batteries, and recharge the system. He also instructs them to keep a daily record of the patient’s experiences with the implant for the provider to review and take into account during future reprogramming. The provider compiles and records the data. Terminology Cochlear implant: An electronic device placed in individuals with hearing problems or for people who cannot hear at all; the device has internal components under the skin and in the ear, and external components on the scalp and behind the ear, as well as a speech processor. Tips Code 92601 is for initial programming of a single implant on a patient younger than 7. See 92602 for subsequent testing on a patient younger than 7. See 92603–92604 for patients 7 and older. short_description: Evaluation of oral and pharyngeal swallowing function Notes: (For motion fluoroscopic evaluation of swallowing function, use 92611) (For flexible endoscopic examination, use 92612-92617)
lay_term: Code 92610 is in the Medicine/Special Otorhinolaryngologic Services Section. It involves special procedures of the ears/nose/throat. Diagnostic/treatment services not generally included in a comprehensive otorhinolaryngologic evaluation or office visit. Explanation In this procedure, a patient's oral and pharyngeal swallowing function is examined usually by a speech–language pathologist (SLP). Evaluation of the oral and pharyngeal swallowing function is a clinical, experimental procedure through which the SLP assesses a patient's capability to chew food, form a bolus, and swallow different types of food and liquids. The physician also evaluates oral motor skills, laryngeal function, reflexes, and wide range of communication problems resulting from damage to the regions of the brain. The physician evaluates tongue tip elevation and movement of the anteroposterior tongue as well as smile/lip pucker/cockle. First the patient presents with a breathy vocal quality and could not initiate the pitch change. The patient is oriented and is helped to understand by slowing rate of speech and using short phrases. The patient can swallow after several seconds but is incapable to trigger a volitional swallow of saliva immediately when asked. The patient might be presented with a variety of foods/textures to determine the oral phase of the swallow and to determine if there are any signs of pharyngeal dysphagia. The SLP evaluates laryngeal elevation, delayed initiation of volitional swallow, choking, and questionable pharyngeal residue. Once patient's oral and pharyngeal swallowing function evaluation is successfully accomplished, the physician can recommend continuation for a nasogastric (NG) tube for nutrition, hydration, and medications, and advices maintaining NPO status. Terminology Auditory: Pertaining to the sense of hearing or to the organs of hearing Dysphagia: Difficulty in swallowing ENT: The medical and surgical specialty diagnosing and treating disorders of the ears; nose and sinuses; throat; and larynx with related regions of the face and neck, tracheobronchial tree, and esophagus. SLPs: Speech–Language Pathologists, also known as speech therapists, who specializes in speech and language (communication) and swallowing disorders. Tips CMS considers 92610 a component of the more comprehensive code, 92611, so you would need to append modifier 59 (Distinct procedural service) to 92610 on the claim form to have both reimbursed when provided on the same day. Also, your documentation would have to support the medical necessity of both services and that your SLP provided them at separate and distinct times. Read Less

short_description: Motion fluoroscopic evaluation of swallowing function by cine or video recording Notes: (For radiological supervision and interpretation, use 74230) (For evaluation of oral and pharyngeal swallowing function, use 92610) (For flexible diagnostic laryngoscopy, use 31575)
lay_term: The provider conducts a study on the inside of the mouth, the voice box, and the food pipe using cine or video recording. He checks whether the patient can swallow properly. Explanation The testing provider conducts an interview of the patient. He tries suitable techniques to evaluate the deficits he has identified in the way of the patient’s swallowing. He studies the oral cavity, larynx, pharynx, and the upper esophagus. Typically, a radiologic provider joins the testing provider and patient for a fluoroscopic evaluation. The testing provider administers edible substances of varying consistencies that include barium contrast to allow the provider to better visualize the anatomy under fluoroscopy as the patient swallows. Cine or video recording documents the test. The testing provider then checks bolus formation, transport, the time taken to swallow, and movement of the pharyngeal wall and the voice box. After all these evaluations, the testing provider reviews the results and makes a detailed report of the encounter. He then recommends various interventions like modifying the diet to assist with swallowing and postures to follow while eating. Terminology Bolus: A rounded mass, such as food during swallowing. Pharynx: Passage starting from the oral and nasal cavities and extending to the esophagus, which is the food pipe, and the larynx, which is the voice box. Tips Speech language pathologists are often the providers who perform 92611. A radiologic provider may perform fluoroscopy and other radiologic services with interpretation for this service. The radiologic provider should report 74230. Read Less

lay_term: The provider carries out testing of the inner lining of the larynx to evaluate the sensory and motor deficits in the laryngeal muscles. short_description: Evaluation of central auditory function, with report; initial 60 minutes
lay_term: The provider assesses central auditory function. He performs this test to detect the extent of the patient’s issues with processing what he hears and occasionally to identify a site of abnormality in the brain. This code represents the first or only hour of testing. Explanation The provider assesses the patient’s auditory mechanisms, such as being able to hear properly in a noisy environment, being able to act according to instructions, and learning new words. The provider selects a battery of tests after assessing the patient using a separately performed and reported routine hearing tests. The provider uses this battery of tests to detect the specific events and environmental factors that may make it difficult for the patient to process what he hears and occasionally to identify the site of abnormality in the brain. The provider performs either electrophysiological tests or behavioral tests. He performs electrophysiological tests to measure the brain's response to sounds. For instance, he may place a special cap with sensors on the head of the patient to measure the electrical activity when the patient hears something. During behavioral tests, the provider commonly performs speech tests by giving certain phrases to the patient and asking her to repeat those phrases. Then the provider assesses how clearly and spontaneously the patient is able to repeat the phrases. This code represents the first or only hour of testing. Terminology Central auditory functions: Auditory mechanism that enables the patient’s brain to respond to what he hears. Tips See +92621 to report each additional 15 minutes. Read Less

lay_term: The provider assesses tinnitus, which is a phantom hearing perception generated within the patient's head: ringing, roaring, static. Tinnitus is a symptom, not a disease. Explanation The provider tests the patient’s ears for tinnitus, which is an abnormal sound heard by the patient due to an ear anomaly. The provider tests two things: first is the intensity of the tinnitus and second is the pitch of the sound heard by the patient. The provider evaluates the pitch and intensity of tinnitus using sound generators. Providers often refer to intensity testing as loudness matching because the provider asks the patient to identify the loudness of the tinnitus based on the loudness of tones presented by the provider. Similarly, terms for the tests to determine the pitch include pitch matching and frequency matching because the patient identifies which external pitch best matches the tinnitus, phantom ringing, roaring, chirping, or static sound heard in the ears that is a symptom of various ear conditions. Tips Documentation in which the provider finds the sound's intensity and tries to locate where the patient's tinnitus resides in frequency terms can help to support the use of this code. This code represents testing on both ears, so if the provider tests only one ear, be sure to append modifier 52 to indicate the reduced service. Read Less

short_description: Evaluation of auditory function for surgically implanted device(s) candidacy or postoperative status of a surgically implanted device(s); first hour
lay_term: The provider tests the auditory functional status of the patient to include sound perception, listening ability, orienting movements, and balancing. The provider performs this evaluation to determine if the patient is a good candidate for a surgically implanted hearing device or to check the efficacy of a previously implanted hearing device. This code represents the first or only hour of evaluation. Explanation The provider checks the patient’s auditory function status. One area the provider checks is whether the patient has sound awareness, which is the ability to determine the presence or absence of sound. He also checks the patient’s ability to differentiate between varying sound types and sound intensities, like loud and soft voice, and high and low pitch sounds. The provider assesses the patient’s hearing ability in general as well as listening abilities in a noisy environment. After evaluation, the provider decides the efficacy of a previously implanted hearing device or whether the patient is a candidate for one. This code represents the first or only hour of evaluation. Terminology Tips For each additional 15 minutes in evaluating the patient after the first hour, report +92627 with 92626. Read Less

short_description: Auditory rehabilitation; prelingual hearing loss
lay_term: The provider conducts auditory training or therapy primarily for pediatric patients whose hearing impairment occurred during or shortly after birth before acquiring language and the ability to speak. Trauma, disease, or genetic reasons may be the cause of the hearing loss. Explanation In this therapy, the provider uses a variety of techniques to teach the patient, usually a child, how to hear. The patient has no prior experience with hearing and is learning to hear through the use of hearing aids or cochlear implants. The provider begins by teaching the identification and characteristics of two sounds. She progresses to more complex skills of learning to identify distinct speech sounds and eventually to discern and recognize speech. The techniques she uses are all intended for the patient to eventually be able to understand speech. Terminology Auditory rehabilitation: Any activity, method, resource, technology, and/or device that facilitates and/or enhances communication and participation in activities in patients with hearing loss. Cochlear implant: An implanted electronic hearing device that helps a profoundly deaf or severely hard of hearing person have a sense of sound by electrically stimulating nerves inside the inner ear. Perilingual hearing loss: A hearing impairment that occurs prior to the acquisition of speech and language. Read Less

short_description: Auditory rehabilitation; postlingual hearing loss
lay_term: The provider conducts auditory training or therapy for children or adults whose hearing impairment occurs after they already learned how to speak. Trauma, disease, or side effects from medicines may be the cause of the hearing loss. Explanation In this therapy, the provider uses a variety of techniques to teach the child or adult patient how to hear through the use of a hearing aid or a cochlear implant. A patient, especially a child, may not have had functional hearing for a period of time to achieve speech understanding and identification of sounds or his hearing may have progressively deteriorated. In either case, the provider may begin by teaching sound awareness and progress to speech recognition, then voice, speech production, and language therapy. The techniques she uses are all meant to help the patient obtain adequate receptive and expressive communication. Terminology Auditory rehabilitation: Any activity, method, resource, technology, or device that facilitates and or enhances communication and participation in activities in patients with hearing loss. Cochlear implant: An implanted electronic hearing device that helps a profoundly deaf or severely hard of hearing person have a sense of sound by electrically stimulating nerves inside the cochlea, or part of the inner ear. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Section Specific Guideline Codes 92920-92944 describe percutaneous revascularization services performed for occlusive disease of the coronary vessels (major coronary arteries, coronary artery branches, or coronary artery bypass grafts). These percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) codes are built on progressive hierarchies with more intensive services inclusive of lesser intensive services. These PCI codes all include the work of accessing and selectively catheterizing the vessel, traversing the lesion, radiological supervision and interpretation directly related to the intervention(s) performed, closure of the arteriotomy when performed through the access sheath, and imaging performed to document completion of the intervention in addition to the intervention(s) performed. These codes include angioplasty (eg, balloon, cutting balloon, wired balloons, cryoplasty), atherectomy (eg, directional, rotational, laser), and stenting (eg, balloon expandable, self-expanding, bare metal, drug eluting, covered). Each code in this family includes balloon angioplasty, when performed. Diagnostic coronary angiography may be reported separately under specific circumstances. Percutaneous transluminal coronary lithotripsy may be reported using 92972 in conjunction with 92920, 92924, 92928, 92933, 92937, 92941, 92943, 92975, as appropriate. Diagnostic coronary angiography codes (93454-93461) and injection procedure codes (93563-93564) should not be used with percutaneous coronary revascularization services (92920-92944) to report: 1.Contrast injections, angiography, roadmapping, and/or fluoroscopic guidance for the coronary intervention, 2.Vessel measurement for the coronary intervention, or 3.Post-coronary angioplasty/stent/atherectomy angiography, as this work is captured in the percutaneous coronary revascularization services codes (92920-92944). Diagnostic angiography performed at the time of a coronary interventional procedure may be separately reportable if: 1.No prior catheter-based coronary angiography study is available, and a full diagnostic study is performed, and a decision to intervene is based on the diagnostic angiography, or 2.A prior study is available, but as documented in the medical record: a.The patient’s condition with respect to the clinical indication has changed since the prior study, or b.There is inadequate visualization of the anatomy and/or pathology, or c.There is a clinical change during the procedure that requires new evaluation outside the target area of intervention. Diagnostic coronary angiography performed at a separate session from an interventional procedure is separately reportable. Major coronary arteries: The major coronary arteries are the left main, left anterior descending, left circumflex, right, and ramus intermedius arteries. All PCI procedures performed in all segments (proximal, mid, distal) of a single major coronary artery through the native coronary circulation are reported with one code. When one segment of a major coronary artery is treated through the native circulation and treatment of another segment of the same artery requires access through a coronary artery bypass graft, the intervention through the bypass graft is reported separately. Coronary artery branches: Up to two coronary artery branches of the left anterior descending (diagonals), left circumflex (marginals), and right (posterior descending, posterolaterals) coronary arteries are recognized. The left main and ramus intermedius coronary arteries do not have recognized branches for reporting purposes. All PCI(s) performed in any segment (proximal, mid, distal) of a coronary artery branch is reported with one code. PCI is reported for up to two branches of a major coronary artery. Additional PCI in a third branch of the same major coronary artery is not separately reportable. Coronary artery bypass grafts: Each coronary artery bypass graft represents a coronary vessel. A sequential bypass graft with more than one distal anastomosis represents only one graft. A branching bypass graft (eg, Y graft) represents a coronary vessel for the main graft, and each branch off the main graft constitutes an additional coronary vessel. PCI performed on major coronary arteries or coronary artery branches by access through a bypass graft is reported using the bypass graft PCI codes. All bypass graft PCI codes include the use of coronary artery embolic protection devices when performed. Only one base code from this family may be reported for revascularization of a major coronary artery and its recognized branches. Only one base code should be reported for revascularization of a coronary artery bypass graft, its subtended coronary artery, and recognized branches of the subtended coronary artery. If one segment of a major coronary artery and its recognized branches is treated through the native circulation, and treatment of another segment of the same vessel requires access through a coronary artery bypass graft, an additional base code is reported to describe the intervention performed through the bypass graft. The PCI base codes are 92920, 92924, 92928, 92933, 92937, 92941, and 92943. The PCI base code that includes the most intensive service provided for the target vessel should be reported. The hierarchy of these services is built on an intensity of service ranked from highest to lowest as 92943 = 92941 = 92933 > 92924 > 92937 = 92928 > 92920. PCI performed during the same session in additional recognized branches of the target vessel should be reported using the applicable add-on code(s). The add-on codes are 92921, 92925, 92929, 92934, 92938, and 92944 and follow the same principle in regard to reporting the most intensive service provided. The intensity of service is ranked from highest to lowest as 92944 = 92938 > 92934 > 92925 > 92929 > 92921. PCI performed during the same session in additional major coronary or in additional coronary artery bypass grafts should be reported using the applicable additional base code(s). PCI performed during the same session in additional coronary artery branches should be reported using the applicable additional add-on code(s). If a single lesion extends from one target vessel (major coronary artery, coronary artery bypass graft, or coronary artery branch) into another target vessel, but can be revascularized with a single intervention bridging the two vessels, this PCI should be reported with a single code despite treating more than one vessel. For example, if a left main coronary lesion extends into the proximal left circumflex coronary artery and a single stent is placed to treat the entire lesion, this PCI should be reported as a single vessel stent (92928). In this example, a code for additional vessel treatment (92929) would not be additionally reported. When bifurcation lesions are treated, PCI is reported for both vessels treated. For example, when a bifurcation lesion involving the left anterior descending artery and the first diagonal artery is treated by stenting both vessels, 92928 and 92929 are both reported. Target vessel PCI for acute myocardial infarction is inclusive of all balloon angioplasty, atherectomy, stenting, manual aspiration thrombectomy, distal protection, and intracoronary rheolytic agent administration performed. Mechanical thrombectomy is reported separately. Chronic total occlusion of a coronary vessel is present when there is no antegrade flow through the true lumen, accompanied by suggestive angiographic and clinical criteria (eg, antegrade “bridging” collaterals present, calcification at the occlusion site, no current presentation with ST elevation or Q wave acute myocardial infarction attributable to the occluded target lesion). Current presentation with ST elevation or Q wave acute myocardial infarction attributable to the occluded target lesion, subtotal occlusion, and occlusion with dye staining at the site consistent with fresh thrombus are not considered chronic total occlusion. Codes 92973 (percutaneous transluminal coronary thrombectomy, mechanical), 92974 (coronary brachytherapy), 92978 and 92979 (intravascular ultrasound/optical coherence tomography), 93571 and 93572 (intravascular Doppler velocity and/or pressure [fractional flow reserve {FFR} or coronary flow reserve {CFR}]), and 92972 (percutaneous transluminal coronary lithotripsy), are add-on codes for reporting procedures performed in addition to coronary and bypass graft diagnostic and interventional services, unless included in the base code. Non-mechanical, aspiration thrombectomy is not reported with 92973, and is included in the PCI code for acute myocardial infarction (92941), when performed. (To report transcatheter placement of radiation delivery device for coronary intravascular brachytherapy, use 92974) (For intravascular radioelement application, see 77770, 77771, 77772) (For nonsurgical septal reduction therapy [eg, alcohol ablation], use 93799) (For percutaneous transcatheter therapeutic drug delivery by intracoronary drug-delivery balloon, see 0913T, 0914T)

short_description: Temporary transcutaneous pacing Notes: (For direction of ambulance or rescue personnel outside the hospital by a physician or other qualified health care professional, use 99288)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider stimulates the contraction of the heart by passing electrical impulses through the heart of the patient with arrhythmia. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized and laid in the supine position with the chest exposed, the provider attaches monitoring electrodes to the patient’s chest which connect to an electrocardiogram machine after noting down the baseline cardiac output rates. These baseline cardiac output rates illustrate the abnormality in the heart rate, which helps to analyze the intensity of electrical shock that the provider will deliver. He then turns on the pacemaker in the patient's chest using the electrocardiogram machine, which sends out electrical impulses through the chest into the heart and stabilizes the cardiac output rhythm. Terminology Cardiac output: Volume of the blood that leaves the heart in one minute, from the right and left ventricle. Electrocardiogram: Painless test to check and record electrical cardiac activity by placing sensors on the skin; abbreviated as ECG or EKG. Pacemaker: Device to regulate abnormal heart beat using electrical impulses. It is implanted into the patient’s chest. Supine: Lying in the face up position. Transcutaneous: Passing across the depth of the skin. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Read Less

lay_term: The provider inflates a balloon–tipped catheter in the blocked area of a pulmonary artery to treat stenosis. This code describes work on a single vessel of the pulmonary artery. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the right internal jugular vein or the right femoral vein and inserts a guidewire through it. He then inserts a balloon–tipped catheter over the guidewire and guides it into either the left or right pulmonary artery. The provider injects a dye and takes angiographic images to examine the blood flow and placement of the catheter into the artery. He advances the balloon–tipped catheter across the lesion in the pulmonary artery and inflates the balloon, which flattens the plaque against the artery wall. This widens the lumen and improves blood flow. The provider finally removes all the equipment, stops the bleeding, and closes the incisions. Terminology Angiography: Imaging of internal organs including blood vessels, arteries, veins, and heart chambers. Angioplasty: Procedure to treat narrowed coronary arteries due to the accumulation of plaque. Balloon catheter: A flexible tube with a balloon at the tip that can be inflated and deflated with a mechanism at the other end. Brachial artery: Blood vessel of the upper arm that runs from the shoulder down to the elbow. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Femoral vein: A large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Internal jugular vein: The blood vessel that drains blood from the neck, brain, and a part of the face to the heart. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Plaque: Yellowish deposits of cholesterol and other lipid material, or fat, in the lining, or intima, of the arteries. Pulmonary artery: The major artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff, affecting its ability to open and close properly. Transluminal: Passing across the lumen, which is the space inside a tubular structure, like an artery. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Tips This code refers to only a single vessel. If the documentation indicates that the provider addressed more than one vessel, you can report the add on code 92998 for each additional vessel treated. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inflates a balloon tipped catheter, or tube, inside a blocked area of a single artery or branch of an artery in the heart to widen a stenosis, or constricted area, that obstructs blood flow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision over the brachial or femoral artery, major arteries in the upper arm and upper leg respectively, and inserts a guide wire through it. He then inserts a guide catheter, or tube, over the guide wire, moving it through the vascular system until he can position the catheter at the opening to the coronary artery. The provider injects a dye and takes an X–ray to examine the blood flow and placement of catheter in the artery. He then advances a balloon tipped catheter to the lesion, or plaque, in the coronary artery and inflates the balloon to flatten the plaque against the artery wall. This restores blood flow in the artery. The provider then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty, or PTCA: Minimally invasive procedure, one that requires only a small incision in the skin, in which a blocked or narrowed artery in the heart is enlarged or cleared with the use of a small balloon attached to a catheter, or tube; inflation of the balloon compresses the blockage and enlarges the artery. Plaque: Yellowish deposits of cholesterol and other lipid material, or fat, in the lining, or intima, of the arteries. Vascular: Pertaining to blood vessels; supplied by blood vessels. He then inserts a guide catheter over the guide wire, moving it through the vascular system until he can position the catheter at the opening to the coronary artery. The provider injects a dye and takes fluoroscopic images to examine the blood flow and placement of catheter into the artery. Then he advances a catheter with a burr or other blade into the coronary vessel to destroy the material blocking the artery. At the same session, he also inserts balloon tipped catheter into the stenosed area and inflates the balloon that flattens the plaque against the artery wall. This removes the plaque that blocks the passage of blood. The provider may also perform an angioplasty, which is where he widens a vessel to open it. The provider finally removes all the equipment, achieves hemostasis, and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Angioplasty: Procedure to treat narrowed blood vessels by unblocking them using a catheter to insert and inflate a balloon within the artery. Atherectomy: Removal of plaque from the lining, or intima, of an artery; also endarterectomy. Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Balloon catheter: A flexible tube with a balloon at the tip that can be inflated and deflated with a mechanism at the other end. Brachial artery: Blood vessel of the upper arm that runs from the shoulder down to the elbow. Burr: Surgical drill. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Coronary arteries:Vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle, such as the right or left coronary artery, left anterior descending, posterior descending, and circumflex. Femoral artery: Large artery in the thigh that supplies oxygen rich blood to the legs. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and other items such as stents. Hemostasis: Process that causes bleeding to cease, which involves a balance of coagulation and clot breakdown. Left coronary artery: One of the major arteries that supplies blood to the left ventricle and atrium of the heart. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Plaque: Yellowish deposits of cholesterol and other lipid material, that is, fat, in the lining, or intima, of the arteries. Right coronary artery: One of the major arteries that supplies blood to the right ventricle and atrium of the heart. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff affecting its ability to open and close properly. Transluminal: Passing across the lumen, which is the space inside a tubular structure, like an artery. Vascular: Pertaining to blood vessels; supplied by blood vessels. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Tips This code includes angioplasty, when performed. That means angioplasty is not required, but you should not report angioplasty separately when the provider performs it. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Section Specific Guideline Codes 92920-92944 describe percutaneous revascularization services performed for occlusive disease of the coronary vessels (major coronary arteries, coronary artery branches, or coronary artery bypass grafts). These percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) codes are built on progressive hierarchies with more intensive services inclusive of lesser intensive services. These PCI codes all include the work of accessing and selectively catheterizing the vessel, traversing the lesion, radiological supervision and interpretation directly related to the intervention(s) performed, closure of the arteriotomy when performed through the access sheath, and imaging performed to document completion of the intervention in addition to the intervention(s) performed. These codes include angioplasty (eg, balloon, cutting balloon, wired balloons, cryoplasty), atherectomy (eg, directional, rotational, laser), and stenting (eg, balloon expandable, self-expanding, bare metal, drug eluting, covered). Each code in this family includes balloon angioplasty, when performed. Diagnostic coronary angiography may be reported separately under specific circumstances. Percutaneous transluminal coronary lithotripsy may be reported using 92972 in conjunction with 92920, 92924, 92928, 92933, 92937, 92941, 92943, 92975, as appropriate. Diagnostic coronary angiography codes (93454-93461) and injection procedure codes (93563-93564) should not be used with percutaneous coronary revascularization services (92920-92944) to report: 1.Contrast injections, angiography, roadmapping, and/or fluoroscopic guidance for the coronary intervention, 2.Vessel measurement for the coronary intervention, or 3.Post-coronary angioplasty/stent/atherectomy angiography, as this work is captured in the percutaneous coronary revascularization services codes (92920-92944). Diagnostic angiography performed at the time of a coronary interventional procedure may be separately reportable if: 1.No prior catheter-based coronary angiography study is available, and a full diagnostic study is performed, and a decision to intervene is based on the diagnostic angiography, or 2.A prior study is available, but as documented in the medical record: a.The patient’s condition with respect to the clinical indication has changed since the prior study, or b.There is inadequate visualization of the anatomy and/or pathology, or c.There is a clinical change during the procedure that requires new evaluation outside the target area of intervention. Diagnostic coronary angiography performed at a separate session from an interventional procedure is separately reportable. Major coronary arteries: The major coronary arteries are the left main, left anterior descending, left circumflex, right, and ramus intermedius arteries. All PCI procedures performed in all segments (proximal, mid, distal) of a single major coronary artery through the native coronary circulation are reported with one code. When one segment of a major coronary artery is treated through the native circulation and treatment of another segment of the same artery requires access through a coronary artery bypass graft, the intervention through the bypass graft is reported separately. Coronary artery branches: Up to two coronary artery branches of the left anterior descending (diagonals), left circumflex (marginals), and right (posterior descending, posterolaterals) coronary arteries are recognized. The left main and ramus intermedius coronary arteries do not have recognized branches for reporting purposes. All PCI(s) performed in any segment (proximal, mid, distal) of a coronary artery branch is reported with one code. PCI is reported for up to two branches of a major coronary artery. Additional PCI in a third branch of the same major coronary artery is not separately reportable. Coronary artery bypass grafts: Each coronary artery bypass graft represents a coronary vessel. A sequential bypass graft with more than one distal anastomosis represents only one graft. A branching bypass graft (eg, Y graft) represents a coronary vessel for the main graft, and each branch off the main graft constitutes an additional coronary vessel. PCI performed on major coronary arteries or coronary artery branches by access through a bypass graft is reported using the bypass graft PCI codes. All bypass graft PCI codes include the use of coronary artery embolic protection devices when performed. Only one base code from this family may be reported for revascularization of a major coronary artery and its recognized branches. Only one base code should be reported for revascularization of a coronary artery bypass graft, its subtended coronary artery, and recognized branches of the subtended coronary artery. If one segment of a major coronary artery and its recognized branches is treated through the native circulation, and treatment of another segment of the same vessel requires access through a coronary artery bypass graft, an additional base code is reported to describe the intervention performed through the bypass graft. The PCI base codes are 92920, 92924, 92928, 92933, 92937, 92941, and 92943. The PCI base code that includes the most intensive service provided for the target vessel should be reported. The hierarchy of these services is built on an intensity of service ranked from highest to lowest as 92943 = 92941 = 92933 > 92924 > 92937 = 92928 > 92920. PCI performed during the same session in additional recognized branches of the target vessel should be reported using the applicable add-on code(s). The add-on codes are 92921, 92925, 92929, 92934, 92938, and 92944 and follow the same principle in regard to reporting the most intensive service provided. The intensity of service is ranked from highest to lowest as 92944 = 92938 > 92934 > 92925 > 92929 > 92921. PCI performed during the same session in additional major coronary or in additional coronary artery bypass grafts should be reported using the applicable additional base code(s). PCI performed during the same session in additional coronary artery branches should be reported using the applicable additional add-on code(s). If a single lesion extends from one target vessel (major coronary artery, coronary artery bypass graft, or coronary artery branch) into another target vessel, but can be revascularized with a single intervention bridging the two vessels, this PCI should be reported with a single code despite treating more than one vessel. For example, if a left main coronary lesion extends into the proximal left circumflex coronary artery and a single stent is placed to treat the entire lesion, this PCI should be reported as a single vessel stent (92928). In this example, a code for additional vessel treatment (92929) would not be additionally reported. When bifurcation lesions are treated, PCI is reported for both vessels treated. For example, when a bifurcation lesion involving the left anterior descending artery and the first diagonal artery is treated by stenting both vessels, 92928 and 92929 are both reported. Target vessel PCI for acute myocardial infarction is inclusive of all balloon angioplasty, atherectomy, stenting, manual aspiration thrombectomy, distal protection, and intracoronary rheolytic agent administration performed. He further inserts a balloon mounted catheter with a stent to the stenosed site. The balloon expands and fits the stent onto the wall of the artery. lay_term: In this procedure the provider makes an incision in the patient’s arm or leg to access the artery. lay_term: As an add–on procedure to another service, the provider performs lithotripsy, which breaks up calcifications, in a coronary (heart) vessel. The approach is percutaneous (through the skin). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and at the same encounter as a primary service, the provider performs percutaneous transluminal coronary lithotripsy. For this percutaneous approach, the provider uses a small opening (such as by needle or small incision) through the skin to access the vascular system. The provider then introduces a guidewire through the opening and uses this guidewire to introduce a specialized catheter and navigate it through the blood vessels to the target coronary (heart) vessel site. The provider performs transluminal coronary lithotripsy, a therapy that fractures a calcified lesion in a coronary vessel, increasing the luminal diameter. The lumen is the hollow space in the blood vessel. The lithotripsy device typically uses sonic (sound) waves introduced through a balloon–based catheter to break calcium deposits. When the lithotripsy procedure is complete, the provider withdraws the catheter system through the site of access and stops the bleeding at that location. Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Transluminal: Passing across or performed by way of the lumen (the interior, open area) of a blood vessel or organ. lay_term: At the same session as treatment of stenosis using any of the appropriate techniques, the provider performs brachytherapy to keep the blocked heart arteries open. In this procedure, the provider places radioactive seeds near the site of the arterial blockage to open up these blocked arteries. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the brachial or femoral artery and inserts a guide wire through it under ultrasound guidance. He then advances a catheter over the guide wire and delivers the radiation device into the site through the catheter. The radioactive seeds are left in place for an appropriate period of time to expose the artery to radiation. Later, the provider removes the radioactive seeds and continues treating the original site of stenosis using the appropriate technique. Terminology Brachial artery: Blood vessel of the upper arm that runs from the shoulder down to the elbow. Brachytherapy: Treatment for cancer in which the provider places a radiation source internally to be near the cancer site. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Femoral artery: Large artery in the thigh that supplies oxygen rich blood to the legs. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and stent. Radioactive seeds: Small seeds about the size of grains that emit radiation into surrounding tissues to destroy cancer cells. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff, affecting its ability to open and close properly. Ultrasound: Use of high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider advances a catheter into a coronary vessel or previously placed graft using ultrasound or optical coherence tomography to view the extent of the blockage, placement of a stent, or other procedure on the heart before or after therapeutic intervention. The left main and ramus intermedius coronary arteries do not have recognized branches for reporting purposes. All PCI(s) performed in any segment (proximal, mid, distal) of a coronary artery branch is reported with one code. PCI is reported for up to two branches of a major coronary artery. Additional PCI in a third branch of the same major coronary artery is not separately reportable. Coronary artery bypass grafts: Each coronary artery bypass graft represents a coronary vessel. A sequential bypass graft with more than one distal anastomosis represents only one graft. guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Cardiovascular monitoring services are diagnostic medical procedures using in-person and remote technology to assess cardiovascular rhythm (ECG) data. Holter monitors (93224-93227) include up to 48 hours of continuous recording. Mobile cardiac telemetry monitors (93228, 93229) have the capability of transmitting a tracing at any time, always have internal ECG analysis algorithms designed to detect major arrhythmias, and transmit to an attended surveillance center. Event monitors (93268-93272) record segments of ECGs with recording initiation triggered either by patient activation or by an internal automatic, pre-programmed detection algorithm (or both) and transmit the recorded electrocardiographic data when requested (but cannot transmit immediately based upon the patient or algorithmic activation rhythm) and require attended surveillance. Long-term continuous recorders (93241, 93242, 93243, 93244, 93245, 93246, 93247, 93248) continuously record and store for greater than 48 hours and up to 7 days or for greater than 7 days up to 15 days. Attended surveillance: is the immediate availability of a remote technician to respond to rhythm or device alert transmissions from a patient, either from an implanted or wearable monitoring or therapy device, as they are generated and transmitted to the remote surveillance location or center. Electrocardiographic rhythm derived elements: elements derived from recordings of the electrical activation of the heart including, but not limited to heart rhythm, rate, ST analysis, heart rate variability, T-wave alternans. Long-term continuous recorders: Continuously record the electrocardiographic rhythm from a device applied to the patient. The electrocardiographic rhythm recording data collected is analyzed and annotated with frequency, duration, and symptomatic rhythm correlations. The processing center technician reviews the data and notifies the physician or other qualified health care professional depending on the prescribed criteria. An initial findings report is generated for physician review and final interpretation. Mobile cardiovascular telemetry (MCT): continuously records the electrocardiographic rhythm from external electrodes placed on the patient's body. Segments of the ECG data are automatically (without patient intervention) transmitted to a remote surveillance location by cellular or landline telephone signal. The segments of the rhythm, selected for transmission, are triggered automatically (MCT device algorithm) by rapid and slow heart rates or by the patient during a symptomatic episode. There is continuous real time data analysis by preprogrammed algorithms in the device and attended surveillance of the transmitted rhythm segments by a surveillance center technician to evaluate any arrhythmias and to determine signal quality. The surveillance center technician reviews the data and notifies the physician or other qualified health care professional depending on the prescribed criteria. ECG rhythm derived elements are distinct from physiologic data, even when the same device is capable of producing both. Implantable cardiovascular physiologic monitor device services are always separately reported from implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) service.

lay_term: The physician or other healthcare professional applies an electrocardiographic, or ECG recorder, to a patient for up to 48 hours to help detect abnormal heart rates and rhythms. The chest electrodes run to a small lightweight recorder, or monitor, which the patient wears on a belt. The device records the heart by continuous rhythm recording and storage, meaning that while the patient goes about his normal activity, the device continuously monitors the electrical activity of the heart, and records and stores the information on the device. After that, the patient returns to the provider and the device is removed. The provider or other qualified healthcare professional then takes the recorded, monitored data, downloads the data onto a computer, and performs a scanning analysis. She then compiles and prints the relevant data and arrhythmias, and along with the patient’s logged diary events, and interprets the results. Report this code for the recording portion of the test only. The recording service includes the placing of the ECG electrodes on the patient’s chest, the data recording, and the device removal. Terminology Arrhythmia: Irregular rate or rhythm of the heartbeat. Logged diary events: A log that the patient keeps to record the times when he has any symptoms and what activity he performed at the time. Other qualified health care professional: A nonphysician professional is an individual who is qualified by education, training, licensure, regulation, when applicable, and facility privileging, when applicable, who performs a professional service within his or her scope of practice and independently reports that professional service. These professionals are distinct from clinical staff. A clinical staff member is a person who works under the supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional and who is allowed by law, regulation, and facility policy to perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service, but who does not individually report that professional service. Other policies may also affect who may report specified services. RNs and LPNs aren't included in the definition because they cannot independently report the professional services that they provide. lay_term: The provider performs a face–to–face evaluation and then repeatedly adjusts and tests the existing parameters of an already implanted single lead or leadless pacemaker system that senses and regulates the heartbeat in a single chamber of the heart. Following his analysis, he reviews the results and prepares a report. This code represents both the professional and technical components of the service. Explanation This code represents the technical and professional components of a service in which a provider or a qualified healthcare professional connects the patient to an electrocardiogram (ECG) monitor, establishing a communication link between a single lead or leadless pacemaker system and the programmer. The provider analyzes and reviews several parameters of the stored pacemaker data, comparing it to current readings. He may make repeated changes to the settings followed by testing the function. He then determines whether to change the programming of the device to optimize performance. This code includes analysis, testing, adjustments, and preparation of a report. Terminology Implanted cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD): A small battery–powered electrical impulse generator device implanted in patients who are at risk of sudden cardiac death. The device is programmed to detect cardiac arrhythmia and correct it by delivering a jolt of electricity. Iterative: Refers to the process of concluding a decision or result based on repetitive action and analysis. Leadless pacemaker: A device usually implanted in the endocardium (inner wall) of a ventricle that can both sense heart rate and rhythm and stimulate contractions; it consists of a generator with a built–in battery and electrode inserted via a catheter with no wires to connect it to a monitor but communicates via magnetic, ultrasound, or electrical waves for device evaluation and programming. Single lead pacemaker system: A device implanted in the patient’s body that senses and regulates the heart’s rhythm in one chamber of the heart only. Tips Electronic analysis to monitor a patient's pacemaker or cardioverter–defibrillator is medically necessary on a regular basis to evaluate the device. Pre and postoperative evaluation of the cardiac rhythm device in patients with implanted cardioverter–defibrillators (ICDs) or who are pacer dependent may be necessary because electromagnetic interference can alter the function of these devices, especially ICDs, in unpredictable ways. They may need reprogramming before and after a surgical procedure. When billing for remote monitoring and trans–telephonic monitoring (TTM) it is not necessary to differentiate between single, dual, or multiple chamber systems. However, in–person programming evaluation represented by code range 93279 to 93285 requires the proper identification and reporting of the type of device the provider is evaluating. lay_term: In this service, the provider performs a face to face evaluation and then optimally adjusts the existing parameters of various operating functions of an already implanted multiple lead defibrillator system. He changes the various operating functions of the system that is responsible for regulating the heart’s rhythm in more than two chambers of the heart. This code represents both the professional and technical components of the service. Explanation This code represents the technical and professional components of a service in which a provider or a qualified healthcare professional connects the patient to a single or multilead electrocardiogram, or ECG monitor, establishing a communication link between the multiple lead implantable cardioverter defibrillator system and the programmer. The provider or other qualified healthcare professional analyzes and reviews several parameters of the stored pacemaker data, comparing it to current readings.
