Explanation This code represents the technical and professional components of a service in which a provider or a qualified healthcare professional connects the patient to an electrocardiogram (ECG) monitor, establishing a communication link between the subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor system and the programmer. He analyzes and reviews several parameters of the data stored in the system, comparing it to current readings. He may make repeated changes to the settings followed by retesting the function. He then determines whether to change the programming of the device to optimize performance. This code includes analysis, testing, adjustments, and preparation of a report. Other qualified healthcare professional: A physician or other qualified health care professional is an individual who is qualified by education, training, licensure or regulation when applicable; and facility privileging as applicable; who performs a professional service within his or her scope of practice and independently reports that professional service, these professionals are distinct from clinical staff who is a person that works under the supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional and who is allowed by law, regulation and facility policy to perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service, but who does not individually report that professional service; other policies may also affect who may report specified services, for example RNs and LPNs aren't included in the definition because they cannot independently report the professional services that they provide. Tips Electronic analysis to monitor a patient's pacemaker or cardioverter defibrillator is medically necessary on a regular basis to evaluate the device. lay_term: In this service, the provider performs a face–to–face evaluation and then optimally adjusts the existing parameters of a single, dual, multiple–lead, or leadless pacemaker system before, during, and/or just after a procedure, then reviews the results and prepares a report. This code represents both the professional and technical components of the service by a physician or other qualified healthcare professional. Explanation This code represents the technical and professional components of a service in which a provider establishes a communication link between the pacemaker and the programmer prior to a planned intervention, such as a test or surgery. The provider reviews several parameters of the data stored in the device, changes one or more parameters, and completes the device re–interrogation to confirm programming. During and/or after the test or surgery, the provider determines whether to return the pacemaker to the original programming. The provider documents the changes in the patient's chart. Report this code if the provider performs the periprocedural device evaluation and programming of the device system parameters before, during, or after a surgery, procedure, or test along with analysis, review, and report by the provider for a single, dual, multiple–lead or leadless pacemaker system. Terminology Dual–lead pacemaker: Pacing and sensing function in only two chambers of the heart, one in the right atrium and one in the right ventricle in a pacemaker or pacing cardioverter–defibrillator. Leadless pacemaker: A device usually implanted in the endocardium (inner wall) of a ventricle that can both sense heart rate and rhythm and stimulate contractions; it consists of a generator with a built–in battery and electrode inserted via a catheter with no wires to connect it to a monitor but communicates via magnetic, ultrasound, or electrical waves for device evaluation and programming. Multiple–lead pacemaker: Pacing and sensing function in three or more chambers of the heart in pacemaker or pacing cardioverter–defibrillator. Periprocedural: Referring to the services that span from the requisite services and preparation prior to the procedure, during the procedure and the post services needed after the procedure. Single–lead pacemaker: Pacing and sensing function in only one chamber of the heart, either atrium or ventricle; in a pacemaker or pacing cardioverter–defibrillator. Additional Info Other qualified healthcare professional: A physician or other qualified health care professional is an individual who is qualified by education, training, licensure or regulation when applicable; and facility privileging as applicable; who performs a professional service within his or her scope of practice and independently reports that professional service, these professionals are distinct from clinical staff who is a person that works under the supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional and who is allowed by law, regulation and facility policy to perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service, but who does not individually report that professional service; other policies may also affect who may report specified services, for example, RNs and LPNs aren't included in the definition because they cannot independently report the professional services that they provide. lay_term: In this service, the provider performs a face–to–face evaluation before or after a surgical procedure and then optimally adjusts the existing parameters of an already implanted single, dual, or multiple lead defibrillator system. He changes the various operating functions for the defibrillator responsible for sensing and regulating the activity from one, two, or more chambers of the heart .This code represents both the professional and technical components of the service . Explanation In this procedure, the provider does a face–to–face, or in person, evaluation of an implantable defibrillator. Using office, hospital, or emergency room equipment, the provider or other qualified healthcare professional retrieves the information the defibrillator stores and measures one or more leads or sensors when present, the battery, and the implanted pulse generator function, as well as data the device collects about the patient's heart rhythm and heart rate. The provider evaluates this information he retrieves to determine the current programming of the device and also to evaluate certain aspects of the device function, such as battery voltage, lead impedance, tachycardia detection settings, and rhythm treatment settings. Report this code if the provider evaluates the interrogation device in person, which includes connection, recording, and disconnection of a single, dual, or multiple implantable defibrillator, along with analysis of heart rhythm derived data elements. Subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor: programmed parameters and the heart rate and rhythm during recorded episodes from both patient-initiated and device algorithm detected events, when present. The data are stored and transmitted by either local telemetry or remotely to an Internet-based file server or surveillance technician. Extraction of data and compilation or report for physician or qualified health care professional interpretation is usually performed in the office setting. In addition, the battery status of the pacemaker is determined by measurement of the paced rate on the electrocardiographic rhythm strip recorded with the magnet applied. For remote monitoring of an implantable wireless pulmonary artery pressure sensor, use 93264. Implantable wireless pulmonary artery sensor: an implantable cardiovascular device used to assist the physician or other qualified health care professional in monitoring heart failure. The device collects longitudinal physiologic cardiovascular data elements from an internal sensor located in the pulmonary artery. The data are transmitted and stored remotely to an Internet-based file server.

lay_term: The provider performs a face–to–face evaluation and optimally adjusts the existing parameters of an already implanted cardiovascular physiologic monitoring system, reviews the results, and prepares a report. This code represents both the professional and technical components of the service by a physician or other qualified health care professional. Explanation The provider interrogates, i.e., retrieves stored data and tests, a cardiovascular physiologic monitoring system. He changes various operating functions for the system responsible for sensing physiologic activity of the heart and major arteries to help evaluate such conditions as unexplained syncope and palpitations. He reviews the data, assessing the appropriateness of the device's function and the current programming parameters. He may review weight, systemic blood pressure, atrial, ventricular, and pulmonary arterial pressures, cardiac output, or intrathoracic impedance measurements. He looks at episodes of data the monitor’s stores to assess history and trends. He also reviews alerts the system generates, along with battery voltage and sensor information to validate the integrity of the system. Report this code if the provider interrogates/evaluates the device including connection, recording, and disconnection of the cardiovascular physiologic monitoring system including analysis of one or more recorded physiologic cardiovascular data elements from all internal and external sensors. Terminology Atrial blood pressure: The force that the blood exerts on the walls of those chambers of the heart that receive blood from all parts of the body. Implantable cardiovascular monitor system (ICM): A device that continuously monitors heart rhythms and records them, for up to 36 months, either automatically performing real time analysis of the heart rhythm or using a patient handheld unit. Intrathoracic impedance: The resistance to blood flow as the blood flows through major blood vessels in the heart. Other qualified healthcare professional: A physician or other qualified health care professional is an individual who is qualified by education, training, licensure or regulation when applicable; and facility privileging as applicable; who performs a professional service within his or her scope of practice and independently reports that professional service, these professionals are distinct from clinical staff who is a person that works under the supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional and who is allowed by law, regulation and facility policy to perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service, but who does not individually report that professional service; other policies may also affect who may report specified services, for example RNs and LPNs aren't included in the definition because they cannot independently report the professional services that they provide. Pulmonary arterial pressures: The force that the blood exerts on the walls of those blood vessels that carry blood to the lungs or the organs that take in atmospheric air to furnish oxygen to the body. Syncope: To faint or pass out. Systemic blood pressure: The force that the blood exerts on the walls of all the blood vessels that supply blood to all the organs and parts of the body. Ventricular blood pressure: The force that the blood exerts on the walls of those chambers of the heart that pump blood to all parts of the body. Read Less

He may review presenting electrograms, patient episodes the device stores, alerts, battery voltage, impedance, pacing, and histograms, which may also include counters. Report this code if the provider includes in his interrogation device evaluation, the connection, recording, and disconnection per patient encounter of a wearable defibrillator system. short_description: Transtelephonic rhythm strip pacemaker evaluation(s) single, dual, or multiple lead pacemaker system, includes recording with and without magnet application with analysis, review and report(s) by a physician or other qualified health care professional, up to 90 days Notes: (Do not report 93293 in conjunction with 93294) (For in person evaluation, see 93040, 93041, 93042) (Report 93293 only once per 90 days)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider evaluates a pacemaker by rhythm strip over the telephone. She reviews the pacemaker data and confirms the function of each of the leads, battery, capture, and sensing by transtelephonic monitoring strip once without the magnet and then again with the magnet over the pacemaker. Therefore, she assesses the pacemaker’s function and the time interval to the next analysis, including the review and report of a single, dual, or multiple lead pacemaker system. Explanation In this procedure, the provider evaluates a pacemaker by rhythm strip over the telephone. She reviews the pacemaker data and confirms the function of each of the leads, battery, capture, and sensing by transtelephonic monitoring strip once without the magnet and then again with the magnet over the pacemaker. Therefore, she assesses the pacemaker’s function and the time interval to the next analysis, including the review and report of a single, dual, or multiple lead pacemaker system. The patient calls the provider on a land line telephone and attaches the phone to a monitoring device. The patient then places the monitoring device with the attached telephone against the implanted pacemaker in his chest. Multiple lead: Pacing and sensing function in three or more chambers of the heart in a pacemaker or pacing cardioverter defibrillator. Pacemaker: A device implanted into the chest that sends electrical impulses to the heart in order to regulate the heart rhythm. Rhythm strip: Multiple electrical vectors, direction as well as magnitude, in determining the position of one point in space relative to another to observe heart rate, regularity, pauses, and basic rhythm. Sensing: The ability of pacemakers to recognize a native electrical signal. Single lead: Pacing and sensing function in only one chamber of the heart, either the atrium or ventricle, in a pacemaker or pacing cardioverter defibrillator. Ventricular: Pertaining to the lower chamber of the heart, the ventricle that receives blood from one or more atria and pumps it by muscular contraction into the arteries. Ventricle: A chamber of the heart which receives blood from a corresponding atrium and from which blood is forced into the arteries. lay_term: In this service the provider evaluates from a remote location an implantable single, dual, or multiple lead defibrillator system. The service includes his interim analyses during a period of up to 90 days, and his technical review and report on the data. Explanation In this procedure, the provider or other qualified healthcare professional remotely evaluates the data from an implantable defibrillator. The provider assesses all device functions, including the programmed parameters, one or more leads, the battery, the devices capture and sensing function, any ventricular tachyarrhythmia therapy, and the patient’s underlying heart rhythm. He then evaluates the data and provides written reports to the ordering provider. Terminology Defibrillator system: A device that continuously senses, monitors, and regulates the heart rate; it can deliver a mild electrical shock to regulate the abnormal or fast rhythm of the heart when needed. Dual lead: Pacing and sensing function in only two chambers of the heart, one in right atrium and one in right ventricle in a pacemaker or pacing defibrillator. Implantable loop recorder system: A small equipment implanted beneath the chest’s skin to record the electrical activity of the heart. Lead impedance: The resistance that the connecting lead presents to the flow of current through it. Multiple lead: Pacing and sensing function in three or more chambers of the heart in pacemaker or pacing cardioverter defibrillator. Other qualified health care professional: A physician or other qualified health care professional is an individual who is qualified by education, training, licensure or regulation when applicable; and facility privileging as applicable; who performs a professional service within his or her scope of practice and independently reports that professional service, these professionals are distinct from clinical staff who is a person that works under the supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional and who is allowed by law, regulation and facility policy to perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service, but who does not individually report that professional service; other policies may also affect who may report specified services, for example RNs and LPNs aren't included in the definition because they cannot independently report the professional services that they provide. Pacemaker: A device implanted in the patient’s body that senses and regulates the heart’s rhythm in two chambers of the heart only. Single lead: Pacing and sensing function in only one chamber of the heart, either atrium or ventricle in a pacemaker or pacing cardioverter defibrillator. Tachyarrhythmia: An abnormal increase in the heart rate above 100 beats per minute along with an irregular heart rhythm. Tachycardia: An abnormal increase in the heart rate during rest above 100 beats per minute. Ventricular: referring to the ventricle of the heart that pumps blood to various parts of the body. Tips According to CPT® guidelines, a remote interrogation device evaluation is a procedure a provider performs for patients with pacemakers, implantable defibrillators, or implantable loop recorders using data he remotely obtains. For the technical portion of these services, report 93296, Interrogation device evaluation(s) (remote), up to 90 days; single, dual, or multiple lead pacemaker system, leadless pacemaker system, or implantable defibrillator system, remote data acquisition(s), receipt of transmissions and technician review, technical support and distribution of results. Code 93296 is for the technical portions of both pacemaker and defibrillator remote monitoring. In general, the professional portion of the service is everything that the provider does, including the supervision, interpretation, and report. lay_term: The technician gathers data, for a period of up to 90 days, from a patient’s single, dual, multiple lead, or leadless pacemaker system or implantable defibrillator system by remotely accessing the device, retrieving information, and conducting a technical review. He then distributes the results to the patient's physicians, providing technical support as necessary. This code represents the technical component of the service only. Explanation At times predetermined by the patient’s physician, a technician uses special equipment and a regular phone line to access and retrieve information stored on a single, dual, multiple lead, or leadless pacemaker system or implantable cardioverter–defibrillator system. He evaluates the date received, such as the programmed parameters of the device, lead integrity, battery status, certain device settings and conditions including capture and sensing functions, the presence or absence of episodes of irregular rhythms, the underlying heart rhythm, and others. When the technician completes his technical review, he sends the results to the patient’s physicians and provides the them with any technical support they need. Single lead, dual lead, and multiple lead pacemakers: Types of pacemakers that perform pacing and sensing functions in one, two, or more chambers of the heart, respectively. Device, leadless: a leadless cardiac pacemaker system that includes a pulse generator with built-in battery and electrode for implantation into the cardiac chamber via a transcatheter approach. Device, single lead: a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator with pacing and sensing function in only one chamber of the heart or a subcutaneous electrode. Device, dual lead: a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator with pacing and sensing function in only two chambers of the heart. Device, multiple lead: a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator with pacing and sensing function in three or more chambers of the heart. Electrocardiographic rhythm derived elements: elements derived from recordings of the electrical activation of the heart including, but not limited to heart rhythm, rate, ST analysis, heart rate variability, T-wave alternans. Implantable cardiovascular physiologic monitor: an implantable cardiovascular device used to assist the physician or other qualified health care professional in the management of non-rhythm related cardiac conditions such as heart failure. The device collects longitudinal physiologic cardiovascular data elements from one or more internal sensors (such as right ventricular pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, left atrial pressure, or an index of lung water) and/or external sensors (such as blood pressure or body weight) for patient assessment and management. Implantable defibrillator: two general categories of implantable defibrillators exist: transvenous implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) and subcutaneous implantable defibrillator (SICD). Implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillators also have pacemaker functions to treat slow heart rhythms called bradycardia. In addition to the tachycardia and bradycardia functions, the implantable pacing cardioverter-defibrillator may or may not include the functionality of an implantable cardiovascular physiologic monitor or a subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor. Interrogation device evaluation: an evaluation of an implantable device such as a cardiac pacemaker, implantable defibrillator, implantable cardiovascular physiologic monitor, or subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor. Using an office, hospital, or emergency room instrument or via a remote interrogation system, stored and measured information about the lead(s) when present, sensor(s) when present, battery and the implanted device function, as well as data collected about the patient's heart rhythm and heart rate is retrieved. The retrieved information is evaluated to determine the current programming of the device and to evaluate certain aspects of the device function such as battery voltage, lead impedance, tachycardia detection settings, and rhythm treatment settings. The components that must be evaluated for the various types of implantable or insertable cardiac devices are listed below. (The required components for both remote and in-person interrogations are the same.) Pacemaker: programmed parameters, with or without lead(s), battery, capture and sensing function and heart rhythm. Implantable defibrillator: programmed parameters, lead(s), battery, capture and sensing function, presence or absence of therapy for ventricular tachyarrhythmias and underlying heart rhythm. Implantable cardiovascular physiologic monitor: programmed parameters and analysis of at least one recorded physiologic cardiovascular data element from either internal or external sensors. Subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor: programmed parameters and the heart rate and rhythm during recorded episodes from both patient initiated and device algorithm detected events, when present. Interrogation device evaluation (remote): a procedure performed for patients with pacemakers, implantable defibrillators, or subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitors using data obtained remotely. All device functions, including the programmed parameters, lead(s), battery, capture and sensing function, presence or absence of therapy for ventricular tachyarrhythmias (for implantable defibrillators) and underlying heart rhythm are evaluated. The components that must be evaluated for the various types of implantable or insertable cardiac devices are listed below. (The required components for both remote and in person interrogations are the same.) Pacemaker: programmed parameters, with or without lead(s), battery, capture and sensing function, and heart rhythm. Implantable defibrillator: programmed parameters, lead(s), battery, capture and sensing function, presence or absence of therapy for ventricular tachyarrhythmias, and underlying heart rhythm. Implantable cardiovascular physiologic monitor: programmed parameters and analysis of at least one recorded physiologic cardiovascular data element from either internal or external sensors. Subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor: programmed parameters and the heart rate and rhythm during recorded episodes from both patient-initiated and device algorithm detected events, when present. Pacemaker: an implantable device that provides low energy localized stimulation to one or more chambers of the heart to initiate contraction in that chamber. Two general categories of pacemakers exist: (1) pacemakers with a subcutaneous generator plus transvenous/epicardial lead(s); and (2) leadless pacemakers. A leadless pacemaker does not require a subcutaneous pocket for the generator. It combines a miniaturized generator with an integrated electrode for implantation in a heart chamber via a transcatheter approach. Peri-procedural device evaluation and programming: an evaluation of an implantable device system (either a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator) to adjust the device to settings appropriate for the patient prior to a surgery, procedure, or test. The device system data are interrogated to evaluate the lead(s) when present, sensor(s), and battery in addition to review of stored information, including patient and system measurements. The device is programmed to settings appropriate for the surgery, procedure, or test, as required. A second evaluation and programming are performed after the surgery, procedure, or test to provide settings appropriate to the post procedural situation, as required. If one performs the pre-surgical service and a separate individual performs the post-surgical service, each reports either 93286 or 93287 only one time. All device functions, including the battery, programmable settings and lead(s), when present, are evaluated. (See also required interrogation device evaluation [remote and in person] components above.) Pacemaker: programmed parameters, lead(s) when present, battery, capture and sensing function, and heart rhythm. Often, but not always, the sensor rate response, lower and upper heart rates, AV intervals, pacing voltage and pulse duration, sensing value, and diagnostics will be adjusted during a programming evaluation. Implantable defibrillator: programmed parameters, lead(s), battery, capture and sensing function, presence or absence of therapy for ventricular tachyarrhythmias and underlying heart rhythm. Often, but not always, the sensor rate response, lower and upper heart rates, AV intervals, pacing voltage and pulse duration, sensing value, and diagnostics will be adjusted during a programming evaluation. Subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor: programmed parameters and the heart rhythm during recorded episodes from both patient initiated and device algorithm detected events. Often, but not always, the tachycardia and bradycardia detection criteria will be adjusted during a programming evaluation. Subcutaneous cardiac rhythm monitor: an implantable or insertable device that continuously records the electrocardiographic rhythm triggered automatically by rapid, irregular, and/or slow heart rates or by the patient during a symptomatic episode. The cardiac rhythm monitor function may be the only function of the device or it may be part of a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator device. The data are stored and transmitted by either local telemetry or remotely to an Internet-based file server or surveillance technician. Extraction of data and compilation or report for physician or qualified health care professional interpretation is usually performed in the office setting. The rhythm strip is evaluated for heart rate and rhythm, atrial and ventricular capture (if observed) and atrial and ventricular sensing (if observed). In addition, the battery status of the pacemaker is determined by measurement of the paced rate on the electrocardiographic rhythm strip recorded with the magnet applied. For remote monitoring of an implantable wireless pulmonary artery pressure sensor, use 93264. Implantable wireless pulmonary artery sensor: an implantable cardiovascular device used to assist the physician or other qualified health care professional in monitoring heart failure. The device collects longitudinal physiologic cardiovascular data elements from an internal sensor located in the pulmonary artery. short_description: Therapy activation of implanted phrenic nerve stimulator system, including all interrogation and programming Notes: (Do not report 93150 in conjunction with 33276, 33277, 33278, 33279, 33280, 33281, 93151, 93152, 93153)
lay_term: The provider performs therapy activation of an implanted phrenic nerve stimulation system, evaluating and programming the device. Explanation Following separately reported implantation of a phrenic nerve stimulation system, the provider performs therapy activation. The timing for activation may be a month or more after implant. The system includes a pulse generator (with electronics and a battery) and one or more leads. Stimulation leads emit electrical impulses to stimulate the phrenic nerve. The phrenic nerve sends signals to the brain which in turn sends signals that stimulate the diaphragm to contract. The contraction of the diaphragm pushes against the lung and results in a more normal breathing pattern. The sensing lead (which is not always present) can help augment the system’s function, such as by sensing breathing. For activation, the provider performs device evaluation and programming services for areas such as rate; pulse amplitude (strength); pulse duration; configuration of waveform (such as shape and frequency of the electrical signal); battery status; electrode selection output modulation (adjusting the strength and pattern of the electrical signals sent by the neurostimulator); cycling; impedance (how much the body’s tissues resist the flow of the electrical signals from the device); and patient compliance (such as amount of use and details about sleep). short_description: Transthoracic echocardiography for congenital cardiac anomalies; complete
lay_term: The provider performs a complete transthoracic echocardiography to obtain images of the heart structures through the chest wall in patients born with heart defects. This study includes visualization of heart chambers, valves, blood flow, and cardiac activity. This service has both a professional and a technical component. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider applies a gel and places a small transducer on the chest wall. The probe generates high–frequency sound waves that bounce off the heart back to the probe, which is connected to a monitor that displays the images of the heart. The gel helps the provider move the probe in different directions on the chest to obtain images of the heart. Standard views for a complete echocardiogram include subcostal, apical, parasternal and suprasternal. The provider views and examines the heart’s movement, as well as the blood flow through the various blood vessels and the valves, and evaluates any congenital abnormalities. Terminology Congenital cardiac anomaly: Defects or abnormities in the heart present since birth. Echocardiogram (Echo): The use of high–frequency sound waves or sonography (ultrasound) to create a two–dimensional image of the heart. Transducer: An electronic device that converts energy from one form to another. Tips If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append modifier 26, Professional component, to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append modifier TC, Technical component, to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. This code describes echocardiography to evaluate congenital cardiac anomalies, but if the provider suspects a congenital issue and does not find one, you should use a noncongenital echocardiography code, such as 93306, Echocardiography, transthoracic, real time with image documentation, includes M mode recording, when performed, complete, without spectral or color Doppler echocardiography. Unlike 93306 and 93307, the descriptor for 93303 doesn't say whether it includes spectral or color–flow Doppler, but it is comparable to 93307. If spectral or color–flow Doppler is performed, consider add–on codes 93320 Doppler echocardiography, pulsed wave and/or continuous wave with spectral display and 93325 Doppler echocardiography color–flow velocity mapping. guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Echocardiography includes obtaining ultrasonic signals from the heart and great vessels, with real time image and/or Doppler ultrasonic signal documentation, with interpretation and report. When interpretation is performed separately, use modifier 26. A complete transthoracic echocardiogram without spectral or color flow Doppler (93307) is a comprehensive procedure that includes 2-dimensional and, when performed, selected M-mode examination of the left and right atria, left and right ventricles, the aortic, mitral, and tricuspid valves, the pericardium, and adjacent portions of the aorta. Multiple views are required to obtain a complete functional and anatomic evaluation, and appropriate measurements are obtained and recorded. Despite significant effort, identification and measurement of some structures may not always be possible. In such instances, the reason that an element could not be visualized must be documented. Additional structures that may be visualized (eg, pulmonary veins, pulmonary artery, pulmonic valve, inferior vena cava) would be included as part of the service. A complete transthoracic echocardiogram with spectral and color flow Doppler (93306) is a comprehensive procedure that includes spectral Doppler and color flow Doppler in addition to the 2-dimensional and selected M-mode examinations, when performed. Spectral Doppler (93320, 93321) and color flow Doppler (93325) provide information regarding intracardiac blood flow and hemodynamics. A follow-up or limited echocardiographic study (93308) is an examination that does not evaluate or document the attempt to evaluate all the structures that comprise the complete echocardiographic exam. This is typically limited to, or performed in follow-up of a focused clinical concern. In stress echocardiography, echocardiographic images are recorded from multiple cardiac windows before, after, and in some protocols, during stress. The stress is achieved by (1) walking on a treadmill; (2) using a bicycle (supine or upright); or (3) the administration of pharmacological agents that either simulate exercise (by increasing heart rate, blood pressure, or myocardial contractility) or alter coronary flow (vasodilation). The patient's ECG, heart rate, and blood pressure are monitored at baseline, throughout the procedure and during recovery. Reports are prepared to evaluate (1) the duration of stress, the reason for stopping, and the hemodynamic response to stress; (2) the electrocardiographic response to stress; and (3) the echocardiographic response to stress. When a stress echocardiogram is performed with a complete cardiovascular stress test (continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, supervision, interpretation and report by a physician or other qualified health care professional), use 93351. When only the professional components of a complete stress test and a stress echocardiogram are provided (eg, in a facility setting) by the same physician, use 93351 with modifier 26. When all professional services of a stress test are not performed by the same physician performing the stress echocardiogram, use 93350 in conjunction with the appropriate codes (93016-93018) for the components of the cardiovascular stress test that are provided. When left ventricular endocardial borders cannot be adequately identified by standard echocardiographic imaging, echocardiographic contrast may be infused intravenously both at rest and with stress to achieve that purpose. Code 93352 is used to report the administration of echocardiographic contrast agent in conjunction with the stress echocardiography codes (93350 or 93351). Supply of contrast agent and/or drugs used for pharmacological stress is reported separately in addition to the procedure code. Code 93355 is used to report transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) services during transcatheter intracardiac therapies. Code 93355 is reported once per intervention and only by an individual who is not performing the interventional procedure. Code 93355 includes the work of passing the endoscopic ultrasound transducer through the mouth into the esophagus, when performed by the individual performing the TEE, diagnostic transesophageal echocardiography and ongoing manipulation of the transducer to guide sizing and/or placement of implants, determination of adequacy of the intervention, and assessment for potential complications. Real-time image acquisition, measurements, and interpretation of image(s), documentation of completion of the intervention, and final written report are included in this code. A range of intracardiac therapies may be performed with TEE guidance. Code 93355 describes TEE during advanced transcatheter structural heart procedures (eg, transcatheter aortic valve replacement [TAVR], left atrial appendage closure [LAA], or percutaneous mitral valve repair). See 93313 for separate reporting of the probe insertion by a physician other than the physician performing the TEE. Report of an echocardiographic study, whether complete or limited, includes an interpretation of all obtained information, documentation of all clinically relevant findings including quantitative measurements obtained, plus a description of any recognized abnormalities. Pertinent images, videotape, and/or digital data are archived for permanent storage and are available for subsequent review. Use of echocardiography not meeting these criteria is not separately reportable. Use of ultrasound, without thorough evaluation of organ(s) or anatomic region, image documentation and final, written report, is not separately reportable. (For fetal echocardiography, see 76825-76828)

short_description: Echocardiography, transthoracic, real-time with image documentation (2D), includes M-mode recording, when performed, complete, with spectral Doppler echocardiography, and with color flow Doppler echocardiography Notes: (For transthoracic echocardiography without spectral and color Doppler, use 93307)
lay_term: The provider uses transducers to obtain two–dimensional (2D) images of the heart structures through the chest wall. He evaluates the anatomy and function of all four heart chambers, valves, adjacent aorta, and wall of the heart. This service has both a professional and a technical component. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider applies a gel and places a small transducer on the chest wall. The probe generates high–frequency sound waves that bounce off the heart back to the probe, which is connected to a monitor that displays the images of the heart. The gel helps the provider move the probe in different directions on the chest to obtain images of the heart. Standard views for a complete echocardiogram include subcostal, apical, parasternal and suprasternal. M–mode recording detects heart motion toward and away from the transducer to evaluate volume of blood being pumped by the heart. Spectral and color–flow Doppler evaluate the blood flowing through the heart valves and demonstrate any leaks. This is a comprehensive exam in which multiple views are obtained and measurements taken to assess both the anatomy and function of the heart. Terminology Color Doppler: A form of pulse wave Doppler in which the energy of the returning echoes is displayed as an assigned color; by convention, echoes representing flow toward the transducer are seen as shades of red, and those representing flow away from the transducer are seen as shades of blue; simultaneously shows visualization of anatomy and flow dynamics. Doppler ultrasound: Use of reflected sound waves to observe blood flow through a vessel; ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Echocardiography: A diagnostic test employing reflected ultrasonic waves to examine the structures and functioning of the heart. M mode: Diagnostic procedure to document the position and motion of the heart and its blood vessels through ultrasound beams from a transducer. Transducer: An electronic device that converts energy from one form to another. Transthoracic echocardiogram: Use of a small probe or transducer to obtain images that can detect an abnormality in the heart. Ultrasound: Use of high–frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. An important distinguishing characteristic of 93306 is that it requires both spectral and color Doppler. If a transthoracic echo service does not include both spectral and color Doppler, you should instead report 93307, Echocardiography, transthoracic, real–time with image documentation, 2D, includes M mode recording, when performed, complete, without spectral or color Doppler echocardiography. lay_term: The provider uses transducers to obtain a two–dimensional (2D) echocardiogram of the heart structures through the chest wall. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider applies a gel and places a small transducer on the chest wall. The probe generates high–frequency sound waves that bounce off the heart back to the probe, which is connected to a monitor that displays the images of the heart. The gel helps the provider move the probe in different directions on the chest to obtain images of the heart. Standard views for a complete echocardiogram include subcostal, apical, parasternal and suprasternal. M mode recording detects heart motion toward and away from the transducer to evaluate volume of blood being pumped by the heart. The provider views and examines the heart’s movement, as well as the blood flow through the various blood vessels and the valves, and evaluates any congenital abnormalities. M mode: Diagnostic procedure to document the position and motion of the heart and its blood vessels through ultrasound beams from a transducer. Transducer: An electronic device that converts energy from one form to another. Transthoracic echocardiogram: Use of a small probe or transducer to obtain images that can detect an abnormality in the heart. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs transesophageal echocardiography, or TEE, with multiple transducers, or probes, or a rotating transducer to obtain a two–dimensional (2D) image of the heart. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs a transesophageal echocardiography, or TEE, which involves using a flexible tube with a transducer at its tip. The probe generates ultrasound in the form of an M mode, producing an image that is similar to a tracing that captures one dimensional motion and position of the heart and its chambers on a paper strip. This procedure is known as two–dimensional motion. She then interprets anatomy, dynamics, and function. Probe: An instrument placed to explore in a wound or the inside of a vessel, organ, or the body; to explore a wound or the inside of a vessel, organ, or the body with such an instrument. lay_term: At the same session as a primary echocardiography service, the provider uses a 3D–capable machine to perform 3D imaging. The provider can view the 3D imaging in real time to assess one or more cardiac structures, such as the cardiac chambers and valves, left atrial appendage, interatrial septum, and interventricular septum. lay_term: The provider performs a complete Doppler echocardiography, which uses high–frequency sound waves to create a two–dimensional image of the heart, while the use of Doppler technology allows determination of the speed and direction of blood flow via spectral display. Explanation At the beginning of the procedure the subject (the person on whom the procedure is performed) is instructed to take off his clothing to the waist level. Women are provided a gown to wear. The person lies down on the examination table. During the examination the room will remain dimly–lit. First the sonographer will apply a gel on the chest wall or thorax of the subject. A number of sticky electrodes will be attached on the chest skin of the subject to receive an EKG report during the test. The sonographer will hold a small hand–held instrument known as the transducer and will move the device over the gel–smeared chest wall skin of the subject. In conjunction with normal echocardiography, the technician performs a Doppler echo. The Doppler transducer is a different one than the normal echo transducer. The sonographer moves the transducer at various angles and at different positions over the location of the heart so that a complete picture of the heart can be obtained. The transducer transmits powerful sound waves that will pass through the gel layer and breast bones and bounce back upon falling onto the heart. The sound waves may be emitted at regular intervals (pulsed) and/or uninterrupted (continuous). To achieve better image recording, the sound waves are targeted as parallel to the blood flow as possible. The echoes received from the heart and the RBCs in blood are converted by a complex computer program into two–dimensional images of the heart that will be displayed on a computer screen. Additional Info Doppler echocardiography is a diagnostic procedure based on the Doppler effect of sound. An echocardiograph uses high–frequency sound waves to assess the velocity and direction of blood flow in the cardiac arteries. The sound waves are transmitted into the body, bounce back, and are again captured by a device called a transducer. These captured waves are converted into images with the help of advanced digital processing technology. The speed and the direction of blood flowing in normal vessels (laminar flow) are synchronized with the pumping action of the heart and the speed of the red blood cells moving along the flow of blood in the arteries in a particular region is always the same. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs echocardiography by administering contrast intravenously to obtain both pre– and poststress images of the heart during stress echocardiography. Explanation In this procedure, the provider performs echocardiography by administering contrast intravenously to have obtain both pre– and poststress images of the heart during stress echocardiography. The provider, typically a nurse, administers a dose of contrast agent intravenously, and the contrast opacifies the left ventricle (LV). Then, the provider, typically a sonographer, takes a prestress contrast image of the LV endocardium. At peak stress or immediately poststress, the nurse administers a second infusion of contrast, and the sonographer obtains poststress images. Lastly, the provider monitors the heart rate until it returns to baseline. Opacifies: To make opaque (nontransparent). lay_term: In this procedure, the provider gains percutaneous venous access through the internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral vein under fluoroscopic guidance. He obtains oxygen saturation measurements that indicate the amount of oxygen the blood is carrying as a percentage of the maximum it could carry, to evaluate cardiac output. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral vein and inserts a catheter through a flexible guide wire under fluoroscopic guidance. She receives X–ray images to facilitate the catheter placement throughout the procedure. She also monitors cardiac rhythm by performing an electrocardiogram, or ECG. She then passes the catheter through the right atrium and the tricuspid valve, into the right ventricle, across the pulmonary valve, and into the pulmonary artery. As the catheter tip passes through the heart into the lungs, the provider obtains pressure measurements the pressure that mounts up within each cardiac chamber and within the main pulmonary artery. She obtains oxygen saturation measurements in the various cardiac chambers to assess for intracardiac shunts and to assess cardiac output. At the end of the procedure, the provider either sews the catheter in place for ongoing monitoring or removes it and achieves hemostasis. Terminology Atrium: One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Cardiac output: The volume of blood pumped per minute by each ventricle of the heart; cardiac output is equal to the stroke volume the amount of blood pumped from a ventricle in a single heartbeat times the heart rate; it is used as a measure of the overall health of the heart. Cardiac rhythm: The rhythm of a beating heart. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Catheterization: Passage of a catheter into a body channel or cavity. Electrocardiogram or ECG: A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Femoral vein: A vein located in the upper leg, which is a continuation of the popliteal vein, which carries blood from knee to thigh and calf muscles to the heart and it carries blood back to the heart from the lower extremities. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and other items such as stents. Hemostasis: Process that causes bleeding to cease, which involves a balance of coagulation and clot breakdown. Internal jugular:Vein located in the neck; it collects blood from the brain and outside of the face and the neck. Intracardiac shunts: A condition in which blood flow in the heart deviates from the normal circuit of the circulatory system. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Pulmonary artery, right pulmonary artery: The major artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Pulmonary valve: The valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery that carries oxygenated blood to the lungs; it prevents backflow of blood from the artery back into the ventricle; the pulmonary valve consists of the right, left, and anterior semilunar cusps. Stroke Volume: The amount of blood pumped by the left ventricle of the heart in one contraction. It is only about two–thirds of the blood in the ventricle is expelled with each beat. Subclavian vein: Vein located below the clavicle, which is the collarbone that connects the sternum, or breastbone, to the scapula, or shoulder blade. Tricuspid valve: The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle; so called because it usually has three cusps or leaflets which may be referred to as anterior meaning toward the front of the heart, posterior meaning toward the back of the heart, and septal meaning nearest the septum or wall between the chambers. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. lay_term: This procedure involves catheter placement in a left sided, systemic cardiac chambers left ventricle or left atrium. It also includes left ventricular injection and measuring left ventricular pressures that mounts within the ventricle. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision into the peripheral artery and inserts a catheter through a flexible guide wire under fluoroscopic guidance. He receives X–ray images to facilitate the catheter placement throughout the procedure. He then passes the catheter into the aortic valve till the left ventricle for evaluating ventricular function. The provider may also inject dye into the catheter to further evaluate the heart’s function with fluoroscopy. At the end of the procedure, the provider either sews the catheter in place for ongoing monitoring or removes it and achieves hemostasis. Terminology Aortic valve: The valve between the left ventricle and the aorta; it keeps blood from flowing backward into the left ventricle, the pumping chamber of the heart; it consists of three semilunar leaflets or cusps, so called because of their crescent moon shape. Catheterization: Passage of a catheter into a body channel or cavity. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and other items such as stents. Hemostasis: Process that causes bleeding to cease, which involves a balance of coagulation and clot breakdown. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Ventriculography: Radiography of the ventricles of the heart after injection of a contrast medium. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs both right and left heart catheterization to evaluate the heart’s function. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral vein and inserts a catheter through a flexible guide wire under fluoroscopic guidance. She receives X–ray images to facilitate the catheter placement throughout the procedure. She also monitors cardiac rhythm by performing an electrocardiogram, or ECG. For right heart catheterization, she then passes the catheter through the right atrium, through the tricuspid valve, and then into the right ventricle, then moves it across the pulmonary valve and into the pulmonary artery. For left heart catheterization, the provider moves the catheter through the aortic valve into the left ventricle. The provider may also inject dye into the catheter to further evaluate the heart’s function with fluoroscopy. At the end of the procedure, the provider either sews the catheter in place for ongoing monitoring or removes it and achieves hemostasis. Terminology Aortic valve: The valve between the left ventricle and the aorta; it keeps blood from flowing backward into the left ventricle, the pumping chamber of the heart; it consists of three semilunar leaflets or cusps, so called because of their crescent moon shape. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Catheterization: Passage of a catheter into a body channel or cavity. Cardiac rhythm: The rhythm of a beating heart. Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Electrocardiogram or ECG: A graphical representation of the electrical activity of the heart. Femoral vein: The large vein in the groin that accompanies the femoral artery in the femoral sheath. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and other items such as stents. Hemostasis: Process that causes bleeding to cease, which involves a balance of coagulation and clot breakdown. Internal jugular: Vein located in the neck; it collects blood from the brain and outside of the face and the neck. Pulmonary artery, right pulmonary artery: The major artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Subclavian vein: Vein located below the clavicle, which is the collarbone that connects the sternum, or breastbone, to the scapula, or shoulder blade. Tricuspid valve: The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle; so called because it usually has three cusps or leaflets which may be referred to as anterior meaning toward the front of the heart, posterior meaning toward the back of the heart, and septal meaning nearest the septum or wall between the chambers. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Ventriculography: Radiography of the ventricles of the heart after injection of a contrast medium. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs coronary angiography, an imaging study of the vessels in the heart. He inserts tubing into an artery, typically in the groin or arm, and threads it into the left side of the heart, where he injects dye. He also injects dye into the left ventricle, the lower chamber on that side, if necessary, and into any prior bypass grafts. He supervises the collection of images and interprets the images to identify narrowing or blockages in the vessels and assess the health of the heart. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the groin, over the femoral artery, or alternative in the upper arm over the brachial or axillary artery. He inserts an introducer sheath into the artery, followed by a guide wire. Under fluoroscopic guidance, he inserts a catheter over the guidewire and sequentially engages the ostia, or openings, in the coronary arteries and any bypass grafts. He injects contrast material, or dye, into the arteries and performs angiograms in multiple views. He then catheterizes the left ventricle and performs a left ventriculogram to measure pressure, volume, and blood flow in the left ventricle. The provider then withdraws the catheters, removes all instruments, and applies pressure and a dressing to the wound. The provider supervises and interprets the images obtained during this procedure. Terminology Angiogram: An image of vessels taken after the injection of a radiographic dye, in a process called angiography. Aorta: The main artery that comes out of the top of the left ventricle of the heart and carries oxygenated blood to the body; it consists of an ascending and descending aorta, which serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Bypass graft: A healthy vessel taken from one area and grafted, or connected, to a blocked or severely narrowed vessel in another area to permit blood flow to bypass, or flow around, the obstruction. Bypass graft angiography: An imaging study of a bypass graft using an injection of dye to assess the flow of blood in the vessel. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Coronary angiography: An imaging study of the vessels in the heart; the study requires insertion of a catheter, or tube, through which dye is injected. Coronary arteries: Vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle, including the right or left coronary artery, left anterior descending, posterior descending, and circumflex. Femoral artery: Vessel that supplies blood to the legs; it diverges from the external iliac artery in the abdomen, which in turn diverges from the common iliac artery and the aorta. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Free arterial graft: An artery harvested for grafting, obtained from a location outside of the graft site, such as an intramammary artery from the chest used in the heart. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and other items such as stents. Internal mammary artery: The artery supplying the thoracic, or chest, wall, mediastinum, the organs and structures in the chest, and diaphragm, the membrane dividing the abdominal and chest cavities; sometimes used for bypass in coronary artery bypass graft surgery. Intraprocedural injection: An injection performed during a procedure, such as during an imaging study. Left heart catheterization: Insertion of a catheter, or tube, into the left side of the heart to view internal structures, inject dye for imaging studies, or treat certain conditions. Left ventriculography: An imaging study of the left ventricle, the lower chamber on the left side of the heart; the study requires insertion of a catheter, or tube, through which dye is injected. Sheath: A protective covering, natural, like a membrane, or artificial, such as an introducer sheath for a needle. Venous graft: A vein used for grafting, typically harvested from the lower leg. Tips This code includes the coronary angiography procedure and the associated imaging supervision and interpretation. There may be rare instances where one provider supervises the radiology service and another provider interprets it. According to Medicare guidelines, each provider should report the radiology code and append modifier 52, Reduced services. Each should also append modifier 26, Professional component, to the code to report only the professional component. Read Less

lay_term: The provider performs right and left heart catheterization with coronary and bypass graft imaging to evaluate heart function. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider takes the steps needed to insert a catheter through a sheath into a blood vessel, such as a femoral vein. The provider uses fluoroscopic guidance and contrast injections as needed throughout the procedure. The provider advances the catheter through the right heart chambers into the pulmonary artery, taking pressure measurements in the various structures. The provider uses a balloon tip to occlude, or block, the pulmonary artery and takes additional measurements, such as diastolic pressure, oxygen saturation, and Fick cardiac output. The provider uses a needle, guidewire, sheath, and catheter under fluoroscopic guidance to access the arterial system and reach the ascending aorta. The provider uses a catheter attachment to measure aortic root pressure and moves the catheter to a coronary artery ostium to evaluate pressure and waveform and obtains various images. The provider repeats the imaging procedure for other coronary ostia as indicated, using additional catheters. The provider then moves another catheter across the aortic valve into the left ventricle, measures pressures, and performs power injection to evaluate the systolic function and the mitral valve. In this service, the provider also performs coronary injections for the assessment of stenosis and coronary artery disease. The provider uses additional catheters to engage the vein and internal mammary artery grafts. The contrast medium is visualized through X–ray technique to generate angiogram images. The provider reviews all images to be sure no additional work is needed. The provider may image the access site to see if a closure device is needed, removes all catheters and instruments, and stops bleeding as required. Ascending aorta: Part of the aorta that rises up from the heart from which the coronary arteries branch off to supply the heart with blood. Bypass graft: A vein from the leg or an inner chest wall artery that replaces a blocked or narrowed vessel in the heart reestablishing a sufficient blood flow to deliver oxygen and nutrients to the heart. Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove fluid, or to keep a passage open. Contrast medium: A substance used in radiology, or X–ray imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body. It can be administered orally or intravenously. It is also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Coronary angiography: X–rays of the arteries of the heart after injecting them with contrast material. Coronary artery disease: It is defined as the deposition of atheromatous plaques inside the walls of coronary arteries supplying the muscle of the heart. Diastolic pressure: Blood pressure when the chambers of the heart are refilling with blood after a contraction of the heart. Femoral vein: Large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that delivers oxygen–rich blood to the leg and pelvic region. Fick cardiac output: Calculation done to determine the oxygen consumed over a certain period of time by measuring the oxygen concentration of the venous and arterial blood. Fluoroscopic guidance: Live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor, which providers use to view body structures while performing procedures. Guidewire: A thin, usually flexible wire used as a guide for placement of larger devices, such as a catheter. Internal mammary artery: Another name for the internal thoracic artery or the blood vessel on either side of the breastbone that is often used as a replacement artery in coronary bypass surgery. Ostium: The openings to the left and right coronary arteries. Oxygen saturation: The concentration of oxygen found in the blood. Stenosis: Abnormal narrowing or constriction. Systolic function: Blood pressure that drives blood out of the heart during a heartbeat, or contraction. Ventriculography: Placement of a catheter into the lower heart chamber, or left ventricle, and injection of contrast medium to visualize the left ventricle and its contractions. Waveform: Visual representation of pressure changes as blood enters or exits a chamber or vessel. lay_term: The provider passes a catheter into the left ventricle of the heart by puncturing the septum, a partition between the ventricles, or by incising the skin between the ribs and accessing the apex (top) of the left ventricle directly. The provider uses this method when the left side of the heart is difficult to access, such as in patients with valve replacement. Explanation During a left heart catheterization procedure, the provider determines that he needs to enter the left ventricle through a transseptal or transapical puncture. He introduces a catheter from the right femoral vein to the right atrium. He punctures the septum under fluoroscopic guidance and passes the catheter into the left atrium or ventricle for measuring pressure, volume, and blood flow. In transapical puncture, he punctures the chest wall and inserts a needle into the left ventricular cavity. The primary procedure then continues. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Left heart catheterization: Insertion of a catheter, or tube, into the left side of the heart to view internal structures, inject dye for imaging studies, or treat certain conditions. Septum: Wall or partition between two cavities or open spaces; examples include the septa between the ventricles and the atria of the heart and the nasal septum. Transapical puncture: Access to the left ventricle through a small incision between the ribs. Transseptal puncture: Access to the left ventricle through an incision in the interatrial septum, the partition between chambers in the heart. Valve: A structure in an organ that can open and close to control the passage of fluid, blood, or other materials; the heart has four valves, the mitral, aortic, pulmonary, and tricuspid. Ventricle: One of the two lower chambers of the heart; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. lay_term: The provider performs Swan–Ganz® catheterization for the direct assessment of pressure in the pulmonary artery, right atrium, right ventricle, as well as the wedge pressure of the left atrium simultaneously in patients with heart failure, valvular regurgitation, acute renal failure, pulmonary edema, pulmonary hypertension, shock, and burns. Explanation A pulmonary artery flow–directed catheter (also referred to as a Swan–Ganz® catheter or right heart catheter) is used in intensive care or cardiac care units on critically ill patients. The points of access are commonly the bigger veins such as the subclavian, internal jugular, brachial, or femoral veins. A Swan–Ganz® catheter may contain 2–6 lumens or tubes that branch out to different areas in the heart for measurement of pressure. Left atrial pressure (left ventricular end–diastolic pressure [LVEDP]) can be measured by creating a wedge in the pulmonary artery through an inflatable balloon at the tip of the catheter. Fluoroscopic guidance is used for correct placement of the catheter. Monitoring equipment connected to the external end of the catheter records pressures at different locations along with cardiac output and oxygen saturation levels in the right atrium and right ventricle. The insertion site is prepared by cleansing and administering a local anesthetic. The provider accesses a vein through an incision in the skin and inserts the catheter through a small incision made in the vein. The veins used for pulmonary artery catheterization include the femoral, internal jugular, subclavian or the brachial veins. The provider advances the catheter to the pulmonary artery via the right atrium under fluoroscopic guidance. The external end of the catheter is connected to the monitoring devices that show the pressure at different lumen locations as well as the oxygen saturation levels in the right atrium and ventricle. Terminology Atrium (pl. atria): One of the two upper chambers of the heart; the left atrium delivers oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins to the left ventricle of the heart, the right receives blood from the major veins and delivers it to the right ventricle. Brachial vein: A large vein in the upper arm that carries blood back toward the heart from the radial and ulnar veins. Diastolic blood pressure: Pressure in the blood vessels when the heart relaxes to let the chambers of the heart refill with blood after a contraction of the heart. Femoral vein: A large vein in the upper thighs and groin area that returns blood to the inferior vena cava from the leg and pelvic region. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the images appear on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Internal jugular vein: The blood vessel that drains blood from the neck, brain, and a part of the face to the heart. Pulmonary artery: Major artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; it branches into the left and right pulmonary artery which correspond to the right and left lung. Subclavian vein: One of the two veins on either side of the body that drains blood from the arm to the heart. Superior vena cava: A wide but short vein that returns blood to the heart from the upper part of the body. Swan–Ganz® catheter: A specialized catheter inserted through a major vein in the neck to enter the right side of the heart as well as the pulmonary artery, the blood vessel bringing blood to the lungs; used to monitor important heart working parameters including blood pressure, especially to monitor a patient after major heart operations. Ventricles of the heart: The two lower chambers of the heart; the right ventricle receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Tips Don't assume every CVP uses Swan–Ganz®. When your anesthesiologist is involved in an extensive heart procedure, he likely places a central venous pressure (CVP) catheter. The line is most often placed in the patient's superior vena cava and may be used for other purposes, including IV fluid delivery, to adjust the patient's blood volume, or for central drug infusion. In addition, your anesthesiologist may place a Swan–Ganz® catheter (SGC) also known as a pulmonary artery (PA) catheter. This catheter can monitor pulmonary artery pressure plus measure cardiac output and other cardiovascular functions. Swan–Ganz® is for specific monitoring and central access. The SGC has multiple ports for central circulation access, including regional anesthesia, RA port, PA port, CVP port, and possibly the main line or introducer. What it means for coding: If documentation shows that your anesthesiologist placed a PA catheter, you'll report 93503 in addition to the appropriate anesthesia code. Reason: When an anesthesiologist places an SGC line, he runs it through the CVP line. So when the CVP line is inserted as part of the procedure of inserting an SGC, the CVP line is considered a component of the line placement and is not reimbursable; only the Swan–Ganz® line is reimbursable. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider passes a catheter into the coronary arteries and injects dye to evaluate heart function in a patient with congenital heart disease. He supervises the collection of images, interprets the images, and makes a report of his findings. Explanation During a cardiac catheterization in a patient with congenital heart disease, the provider introduces a catheter into the coronary arteries, under fluoroscopic guidance. The provider injects dye into one or more arteries and checks the blood flow, pressure and catheter position. He may perform multiple injections and obtain multiple views. He supervises the collection of images, interprets the images, and makes a report of his findings. Terminology Cardiac catheterization: The insertion of a catheter, or tube, into a major vessel in the groin or another location, and advanced to the heart to perform diagnostic tests, such as dye studies, and therapeutic procedures. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Congenital heart disease: A general term for a problem with the heart's structure or function due to abnormal heart development before birth; often divided into two types, cyanotic, a blue discoloration caused by low oxygen levels, and noncyanotic or acyanotic; many congenital heart defects occur unassociated with other diseases but association with other genetic and chromosomal syndromes is not uncommon. Congenital heart catheterization: Cardiac catheterization performed in a patient with congenital heart disease, which is heart defects present at birth. Coronary arteries: Vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle, such as the right or left coronary artery, left anterior descending, posterior descending, and circumflex. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Tips Because +93563 is an add on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code. This code includes moderate sedation services, according to coding guidelines, so you should not report sedation separately. Read Less
