Explanation The provider applies electrodes on the wrists or ankles of the patient and passes a mild electric current through the electrodes. He then measures the resistance of the tissues to the electric current at one or more frequencies, analyzes it, and converts the data using an established equation to determine the fluid levels in the tissues. Terminology Bioimpedance spectroscopy, or BIS: A procedure that uses electrodes placed on the skin to send mild electric current through a patient's tissues; the results indicate the amount of intracellular and extracellular fluid in the tissues. Electrodes, or leads: Insulated wires that can transmit and receive electrical impulses Lymphedema: Accumulation of fluid within the spaces between cells in the tissues that causes swelling; the condition typical results from a disorder of the lymphatic system or kidneys. short_description: Duplex scan of extracranial arteries; complete bilateral study Notes: (Do not report 93880 in conjunction with 93895)
lay_term: Duplex scanning of arteries for the evaluation of blood flow is a type of non–invasive vascular diagnostic process. A physician can visualize and selectively assess the flow patterns of peripheral vessels using real–time ultrasound imaging and pulsed Doppler. The presence of arterial stenosis, occlusion, and identification of incompetent veins can also be achieved through this process. Explanation The physician or a technician performs the duplex scanning procedure by holding a probe on the skin surface. The probe emits short ultrasonic pulses which travel into the body. When the ultrasound pulse collides with a soft tissue, it gets reflected and arrives back to the probe as an echo. Echoes from stationary structures come back to the probe with the same frequency, but in moving targets, echoes return with a higher or lower frequency. The scanner can detect even minute changes in frequency and can calculate the speed and direction of blood flow. Successive pulses from the probe and echoes generated through the body together create an image of a targeted plane in the body. During this procedure, the physician examines vascular flow of both sides of the head and neck. Terminology Doppler: A technique to measure the flow of blood in a blood vessel. Duplex Doppler scan: A method of visualizing and selectively assessing the flow patterns of peripheral arteries and veins using ultrasound imaging and pulsed Doppler. Tips National Correct Coding Initiative edits don't prevent you from reporting carotid Doppler (93880) on the same day as venous Doppler (93970 and 93971), but your payer may question the medical necessity of performing both services on the same day. Doctors don't usually order both of these exams for the same patient on the same date of service. Code 93880: Indications for noninvasive physiologic cerebrovascular studies (including 93880, Duplex scan of extracranial arteries ...) include neck trauma, stroke and pulsatile tinnitus. The studies may also be appropriate before a patient with systemic atherosclerosis has coronary artery bypass grafting or after a patient has carotid surgery. Codes 93970 and 93971: Indications for peripheral venous exams (93970–93971, Duplex scan of extremity veins ...)" are separated into three major categories: deep vein thrombosis, chronic venous insufficiency, and vein selection for arterial surgery. Studies, which are medically necessary to determine subsequent treatment, are covered." Check with the referring physician to identify the reasons why the patient needs both exams. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline A complete transcranial Doppler (TCD) study (93886) includes ultrasound evaluation of the right and left anterior circulation territories and the posterior circulation territory (to include vertebral arteries and basilar artery). Use TCD study codes (93886, 93888, 93892, 93893) when a single study is performed. Use 93896, 93897, 93898, when a vasoreactivity study, emboli detection without intravenous microbubble injection, or venous-arterial shunt detection with intravenous microbubble injection is performed in conjunction with a complete TCD on the same day. Section Specific Guideline Vascular studies include patient care required to perform the studies, supervision of the studies and interpretation of study results with copies for patient records of hard copy output with analysis of all data, including bidirectional vascular flow or imaging when provided. Duplex scan (eg, 93880, 93882) describes an ultrasonic scanning procedure for characterizing the pattern and direction of blood flow in arteries or veins with the production of real-time images integrating B-mode two-dimensional vascular structure, Doppler spectral analysis, and color flow Doppler imaging. Codes 93922, 93923, 93924 describe the evaluation of non-imaging physiologic recordings of pressures with Doppler analysis of bi-directional blood flow, plethysmography, and/or oxygen tension measurements appropriate for the anatomic area studied. Limited studies for lower extremity require either: (1) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries plus bidirectional Doppler waveform recording and analysis at 1-2 levels; or (2) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries plus volume plethysmography at 1-2 levels; or (3) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries with transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements at 1-2 levels. Alternatively, a complete study may be reported with measurements at a single level if provocative functional maneuvers (eg, measurements with postural provocative tests, or measurements with reactive hyperemia) are performed. Complete studies for upper extremity require either: (1) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and bidirectional Doppler waveform recording and analysis at 3 or more levels; or (2) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and volume plethysmography at 3 or more levels; or (3) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements at 3 or more levels. Potential levels include arm, forearm, wrist, and digits. Alternatively, a complete study may be reported with measurements at a single level if provocative functional maneuvers (eg, measurements with postural provocative tests, or measurements with cold stress) are performed.

Terminology Atherosclerosis: A disease characterized by deposition of fatty material on the inner walls of the arteries. Atherosclerotic burden: The sum or extent of atherosclerotic disease. short_description: Transcranial Doppler study of the intracranial arteries; complete study
lay_term: The provider performs an ultrasound of the arteries inside the head using Doppler technique to study the flow and speed of blood through the arteries. He performs the procedure to assess blood flow to the brain. Providers may order the test to determine whether there is an artery occlusion or stenosis that could result in cerebrovascular diseases such as stroke and brain hemorrhages. Providers also may order the test as a screening study for children with particular conditions, such as sickle cell anemia. Explanation The provider applies a gel to the skin, typically over the base of the skull and the area over the ears. The gel improves contact between the transducer and the skin and helps the sound waves penetrate the skin better. The provider holds the transducer in place on the skin's surface to record blood flow information. In a complete study, the provider evaluates the right and left anterior circulation territories and the posterior circulation territory. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body. Basilar artery: One of the arteries that supply blood to the brain. Doppler ultrasound: An imaging procedure that records sound waves reflecting off moving objects, such as blood, to measure their speed and other aspects of how they flow. Hemorrhage: Bleeding, typically used to refer to active or significant bleed. Intracranial: Inside of or including the skull. Noninvasive: Refers to a procedure that does not involve a surgical incision. Occlusion: A blockage or closure in a vessel or organ. Posterior: Closer to the back part of the body. Sickle cell anemia: A genetic disease in which an individual produces red blood cells shaped like a crescent or sickle; these blood don't last as long as normal, round red blood cells, which leads to anemia; when the sickle cells get stuck in blood vessels, blocking blood flow, it can cause pain and organ damage. Stenosis: Narrowing of a vessel or other structure; a stenosed valve becomes stiff affecting its ability to open and close properly. Stroke: Lay term for a cerebrovascular accident, or CVA; an ischemic stroke happens when a blood clot blocks flow to the brain; a hemorrhagic stroke happens when a blood vessel breaks and bleeds into the brain; transient ischemic attack, or TIA, refers to mini strokes that occur when the blood supply to the brain is briefly interrupted. Transcranial: Through the skull. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. Vertebral arteries: Major arteries that supply blood to the brain. Tips Transcranial Doppler, or TCD, study is a noninvasive diagnostic ultrasound evaluation of the intracranial arteries. To qualify as complete, 93886 documentation must show ultrasound evaluation of the right and left anterior circulation territories and the posterior circulation territory to include vertebral arteries and basilar artery. To report a limited transcranial study, report 93888. Read Less

lay_term: The provider performs an ultrasound of the arteries inside the head using Doppler technique to study the flow and speed of blood through the arteries. The provider injects a microbubble to enhance the imaging. The provider performs this study to search for venous–arterial shunt, an abnormal connection between the venous and arterial systems. Explanation The provider applies a gel to the skin, typically the base of the skull and the area over the ears. The gel improves contact between the transducer and the skin and helps the sound waves penetrate the skin better. The provider holds a transducer in place on the skin’s surface to record blood flow information. The provider injects microbubble contrast into the patient’s vein and checks for venous–arterial shunt signals in the Doppler waveform. A venous–arterial shunt is an abnormal pathway where blood flows directly from veins (which normally carry deoxygenated blood) into arteries (which carry oxygen–rich blood). The provider monitors the Doppler signal for the presence of these microbubbles, which would indicate an abnormal connection between the venous and arterial systems, suggesting the presence of a venous–arterial shunt. Terminology Doppler ultrasound: An imaging procedure that records sound waves reflecting off moving objects, such as blood, to measure their speed and other aspects of how they flow. Intracranial: Inside of or including the skull. Transcranial: Through the skull. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand–held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. The study evaluates how well the intracranial arteries respond to changes in carbon dioxide levels, which can affect blood vessel tone and blood flow. The provider positions the TCD ultrasound probe on specific areas of the head to measure blood flow velocities and flow velocity changes in intracranial arteries. These measurements help assess the ability of blood vessels to dilate or constrict. lay_term: Noninvasive arterial diagnostic procedures are performed to examine the rate of blood flow in an area and to assess the presence of a blockage in the upper and lower extremity arteries. Plethysmography, segmental blood pressure measurements, and Doppler waveform analysis are few of the tests that can be performed under this category. Explanation Segmental pressure measurement is one of the important examinations that a physician may perform to evaluate blood flow patterns and blockage in the arms and legs. During this process, the physician places two or three pneumatic blood pressure cuffs on the arms or legs at various levels (proximal thigh, distal thigh, foot, ankle, calf, etc.). The cuffs are inflated above the normal systolic blood pressure and then deflated slowly. Blood pressure measurements are taken using a Doppler instrument. Volume changes in the upper and lower extremity segment below the cuff are translated into pulsatile pressure, which is detected by a transducer and displayed as a pressure pulse contour. Several functional maneuvers are also performed for complete bilateral study. A high–level drop in pressure between two adjacent cuffs indicates the presence of a blockage or stricture inside the artery at that part of the extremity. The precision rate of identifying a blockage in an artery via this process is quite high (almost 97%). Terminology Doppler: A technique to measure the flow of blood in a blood vessel. Plethysmography: A noninvasive procedure that measures the amount of blood flow present in an organ or artery or part of the body. This is used to diagnose deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and arterial occlusive disease. Tips This code is for a bilateral study, so do not append modifier 50 when the procedure is performed bilaterally. The Ankle-Brachial Index (or ABI) is reportable with 93922 or 93923 as long as simultaneous Doppler recording and analysis of bidirectional blood flow, volume plethysmography, or transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements are also performed. Duplex scan (eg, 93880, 93882) describes an ultrasonic scanning procedure for characterizing the pattern and direction of blood flow in arteries or veins with the production of real-time images integrating B-mode two-dimensional vascular structure, Doppler spectral analysis, and color flow Doppler imaging. Physiologic studies Noninvasive physiologic studies are performed using equipment separate and distinct from the duplex ultrasound imager. Codes 93922, 93923, 93924 describe the evaluation of non-imaging physiologic recordings of pressures with Doppler analysis of bi-directional blood flow, plethysmography, and/or oxygen tension measurements appropriate for the anatomic area studied. Limited studies for lower extremity require either: (1) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries plus bidirectional Doppler waveform recording and analysis at 1-2 levels; or (2) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries plus volume plethysmography at 1-2 levels; or (3) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries with transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements at 1-2 levels. Potential levels include high thigh, low thigh, calf, ankle, metatarsal and toes. Limited studies for upper extremity require either: (1) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and bidirectional Doppler waveform recording and analysis at 1-2 levels; or (2) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and volume plethysmography at 1-2 levels; or (3) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements at 1-2 levels. Potential levels include arm, forearm, wrist, and digits. Complete studies for lower extremity require either: (1) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries plus bidirectional Doppler waveform recording and analysis at 3 or more levels; or (2) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries plus volume plethysmography at 3 or more levels; or (3) ankle/brachial indices at distal posterior tibial and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries with transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements at 3 or more levels. Alternatively, a complete study may be reported with measurements at a single level if provocative functional maneuvers (eg, measurements with postural provocative tests, or measurements with reactive hyperemia) are performed. Complete studies for upper extremity require either: (1) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and bidirectional Doppler waveform recording and analysis at 3 or more levels; or (2) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and volume plethysmography at 3 or more levels; or (3) Doppler-determined systolic pressures and transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements at 3 or more levels. Potential levels include arm, forearm, wrist, and digits. Alternatively, a complete study may be reported with measurements at a single level if provocative functional maneuvers (eg, measurements with postural provocative tests, or measurements with cold stress) are performed.

short_description: Noninvasive physiologic studies of lower extremity arteries, at rest and following treadmill stress testing, (ie, bidirectional Doppler waveform or volume plethysmography recording and analysis at rest with ankle/brachial indices immediately after and at timed intervals following performance of a standardized protocol on a motorized treadmill plus recording of time of onset of claudication or other symptoms, maximal walking time, and time to recovery) complete bilateral study Notes: (Do not report 93924 in conjunction with 93922, 93923)
lay_term: The provider assesses blood flow in the arteries of the legs before and after exercise using various techniques, such as bidirectional Doppler waveform analysis, or volume plethysmography, and measurement of ankle brachial indices. He monitors symptoms and exercise tolerance. Providers use plethysmography to diagnose deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, and arterial occlusive disease. Explanation The provider places blood pressure cuffs on the legs and arms at the appropriate levels. He obtains Doppler signals from the arteries in the legs by holding a small probe against the subject's skin. The provider applies blood pressure cuffs to the arms and lower legs and compares the differences in pressure between the arms and the ankles, a technique referred to as ankle brachial index. The patient is asked to perform some exercise, such as walking on a treadmill. He takes blood pressures immediately after exercise and at various times during the rest period following exercise. He monitors symptoms and exercise tolerance as well as the time needed to recover from exercise. Terminology Bilateral: On two sides; opposite of unilateral. Claudication: A condition characterized by leg pain and cramping, especially in the calf that occurs the muscles of the legs do get enough blood and oxygen when they are working harder, such as during exercise or walking; when severe, claudication may occur even when at rest; also called peripheral artery disease or PAD and peripheral vascular disease or PVD. Doppler ultrasound: An imaging procedure that records sound waves reflecting off moving objects, such as blood, to measure their speed and other aspects of how they flow. Noninvasive: Refers to a procedure that does not involve a surgical incision. Plethysmography: A noninvasive procedure to measure the amount of blood flow present in an organ or artery or other part of the body; providers use plethysmography to diagnose deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, and arterial occlusive disease. Transcutaneous oxygen tension measurement, or TCOM: Use of an electrode or electrodes placed directly on the skin to measure oxygen perfusion in order to determine if a wound or sore is getting the necessary amount of oxygen to heal. Tips Providers perform noninvasive arterial diagnostic procedures to examine the rate of blood flow and to assess the presence of blockage in the lower extremity arteries. This category of tests includes plethysmography, transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements, or TCOM, and Doppler waveform analysis. No need to add modifier 50 for a bilateral study as that is already mentioned in the Code Descriptor. This procedure includes the use of a simple hand–held device. CPT® includes a range of codes for arterial Doppler studies on the extremities. Coding will vary depending on if the diagnostic test was a limited or complete study, if the study followed a treadmill stress test, and or if the study included the criteria for a Duplex scan. For some providers, coding may also depend on the diagnosis code. Check your provider's documentation and review the options in code family 93922 to 93931, Noninvasive extremity arterial studies, including digits, to ensure you choose correctly. Read Less

short_description: Duplex scan of lower extremity arteries or arterial bypass grafts; unilateral or limited study Notes: (Do not report 93926 in conjunction with 93986 for the same extremity)
lay_term: The provider performs a duplex ultrasound scan of the lower extremity arteries or bypass grafts. Providers perform noninvasive arterial diagnostic procedures to examine the rate of blood flow and to assess the presence of blockage in the lower extremity arteries on just one side. Explanation With the patient lying on an exam table, the provider applies a gel to the area of the leg being studied. The gel improves contact between the transducer and the skin and helps the sound waves penetrate the skin better. The provider then presses the transducer firmly against the skin and sweeps it back and forth over the area to be examined. A duplex scan adds visualization and an imaging component to the Doppler waveform study. The test usually takes about 30 minutes. Terminology Bypass graft: Placing a vein graft between an obstructed artery and a nonobstructed artery, or before and after an obstruction in a single artery to reestablish blood flow; providers may also anastomose two arteries together in such a way as to bypass an obstruction in one of the arteries. Duplex ultrasound scan: A duplex ultrasound scan combines traditional ultrasound, the use of sound waves that bounce off blood vessels to create images, with Doppler ultrasound, which records sound waves reflecting off moving objects, such as blood, to measure their speed and other aspects of how they flow; color Doppler produces color coded images of blood flow that are overlaid on the black and white anatomical images produced by the device. Noninvasive: Refers to a procedure that does not involve a surgical incision. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. Unilateral: On a single side; opposite of bilateral, on two sides. Tips For a complex duplex scan of both lower extremities, report 93925. CPT® includes a range of codes for arterial Doppler studies on the extremities. Coding will vary depending on if the diagnostic test was a limited or complete study, if the study followed a treadmill stress test, and or if the study included the criteria for a Duplex scan. For some providers, coding may also depend on the diagnosis code. Check your provider's documentation and review the options in code family 93922 to 93931, Noninvasive extremity arterial studies, including digits, to ensure you choose correctly. When your provider performs spectral and color Doppler evaluation of the extremities, you should use one of the following appropriate codes: Code 93925 or 93926, Duplex scan of lower extremity arteries or arterial bypass grafts; bilateral or unilateral/limited study respectively; Code 93930, Duplex scan of upper extremity arteries or arterial bypass grafts; complete bilateral study, or 93931, Duplex scan of upper extremity arteries or arterial bypass grafts; unilateral or limited study; Or code 93970, Duplex scan of extremity veins including responses to compression and other maneuvers; complete bilateral study, or 93971, Duplex scan of extremity veins including responses to compression and other maneuvers; unilateral or limited study, Do not report 93926 for a unilateral noninvasive physiological study. Instead, look to 93922, Noninvasive physiologic studies of upper or lower extremity arteries, single level, bilateral, e.g., ankle brachial indices, Doppler waveform analysis, volume plethysmography, transcutaneous oxygen tension measurement, or 93923, Noninvasive physiologic studies of upper or lower extremity arteries, multiple levels or with provocative functional maneuvers, complete bilateral study, e.g., segmental blood pressure measurements, segmental Doppler waveform analysis, segmental volume plethysmography, segmental transcutaneous oxygen tension measurements, measurements with postural provocative tests, measurements with reactive hyperemia. Important: Codes 93922 and 93923 describe bilateral services, so if for some reason the provider performs and documents a unilateral study, you should append modifier 52, Reduced services, to the code to indicate that the provider did not perform the full service the code describes. Common pitfall: Reporting 93926 for a unilateral noninvasive study is tempting because you'll see the term unilateral when you quickly scan the codes. But you should report 93926 only if your provider performs the duplex scan. Code 93926 does not apply to the noninvasive physiologic studies that 93922 and 93923 describe. Read Less

short_description: Duplex scan of extremity veins including responses to compression and other maneuvers; complete bilateral study Notes: (Do not report 93970 in conjunction with 93985, 93986 for the same extremity[ies])
lay_term: The provider performs an ultrasound scanning procedure called a duplex scan to characterize the pattern and direction of blood flow in extremity veins (arms or legs). This is a complete, bilateral imaging study that includes assessing the patient’s response to maneuvers such as compression. Explanation The provider spreads a gel over the patient’s skin at the areas to be tested. The provider moves the ultrasound probe (transducer) over the skin of the extremities (arms or legs). The probe emits short ultrasonic (sound wave) pulses that travel into the body. When the ultrasound pulse collides with a soft tissue, the sound waves reflect to the probe as an echo. A computer converts the sound wave data into real–time images. Duplex scans combine conventional (B–mode, two dimensional) ultrasound imaging of the vascular structure and Doppler ultrasound, in which sound waves bounce off moving blood cells, causing a change in pitch known as the Doppler effect. The scan includes Doppler spectral analysis that shows blood flow information on a graph, which can help reveal blockage, and color flow Doppler imaging that changes sound waves into colors that show the speed and direction of blood flow. During the service, the provider also performs maneuvers to observe changes in the flow inside the veins. An example is compression using blood pressure cuffs. This is a complete, bilateral study. The provider documents the images and interpretation of the results. Terminology B mode ultrasound: Imaging technique using high–frequency sound waves to provide a cross sectional, two–dimensional view in gray scale imaging; also known as bright scan or B scan ultrasound. Tips See 93971 for a unilateral or limited study. If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC. Note, however, that payer policy may exempt hospitals from appending modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Duplex scan of arterial inflow and venous outflow of abdominal, pelvic, scrotal contents and/or retroperitoneal organs; complete study
lay_term: The provider performs a complete study of the abdominal, pelvic, scrotal, and or retroperitoneal organs using duplex ultrasound. He performs the procedure to examine the vascular supply to the organs involved as well as the venous return. Explanation With the patient lying face up on an exam table, the practitioner applies a gel on the skin over the abdominal, pelvic, scrotal, and retroperitoneal area. The gel improves contact between the transducer and the skin and helps in the transmission of the sound waves. A duplex ultrasound machine sends high frequency sound waves through a probe, also called a transducer. The transducer is then pressed against the skin and moved over the area being studied. The machine creates images of the structures in those areas, and a monitor displays the images. The test usually takes about 30 minutes. Terminology Duplex ultrasound scan: A duplex ultrasound scan combines traditional ultrasound, the use of sound waves that bounce off blood vessels to create images, with Doppler ultrasound, which records sound waves reflecting off moving objects, such as blood, to measure their speed and other aspects of how they flow. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity that attaches various organs to the abdominal wall. Retroperitoneal: Behind and outside the peritoneum. Scrotum: The sac that contains the testes, or testicles. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Ultrasound transducer: A small hand held device that resembles a microphone and attaches to an ultrasound scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high frequency sound waves into the body and then detects the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. lay_term: The provider performs a duplex ultrasound scan of the arteries and veins in both upper extremities to assess vascular supply and venous return in the arm prior to establishing hemodialysis access. Explanation With the patient lying face up on an exam table, the practitioner applies a gel on the skin of both upper extremities. The gel improves contact between the transducer and the skin and helps in the transmission of the sound waves. A duplex ultrasound machine sends high–frequency sound waves through a transducer. The transducer is then pressed against the skin and sweeps it back and forth over the area being studied. The transducer captures the sounds waves being reflected back and a computer creates color–coded images of blood flow in the vessels in the area being studied. These colored images are overlaid on black and white anatomical images produced by the device and displayed on a monitor. The provider uses the images to assess the speed, direction, and amount of blood flow in the vessels of the upper extremities. The test usually takes about 30 minutes. Terminology Duplex Doppler scan: A method of visualizing and selectively assessing the flow patterns of peripheral arteries and veins using ultrasound imaging and pulsed Doppler. short_description: Ventilation assist and management, initiation of pressure or volume preset ventilators for assisted or controlled breathing; hospital inpatient/observation, each subsequent day
lay_term: Use this code for each subsequent day managing ventilator settings for a patient who cannot breathe on his own. Explanation Use this code for the initial setting of ventilator parameters for a patient who cannot breathe on his own. The service is performed for a hospital inpatient or observation patient, each subsequent day of treatment. In assisted or controlled breathing, a ventilator delivers preset breaths in coordination with the respiratory effort of the patient. The provider examines the patient and determines that the patient requires ventilation. Depending on whether the patient has reduced oxygen readings or apneic spells, the provider sets the ventilator settings to assist or to breathe for the patient. The provider sedates the patient so as to facilitate optimal ventilation and prevent the patient from fighting the ventilator tube. During weaning, or removing a patient from a ventilator, he gradually changes the modes of mechanical ventilation to allow the patient to resume breathing on his own. Terminology Continuous negative pressure ventilation, or CNP: Rarely used, CNP ventilation involves placing the patient in a chamber that reduces external pressure on the chest and allows the lungs to expand and fill with oxygen blown into the chamber. Positive airway pressure ventilation: In positive airway pressure ventilation, the provider places an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy to force oxygen into the lungs; settings on the ventilator allow the pressure to increase and decrease facilitating the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide; positive airway pressure may be intermittent, as in IPPB, or continuous, as in CPAP, which pumps air under pressure into the airway through a mask or nasal prongs, keeping the windpipe open during sleep. Acute respiratory distress: Sudden onset of difficulty breathing or periods of apnea, or failure to breathe. Sedation: A calm or sleep state induced by a medication referred to as a sedative. Ventilator: A mechanical device that provides breathing assistance to a patient or, if necessary, breathes for the patient. Weaning: The gradual step down of mechanical assistance to allow the patient to become self sufficient. Tips The general rule is that you cannot report ventilation therapy with an E/M service. However, your code choice lies on deciding whether to report the ventilation therapy or roll the work into the E/M level. Notes for these encounters will likely lead you to the proper code choice: If the provider focuses on ventilation management services during the encounter and does not document key components warranting an E/M, report a ventilation management code only. But if the notes describe an encounter in which the provider performs ventilation management during the course of a larger E/M, report the E/M code. Read Less

short_description: Spirometry, including graphic record, total and timed vital capacity, expiratory flow rate measurement(s), with or without maximal voluntary ventilation Notes: (Do not report 94010 in conjunction with 94150, 94200, 94375, 94728)
lay_term: The provider or technician administers a spirometry test to assess the patient's respiratory function. The spirometer is attached to a computer that records the total and timed vital capacity (maximum expired air) and expiratory flow rate (speed of expiration) and displays the results as a graph. The patient may or may not be required to exhale rapidly over 12 to 15 seconds after deep breathing. Explanation During this test, the patient is asked to stand or sit up straight. The patient breathes in and then blows hard into the spirometer's mouthpiece for 5 to 6 seconds until he feels his lungs completely empty of air. The technician may repeat this test several times for the best result. Later, the result is interpreted by the physician. The device measures the flow and volume of air during inhalation and exhalation. The result is represented in a graphic format where the X axis represents the volume of air and the Y axis represents the rate of airflow. Spirometry, also known as a pulmonary function test (PFT), measures the functionality of the lungs. Respiratory disorders such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and pulmonary fibrosis can be evaluated via spirometry. Terminology Expiratory flow rate (EFR): Maximum speed of expiration, a measure of a person's ability to breathe out air, as measured by a small hand–held device called a peak flow meter; also called peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR). Maximal voluntary ventilation (MVV): The total volume of air that can be exhaled during 12 to 15 seconds of rapid, deep breathing; also called maximum breathing capacity (MBC). Timed vital capacity: The maximal amount (volume) of air that can be forcibly breathed out during a short period of time. Vital capacity: Measure of the maximal amount (volume) of air that a patient exhales following a maximal inspiration; it equals the inspiratory reserve volume (the amount of air that can be forcefully inhaled following a normal inhalation) plus tidal volume (the normal volume of air breathed in and out during normal respiration) plus expiratory reserve volume (the amount of air remaining in the lungs after exhaling). Tips For pulmonary function testing on infants and children, see codes 94011 to 94013. For patient–initiated spirometry over a 30–day period, see codes 94014 to 94016. For a viral capacity test as a separate procedure, see 94150. For a test of maximum breathing capacity/maximal voluntary ventilation, see 94200. Read Less

short_description: Measurement of lung volumes (ie, functional residual capacity [FRC], forced vital capacity [FVC], and expiratory reserve volume [ERV]) in an infant or child through 2 years of age
lay_term: The provider performs a pulmonary function test for an infant or child up to two years old to measure the amount of air in the lungs at different points during breathing, using a technique to determine a range of lung conditions. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses a technique known as raised volume rapid thoracoabdominal compression, or RVRTC, to obtain lung volume measurements. The provider places the patient in a pneumatic jacket–like device and takes a series of measurements before, during, and after using the device to mechanically squeeze the patient’s chest after inflating the infant’s lungs several times. The measurement the provider takes includes FRC, or the functional residual capacity, which measures the amount of air remaining in the lungs after a regular undisturbed breath. FRC measurement techniques include gas dilution methods, such as the helium dilution technique or nitrogen washout technique, which measure the lung volume at the central airways. Another option is plethysmography using a whole–body infant plethysmograph, a device that measures changes in volume of all the thoracic gas, including gas that is communicating and not communicating with the central airways. The provider also measures the FVC, or forced vital capacity, meaning the total amount of air when exhaling, and the ERV, or expiratory reserve volume, that measures the additional amount of air that the patient can expel from the lungs after a normal breath. If appropriate you can report 94013 twice on the same day, such as before and after bronchodilator. Read Less

lay_term: The spirometry test is performed with a spirometer. The instrument displays a graphical representation, known as a spirogram, of the test results. The basic forced volume vital capacity (FVC) test is done by asking the patient to inhale and exhale air through the sensors of the device. The speed and volume of the air is measured and the result is displayed on a graph. A bronchodilator drug is also given to the patient and the spirometry test is performed before and after the drug administration to find out the difference between results obtained in two different phases. The difference in results helps to deduce the responsiveness of the respiratory system to the bronchodilator. Explanation In a spirometer, a mouthpiece is attached with a sensor and graph plotter. Usually the patient is asked to take the deepest breath he can, and then exhale into the mouthpiece as hard as possible (forced exhalation), and for as long as possible. While assessing possible upper airway obstruction, the patient is asked to do a rapid inhalation (inspiration) just after the forced exhalation. Sometimes, a few variations in the process can be seen when the test will be preceded by a period of quiet breathing in and out from the sensor (tidal volume), or the rapid breath in (forced inspiration part) will take place before the forced exhalation. Soft nose clips are used to make sure that no air is escaping through the nose and the full amount of air is entering the mouthpiece through mouth only. The spirometer records the in– and outflow of air and uses a microprocessor to calculate and finally plot the airflow. Spirometry is also used to assess lung function over a period of time, and many times to determine the efficiency of bronchodilator drugs such as Albuterol or Combivent, that are available in aerosol form. Spirometry is performed before and after inhaling the bronchodilator to record the difference between the two results. This helps to evaluate the efficacy of the bronchodilator, based on the responsiveness of the respiratory system to the drug. short_description: Maximum breathing capacity, maximal voluntary ventilation Notes: (Do not report 94200 in conjunction with 94010, 94060)
lay_term: The provider measures the largest volume of air that a patient can voluntarily breathe while the patient breathes as deeply and quickly as possible for a specified period of time. short_description: Breathing response to hypoxia (hypoxia response curve) Notes: (For high altitude simulation test [HAST], see 94452, 94453)
lay_term: The provider performs a pulmonary function test to determine the lungs’ responses to an inadequate supply of oxygen. Explanation In this exam the provider measures a patient’s lung function using one of several approaches, such as an open–circuit nitrogen washout or a closed–circuit helium dilution technique. When the provider uses these techniques, he measures the lung volume by having a patient breathe nitrogen or helium gas through a tube for a specified period of time. He then measures the change in concentration of the gas in a chamber attached to the tube after the patient is done breathing. By knowing the concentration of the gas before starting the test and the volume of the spirometer, he calculates the amount of gas in the patient's lungs at the start of the test along with the functional residual capacity of the patient’s lungs and the residual volume as required. During the test, the provider decreases oxygen saturation and takes oxygen measurements through various methods, such as rebreathing, end–tidal forcing, or pulse oximeter readings, which measure or help calculate and assess the ventilatory response to hypoxia. Terminology End–tidal forcing: Technique that sets oxygen and carbon dioxide to desired levels by altering the inspired gas partial pressures at the end of a normal exhale on a breath–by–breath basis using computer–controlled feedback. Hypoxia: An inadequate supply of oxygen in blood or tissue. Pulse oximeter: Device that indirectly measures the oxygen saturation of a patient's blood. Rebreathing: Partial or complete inhalation of previously exhaled gases. lay_term: The patient breathes a low oxygen mixture while the provider monitors the patient’s oxyhemoglobin saturations. The provider interprets the results and creates a report. lay_term: The provider performs complex cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) to evaluate the heart and lung function. The procedure includes measuring minute ventilation (the volume of gas exhaled). Minute ventilation helps estimate ventilation to perfusion ratio, thereby assessing pulmonary function. Explanation In this test, the provider measures physiological parameters like heart rate, blood pressure, ventilation to perfusion ratio, and oxygen saturation during rest and exercise. He also checks lung volumes and assesses the impact of exercise on them. The provider has the patient walk on a treadmill to evaluate the exercise ability of patients with moderate to advanced lung diseases. The provider monitors the patient’s oxygen saturation, heart rate, and dyspnea during and after exercise. The test includes measuring the patient’s oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production in the blood by taking a blood sample during the test. The procedure also includes continuous electrocardiogram recording during the exercise by placement of chest electrodes. CPET assesses pulmonary, cardiac, and skeletal system functioning, and is more useful than the pulmonary stress testing alone. Terminology Dyspnea: Shortness of breath. Spirometry: Also known as a pulmonary function study; is a diagnostic test to measure the functionality of the lung. Tips If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Physician or other qualified health care professional services for outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation; without continuous oximetry monitoring (per session)
lay_term: The provider performs services related to a session of outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation, a treatment program that helps a patient who has a chronic respiratory illness. Typical sessions include education and exercise. The session does not involve continuous oximetry monitoring. Explanation Pulmonary rehabilitation is a treatment program aimed at helping a patient with chronic respiratory disease improve their quality of life. This treatment protocol helps the patient reduce their shortness of breath, increase their exercise tolerance, and improve their general well–being. A typical session includes curriculum–based education on topics such as self–management and advance care planning, tailored to the patient’s needs. The session also includes provider–prescribed exercise based on the patient’s individualized treatment plan. Examples of exercise equipment used include treadmills, bikes, steppers, upper body ergometers (UBEs; a device where the patient uses arm cranks in a motion like legs pedaling a bike), pulleys, and balance boards. The provider assesses the patient’s outcomes. One unit of this code represents a single session that does not involve continuous oximetry monitoring to measure the level of oxygen in the blood. Terminology Respiratory: Pertaining to the structures and/organs involved in breathing and exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide, that is, the nose, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and lungs. Tips For a session with continuous oximetry monitoring, see 94626. Payer policy may dictate specific requirements for pulmonary rehab coverage. Read Less

short_description: Continuous inhalation treatment with aerosol medication for acute airway obstruction; first hour Notes: (For services of less than 1 hour, use 94640)
lay_term: The provider administers inhalation aerosol treatment with medication for up to an hour. He performs the procedure to treat acute airway obstruction. Explanation The provider discusses the procedure with the patient, parent, or guardian. He explains what will occur during continuous inhalation as well as the risks and benefits. The provider or nonphysician practitioner, or NPP, performs the treatment. Generally, the provider carries out inhalation therapy, or aerosol drug administration, by two means. First, through a nebulizer, a mechanical pump that produces a fine mist in which the drug is dispersed via a face mask. Second, through a hand held, nebulized aerosol device or puffers, which uses the effects of a pressurized gas to create and disperse the drug into a fine mist or spray. After he completes the treatment, he discusses next steps with the patient or the patient's parent or guardian. Use this code for first hour of treatment only. Terminology Acute: A medical condition or injury of sudden onset, sometimes severe in nature, and typically last a short period of time; opposite of chronic. Aerosol generator: A device that produces aerosol suspensions, as for inhalation therapy. Albuterol: An inhaled bronchodilator. Asthma: A respiratory disease that prevents the lungs from fully expanding, often in response to an allergen, a substance, such as pollen, dust, dander, venom, etc., which triggers an allergic response. short_description: Continuous negative pressure ventilation (CNP), initiation and management
lay_term: The provider initiates continuous negative pressure ventilation in a patient whose cannot breathe on his own due to paralysis or some other pathology. Explanation The provider initiates high frequency oscillation using an airtight cuirass, a negative pressure full body respirator, placed around the chest wall. Negative pressure ventilation, or NPV, works by exposing the chest wall's surface to subatmospheric pressures thereby expanding the lungs and drawing air into it. The provider adjusts the settings and manages the continuous negative pressure ventilation, or CNP. Terminology Subatmospheric pressure: Lower pressure than the atmospheric pressure, which is generally the pressure of the air around us and at sea level, designated as 1 atm; pressure decreases with increased elevation and increases with lower elevations, e.g. diving below the sea level. Tips Hint: When your provider performs 94662, you'll need to decide whether to report the ventilation therapy or roll the work into the E/M level. Notes for these encounters will likely lead you to the proper code choice: If the provider focuses on ventilation management services during the encounter and does not document key components warranting an E/M, report a ventilation management code only. But if the notes describe an encounter in which the provider performs ventilation management during the course of a larger E/M, report the E/M code. Read Less

short_description: Oxygen uptake, expired gas analysis; rest and exercise, direct, simple
lay_term: The provider collects the patient’s expelled air during rest and exercise, and uses it to determine the patient’s oxygen uptake. Explanation The provider prepares the testing system for collecting the patient’s exhaled breath. For instance, in a typical test, the patient breathes in through a special device that allows for air to come in but collects all expelled air in a device such as a Douglas bag, an inflatable bag designed for this purpose. The provider performs expired air collection both with the patient at rest and during exercise, such as a set time on an exercise bike or treadmill. The provider then uses a gas analyzer to measure the patient’s oxygen consumption rate based on the collected expired air. Tips The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule divides this code into professional and technical components, so if you are reporting only the professional interpretation for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. Appending modifier TC indicates you are reporting only the technical component for the service. lay_term: The provider performs a pulmonary function test, or PFT, to determine the patient’s lung volumes, such as total lung capacity, residual volume, and functional residual capacity. The testing also may include checking airway resistance. Explanation The testing provider sets up the testing instruments. This set up may involve having the patient sit in a specially designed small room, often called a body box. A mouthpiece attached to a measuring device measures volume and pressure changes as the patient breathes. Another approach uses belts wrapped around the patient to sense changes in the chest and abdomen. The provider may also ask the patient to perform panting to check airway resistance. The provider interpreting the results reviews the pressure volume curves created during testing as well as the pressure and flow results if the patient also completed the airway resistance test. The provider checks for errors, interprets the results, and documents the interpretation in the medical record. Providers may order this test for patients with symptoms affecting the lungs, such as shortness of breath, or conditions such as emphysema or lung cancer. Functional residual capacity, lungs: The volume of air left in the lungs after the patient breathes out normally. Plethysmography: Measurement of volume changes in a body part. Residual volume, lungs: The volume of air left in the lungs after the patient breathes out as much as possible. Total lung capacity: The volume of air in the lungs after the patient breathes in as much as possible. short_description: Gas dilution or washout for determination of lung volumes and, when performed, distribution of ventilation and closing volumes Notes: (Do not report 94727 in conjunction with 94726)
lay_term: The provider performs a pulmonary function test, or PFT, to assess the patient’s lung volumes using gas dilution or washout techniques that compare a known concentration of an inhaled gas with the patient’s exhaled breath. The provider also may test the patient’s ventilation distribution and closing volumes. Explanation The testing provider sets up the testing instruments. In a typical gas dilution test, the provider places a nose clip on the patient and has the patient breathe into a mouthpiece attached to a measuring device. The patient breathes in a known amount of a gas, usually helium. The patient follows the provider’s instructions on breathing throughout the test. The instruments measure the final exhaled concentration of helium, typically to calculate the functional residual capacity. In a typical washout test, the provider has the patient breathe in a known amount of nitrogen and then has the patient breathe only oxygen so the nitrogen washes out of the patient’s lungs. The instruments measure the volume of air exhaled and the concentration of nitrogen present. The variation between initial nitrogen concentration and final concentration reveals the volume, typically functional residual capacity. The provider may also check distribution of ventilation, meaning airflow, and closing volumes, the lung volume inflated when the small airways close as the patient breathes out. The provider performing the interpretation reviews the curves measured during the test and documents the interpretation in the medical record. Providers may order this test for patients with symptoms affecting the lungs, such as shortness of breath, or conditions such as emphysema or lung cancer. Terminology Functional residual capacity, lungs: The volume of air left in the lungs after the patient breathes out normally. short_description: Airway resistance by oscillometry Notes: (Do not report 94728 in conjunction with 94010, 94060, 94070, 94375, 94726)
lay_term: The provider performs pulmonary function testing (PFT) using sound waves to check airway resistance. Explanation The testing provider sets up the testing instruments. The patient breathes normally through a pneumotachograph, which is a device that records the airflow to and from the lungs. The device overlays sound waves on the patient’s breathing. A device uses the sound waves and the patient's airflow to calculate the airway resistance. The provider may use bronchodilators, substances that help open the airways, during the test. The provider performing the interpretation reviews the data from the test and checks for errors. She interprets the results and records them in the medical record. Providers may use this test for patients with lung–related conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Terminology Asthma: A disease that causes the airways of the lungs to swell and narrow, leading to wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and coughing. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): A progressive lung disease in which obstruction in the flow of air disturbs the normal breathing pattern; emphysema or chronic bronchitis are the two most common types of COPD. Chronic: A condition that is long–lasting, typically slow to develop, and with symptoms of less severity than an acute condition (one of sudden onset). lay_term: The provider monitors the patient’s oxygen saturation overnight using a sensor on the ear or finger. Explanation The provider places a sensor, such as one in the form of a clip, on the patient’s earlobe or fingertip. Oxygen saturation, sometimes called O2 sat, is the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen molecules. Hemoglobin is the protein in the red blood cell that carries oxygen to the tissue and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs. The sensor transmits the data to a computer unit that displays the result. short_description: Pediatric home apnea monitoring event recording including respiratory rate, pattern and heart rate per 30-day period of time; review, interpretation and preparation of report only by a physician or other qualified health care professional Notes: (When oxygen saturation monitoring is used in addition to heart rate and respiratory monitoring, it is not reported separately) (Do not report 94774-94777 in conjunction with 93224-93272) (Do not report apnea recording device separately) (For sleep study, see 95805-95811)
lay_term: This service is used is to report home apnea monitoring for a period of 30 days. Apnea monitors identify and warn of life–threatening events in neonates at risk for recurrent apnea, bradycardia, and hypoxemia after hospital discharge. This procedure includes the review and interpretation of data and preparation of the report. Explanation A pediatric home apnea monitor is a device that detects respiratory rate and heart rate. In a home setting, and upon the physician's or other qualified healthcare professional's order, the provider attaches stick–on patches or a belt to the infant's chest or stomach. Usually, a home monitoring company will teach parents how to operate the monitor. Depending on the gravity of the infant's apnea, the monitor will be used for a 30–day period of time. Report this code for the monitoring, review, and report carried out during that period. Terminology Other qualified healthcare professional: A "physician or other qualified healthcare professional" is an individual who is qualified by education, training, licensure/regulation (when applicable), and facility privileging (when applicable) who performs a professional service within his/her scope of practice and independently reports that professional service. These professionals are distinct from 'clinical staff.' A clinical staff member is a person who works under the supervision of a physician or other qualified health care professional and who is allowed by law, regulation and facility policy to perform or assist in the performance of a specified professional service, but who does not individually report that professional service. Other policies may also affect who may report specified services. RNs and LPNs aren't included in the definition because they cannot independently report most of the professional services that they provide. Tips If the physician performs a separately identifiable E/M service, you may report the appropriate E/M code with modifier 25. Code 94777 is only for interpretation and report by a physician or other qualified health care professional, in other words, the professional component of an apnea monitoring service. If the services provided include monitor attachment, monitoring, download of data, review, interpretation, and report, see 94774. For pediatric apnea monitor attachment only (includes hook–up, initiation of recording and disconnection), see 94775. For pediatric home apnea monitoring, download of information, receipt of transmission(s) and analyses by computer only, see 94776. Do not report these codes with electrocardiographic monitoring codes. Additional Info Example: An infant that was born at 24 weeks' gestation has residual lung disease of prematurity necessitating prolonged low–flow oxygen. She has also suffered a grade II intraventricular hemorrhage. She is now 36 weeks postconception, on full enteral feedings, and has continued to have occasional episodes of self–stimulated apnea lasting more than 15 seconds. Her providers and parents wish to send her home but are concerned about the possibility of unwitnessed prolonged apnea requiring intervention. They agree to send the patient home with heart rate and respiratory monitoring during unattended periods and sleep. The physician receives the downloaded information via computer disk or printout. The patterns are reviewed and the periods of abnormal respiratory rate or heart rate are identified and quantified. The significance of these abnormalities is summarized in a written report with recommendations for continuation or discontinuation of the monitoring. You would report this scenario with 94777. short_description: Nitric oxide expired gas determination
lay_term: The provider performs a test involving nitric oxide exhaled by a patient into a nitric oxide monitoring system. The test helps with checking the level of inflammation in the airways of a patient who is suspected to have or is confirmed to have an airway inflammation disease such as bronchial asthma. Explanation The provider instructs the patient to inhale air, that is free of nitric oxide, to the maximum of what the patient can inhale. Then he asks the patient to immediately exhale the air into a nitric oxide monitoring system. The provider measures the amount of nitric oxide that the patient exhales. The provider performs this test before and after a patient has started anti–inflammatory treatment for confirmed or suspected inflammatory diseases of the airway. The provider performs this test to check whether the anti–inflammatory treatment that the patient is taking is appropriate or not. The provider also checks whether the patient’s asthma is under control. short_description: Inhalation bronchial challenge testing (not including necessary pulmonary function tests), with histamine, methacholine, or similar compounds Notes: (For pulmonary function tests, see 94060, 94070)
lay_term: Providers use the bronchial challenge test, also known as a histamine challenge test or a methacholine challenge test, to assist in the diagnosis of asthma. The test involves the patient inhaling the test substance. This code represents the technical component of the service only. Explanation This code represents the technical component of a service in which the provider uses chemicals to perform a test when the patient has a specific allergy. The provider uses a histamine, methacholine, or similar compounds to detect how the airways respond. These compounds constrict the bronchioles, which are tubes through which air passes from the nose to the lungs after a person breathes. The provider allows the patient to inhale the substance, to which the patient is in frequent exposure, and checks if the patient is allergic to it. The provider then records the allergic reaction, which includes further contraction of the bronchioles, reflecting the changes in inhalational capacity of the patient. This test does not include pulmonary function tests, such as 94060 and 94070. The provider prepares a report after he finishes doing the test. Terminology Histamine: Chemical substance found in some of the body’s cells, which is responsible for many allergic reactions in the body. Methacholine: Substance used to assess airway responsiveness in patients with asthma; it enhances secretion and smooth muscle activity. Tips Code 95070 represents the technical component of the service only, so you should not append modifier 26 or TC. This code does not include payment for the pulmonary function tests required to evaluate the patient's prolonged post exposure bronchospasm, so you should report codes such as 94070 in addition to 95070. short_description: Ingestion challenge test (sequential and incremental ingestion of test items, eg, food, drug or other substance); initial 120 minutes of testing
lay_term: The provider performs this test to identify which foods, drugs, or other substances trigger an allergic response in an individual. Explanation In this test, the provider supplies the patient a particular food, drug, or other substance which he carefully plans to test the patient for the allergen. Next, the patient tastes the food and the provider observes him for allergic symptoms. If symptoms appear the test ends and the provider confirms that the particular allergen is a cause of hypersensitivity to the patient. But if no symptom is apparent and enough time passes without any reaction, the provider confirms that the particular food is safe for consumption by the patient. During the test, the provider slowly and sequentially increases the amount of the food or drug the patient ingests to determine if a substance causes an allergic reaction when the patient ingests the food in a larger quantity only or in cases of multiple substances testing, in combination with another item. Use this code for allergic response testing initial 120 minutes after sequential and incremental ingestion. Terminology Allergy: An adverse reaction that the body has in response to a particular food or substance. Ingestion: The act of consuming something into body by mouth. Tips Use code 95076 one time per patient encounter, regardless of the number of items the provider tests. Read Less
guidelines: Medicine Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Codes 95076 and 95079 are used to report ingestion challenge testing. Report 95076 for initial 120 minutes of testing time (ie, not physician face-to-face time). Report 95079 for each additional 60 minutes of testing time (ie, not physician face-to-face time). For total testing time less than 61 minutes (eg, positive challenge resulting in cessation of testing), report an evaluation and management service, if appropriate. Patient assessment/monitoring activities for allergic reaction (eg, blood pressure testing, peak flow meter testing) are not separately reported. In an ingestion challenge test, the provider identifies which foods, drugs, or other substances trigger an allergic response in an individual. Explanation In this test, the provider supplies the patient a particular food, drug, or other substance which he carefully plans to test the patient for the allergen. Next, the patient tastes the food and the provider observes him for allergic symptoms. If symptoms appear the test ends and the provider confirms that the particular allergen is a cause of hypersensitivity to the patient. short_description: Professional services for allergen immunotherapy in the office or institution of the prescribing physician or other qualified health care professional, including provision of allergenic extract; single injection
lay_term: This procedure is part of a series of injections the provider administers over time, gradually increasing quantities of a specific allergenic extract to achieve clinical tolerance of those allergens. Use this code when the provider administers a single injection at the session. Explanation Allergen immunotherapy involves periodic, gradual administration of purified allergen extracts via injection, with the aim of overcoming or minimizing allergic reaction, so that a patient can develop tolerance to the allergens with fewer or no symptoms. An allergic reaction is the result of the body's reaction to a specific substance that otherwise seems to be quite harmless, but can cause a severe reaction in a person allergic to the substance. Allergy shots decrease the sensitivity to allergens and often lead to lasting relief of allergy symptoms. In this procedure, the provider prepares the allergic extracts and also provides the immunotherapy. Use this code when the provider administers a single injection of allergenic extract. Tips Use 95125 when the provider prepares the allergic extracts and administers two or more injections. Read Less

lay_term: A provider analyzes and interprets data from a patient’s continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and writes a report based on interpretation. This code represents the professional component of the service only. Explanation This code represents the professional component of a service in which a patient has undergone continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) for at least 72 hours. The provider reviews the data collected from monitoring, analyzes it, interprets it, and creates a written report. Reports may include information such as assessment of current treatment and necessary treatment adjustments. CGM systems monitor and record blood glucose levels by measuring glucose levels in interstitial fluid. The monitor either provides the data in real–time for patient response or stores it for later download and review by a provider. Typical patients may have trouble regulating blood glucose because of type 1, type 2, or gestational diabetes. Terminology Interstitial fluid: Fluid between the cells of the body. Tips You may report this code a maximum of one time per month. Code 95251 represents the professional component of the service only, so you should not append modifier 26 or TC. For the technical component, the rendering provider should report 95250. Technical services include hooking–up the device, recording, disconnecting the device, and downloading and printing data. lay_term: A patient undergoes a sleep study with no provider physically present. Parameters recorded include heart rate, blood oxygen concentration, respiratory analysis, and the amount of time sleeping. Explanation The provider uses a diagnostic service called a sleep test to assess a patient for various sleep disorders. The test described by this code is unattended, meaning no provider such as a technologist is present with the patient at the time of recording. This test records the patient’s heart rate and oxygen saturation, meaning oxygen’s concentration in the blood. The test also involves respiratory analysis using a method such as airflow, which is air movement while the patient breathes, or peripheral arterial tone, which uses plethysmography to measure blood volume changes in a digit, an indirect method of measurement used for respiratory analysis. The test also records sleep time, which may involve identifying the patient’s sleep levels using methods such as electroencephalography or EEG, electromyography or EMG, and electrooculography or EOG. Actigraphy, which records movement, also can determine sleep time. Tips Code 95800 requires at least six hours of recording. You may report the code for less than six hours, but you must append reduced services modifier 52. If documentation does not include sleep time, see 95801. If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Polysomnography; younger than 6 years, sleep staging with 4 or more additional parameters of sleep, attended by a technologist
lay_term: A patient under the age of 6 undergoes an attended sleep study with identification of sleep levels and at least four additional sleep parameters. Explanation The provider uses a diagnostic sleep test service called polysomnography to assess a patient under age 6 for various sleep disorders. The test described by this code is attended, meaning a provider such as a technologist is present with the patient at the time of recording. This test requires sleep staging, which identifies the patient’s sleep levels using 3–lead electroencephalography or EEG, electromyography or EMG, and electrooculography or EOG. The test additionally requires a minimum of four additional parameters. One typical parameter is electrocardiogram, or ECG, which records the heart’s electrical activity. Another possibility is airflow from the nose and/or mouth as the patient breathes. A third option is respiratory effort measured by transducers or EMG. The provider may request monitoring of oxyhemoglobin saturation, which is the amount of oxygen combined with hemoglobin in the blood, or capnography, which measures carbon dioxide levels. You may also see bilateral anterior tibialis EMG, which records the electrical activity of the anterior tibialis muscles in both legs to identify leg movement during sleep. Tips Code 95782 requires at least seven hours of recording. You may report the code for less than six hours, but you must append reduced services modifier 52. If a provider also initiates continuous positive airway pressure therapy or bi–level ventilation, see 95783. If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components. Read Less

short_description: Electrocorticogram from an implanted brain neurostimulator pulse generator/transmitter, including recording, with interpretation and written report, up to 30 days Notes: (Report 95836 only once per 30 days) (Do not report 95836 in conjunction with 95957) (For programming a brain neurostimulator pulse generator/transmitter when performed in conjunction with ECoG [95836], see 95983, 95984)
lay_term: The provider analyzes an electrocorticogram (ECoG) recording from a previously placed brain neurostimulator pulse generator or transmitter system. He interprets the results and prepares a written report. Explanation The provider analyzes an ECoG (a recording of the brain’s electrical activity) to assess functioning of a brain neurostimulator pulse generator/transmitter system. He analyzes cortical potentials and compares them to previous recordings from before and after implantation of the neurostimulator system. He also interprets post–stimulation recordings. He assesses brain activity such as flat, burst suppression, burst suppression/delta, delta, delta/theta, theta/alpha waveforms, which are classified according to their frequency, amplitude, shape, and sometimes location and similar to those that might be seen on an electroencephalogram (EEG). He examines the relationship between recorded data and clinical events or electrical stimulation from the neurostimulator pulse generator. He prepares a report. This code can be reported only once during a 30–day period. short_description: Range of motion measurements and report (separate procedure); each extremity (excluding hand) or each trunk section (spine)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider measures the range of motion of a single section of spine or a single extremity, excluding the hand. Passive range of motion is when an external force or provider moves the joint through the range of movement without any effort by the patient. In this procedure, the provider measures the range of motion of a spine section or an extremity, not including hands. He then prepares a formal report. short_description: Cholinesterase inhibitor challenge test for myasthenia gravis
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider injects the drug Tensilon, generic name edrophonium, or another cholinesterase inhibitor into the vein of the patient suspected of having myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular disease characterized by muscle weakness and fatigue. Explanation Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular disease characterized by varying degrees of muscle weakness and fatigue. The cause of muscle weakness is circulating antibodies that block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This block inhibits the muscle stimulation function of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. The goal of this test is to administer an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor drug, such as edrophonium, that blocks the enzymatic effect of the acetylcholinesterase enzyme, thereby prolonging the presence of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Thus, acetylcholine is able to stimulate the muscle contraction for a longer time, reducing the muscle fatigue or weakness. Providers use this test to diagnose myasthenia gravis and to differentiate it from other diseases. This test is also known as a Tensilon test. Terminology Acetylcholinesterase: An enzyme that breaks up acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter. Neuromuscular junction: A junction between a nerve and a muscle. The provider can also hear the electrical activity in the form of popping sounds with the help of the loudspeaker connected to the computer. short_description: Needle electromyography using single fiber electrode, with quantitative measurement of jitter, blocking and/or fiber density, any/all sites of each muscle studied
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider does the recording and study of electrical activity of a muscle using a single fiber electrode, a special needle electrode that has a very small recording surface. The goal is to identify electrical activity from an individual muscle fiber. He measures the parameters like jitter, blocking, and fiber density from any/all sites of each muscle tested. Explanation Single fiber needle electromyography is a selective EMG recording technique that allows the identification of electrical activity from an individual muscle fiber. In this procedure, the provider uses a special electrode that has a small recording surface that allows measuring electrical activity from the selected muscle fiber. The provider uses this test most commonly for diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. He measures the parameters like jitter and blocking with or without fiber density at one or more sites of the muscle studied. Jitter is an indicator of irregularity of neuromuscular transmission. Blocking is an indicator of failure of transmission. Fiber density is the density of muscle fibers within a motor unit. Terminology Motor unit: Made up of a single motor neuron along with all the muscle fibers it supplies. Myasthenia gravis: A neuromuscular disease characterized by varying degrees of muscle weakness and fatigue. Tips If the provider studies action potentials from individual muscle fibers, you should select 95872. Report 95872 for tests such as a neuromuscular transmission test. You should report one unit of 95872 for each muscle the provider tests, according to coding guidelines.
